News.title: Acrobat who suffered devastating injuries including broken bones after horror 15ft plunge is now SUING circus for £12m
News.content:
AN ACROBAT is suing Cirque du Soleil for a whopping £12million after plunging 15 feet during a performance without a safety net underneath.

Russian Mariia Konfektova, who holds the Guinness World Record for most seated aerial hoop rotations in 30 seconds, sustained multiple injuries in the “life-changing” fall during the Kooza show in Portland, Oregon.



Footage shows her suspended in the air, spinning on a ring, when she lost her grip and plummeted face-first on the hard stage floor.

A personal injury lawsuit has finally detailed the full extent of her injuries – 11 broken bones, fractures to her lower back, wrist, skull and at least seven bones in her face, as well as a concussion and double vision.



Konfektova had to undergo multiple surgeries, The Oregonian reported.

She said she has been left with permanent injuries, according to the lawsuit.

As a result, the artist is seeking the whopping sum from the largest contemporary circus producer in the world.

According to the lawsuit, Cirque du Soleil did not provide adequate safety equipment, including mats, nets or other equipment to mitigate harm from a fall.

It also alleged that Cirque du Soleil ignored concerns the performer raised about the rigging for the hoop she fell from, and that the circus fired her when she returned to work and continued raising safety concerns after the accident.

A GoFundMe set up by the artist detailed how she continues to live with “persistent double vision and other long-term complications”.



“Although I survived and worked hard to recover, I continue to live with persistent double vision and other long-term complications,” Konfektova said.

“Recent medical evaluations confirmed ongoing problems affecting my vision, jaw, facial symmetry, breathing, and daily life…”

She added: “Unfortunately, ongoing medical, insurance, legal, and immigration complications have made my situation increasingly difficult.



“My access to treatment remains uncertain, and I cannot fully return to my profession while my future surgeries are still ahead of me.”

Konfektova is among 16 performers who have suffered notable injuries during their career with Cirque du Soleil over the past 20 years.

The Oregonian reported that three were so catastrophic that the victims died – in Montreal in 2009, Las Vegas in 2013 and Tampa in 2018.

Almost all of the accidents involved falls ranging from 10 feet to 94 feet.

Shortly after the frightening fall, Cirque du Soleil said Konfektova was “recovering and being cared for by our medical and coaching team”.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

A statement explained she had fallen on her head and was hospitalised, but left the full extent of her injuries unclear.

The Sun has reached out to Cirque du Soleil for a comment.

News.title: Five arrested as cops shut down illegal rave in quaint rural village
News.content:
RAVING MAD Five arrested as cops shut down illegal rave in quaint rural village

FIVE people have been arrested after police shut down an illegal rave in a sleepy rural village.

The quiet town was plunged into chaos in the early hours of Sunday as furious locals were kept awake due to the raucous unlicensed event.



Local police received reports of a disturbance shortly after 1am on Sunday near Thursford Road in Little Snoring.

But nearby residents were doing anything but snoring as the noisy rave went on – with many complaining of the loud music on social media.



Cops rushed to the scene near Fakenham, seizing sound equipment, vehicles and generators.

Officers also closed the entrance to the venue in order to prevent further people from attending.

The event was monitored closely by authorities all throughout the night and into the early hours of Sunday morning.

Ravers were then ordered to leave and disperse.

By late morning, many had begun to leave the site.

The five suspects were cuffed in connection with the event on suspicion of offences including drug driving, drink driving, possession of a class A with intent to supply and carrying on a licensable activity without a licence.



An investigation has been launched to identify who organised the event.

Superintendent Craig Miller said: “We are committed to doing everything we can to prevent, disrupt and stop these events from taking place, while reducing their impact on local communities.

“I would like to thank the landowner and members of the local community for their patience and understanding while we worked to shut down the event as quickly and safely as possible.

“Unauthorised music events such as this can cause significant disruption and often result in damage to the natural environment. As they are not required to meet recognised safety standards, they can also place attendees at risk.

“Our work does not end with the closure of the event, and investigations into those responsible and the circumstances surrounding it will continue.”



Patrick Galbraith, a Great Snoring local, told Eastern Daily Press he went to the site of the rave on Sunday morning.

He said an officer told him they needed riot shields to break up the event.

The resident said: “The people at the rave were very friendly.

“A young raver apologised for snorting a white substance off his phone in front of me.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He added: “I later bumped into the police who said they could not ‘go down there’ without riot shields.



“This surprised me as there were not that many ravers.”

News.title: ‘We’ll stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes,’ Burnham will vow today as he visits Kyiv on first foreign trip as PM
News.content:
ANDY Burnham will today vow Britain will stand with Ukraine “for as long as it takes” as he visits Kyiv on his first foreign trip as PM.

He will mark Ukraine’s Independence Day alongside President Zelensky.



Mr Burnham will also chair his first meeting of the UK and France-led Coalition of the Willing.

The PM said: “The friendship between our two countries will long outlast Russia’s illegal war.



“In both the fight and in the rebuilding to come, we will stand with Ukraine.

“And deliver opportunities for people across both our countries.



“Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve.

“We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace.”

It comes after Moscow warned Britain would face “consequences” over the reported use of UK-made drones in Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia.

He will also accept an award recognising the UK’s support.



Britain has authorised defence giant MBDA to release info on missile components, so they can be assembled in Ukraine.

News.title: Man, 52, dies after horror double stabbing at seaside town – as cops arrest suspect, 21, and launch murder probe
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

KNIFE HORROR Man, 52, dies after horror double stabbing at seaside town – as cops arrest suspect, 21, and launch murder probe

COPS have launched a murder probe after a man died in a horror seafront stabbing.

The brutal attack is said to have happened in the early hours – at around 4.45am – in the harbour area of Ramsgate, Kent.



Police were called after reports of a man carrying a knife.

Officers and paramedics rushed to the scene and found two men suffering injuries consistent with being stabbed.



A 52-year-old man was found injured in Harbour Street, while a 48-year-old was discovered in nearby Harbour Parade.

Both were rushed to a local hospital with serious injuries.



But the 52-year-old was later pronounced dead.

His next of kin have been informed.

The second victim has since been discharged from hospital.

A 21-year-old British man was arrested shortly afterwards and remains in custody as detectives probe the horror.



Cops are not looking for anyone else in connection with the attack.

Large parts of the harbour remain cordoned off, including Harbour Street and sections of the seafront near the Royal Victoria Pavilion Wetherspoon pub.

Forensics officers have been scouring the scene, with investigators seen working inside the cordon on Harbour Street.

A taxi believed to be linked to the incident is also being examined after it crashed onto concrete bollards on the pavement near the seafront, Kent Online reports.

A forensic officer was seen photographing the cab as the investigation continued this morning.



Pictures from the scene show the taxi partially mounted on the bollards, with police tape surrounding the area.

Several businesses in Harbour Street, including the Silver Compass Sports Bar, have been unable to open.

Kent Police said inquiries into the circumstances of the stabbing are continuing.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Extra patrols will also be carried out across Ramsgate today.

Anybody with information is asked to contact Kent Police, quoting reference 46/139262/26.

News.title: Two women, 19 and 20, arrested after boy, three, is left fighting for his life following plunge from first-floor window
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

HORROR FALL Two women, 19 and 20, arrested after boy, three, is left fighting for his life following plunge from first-floor window

COPS have arrested two women as a three-year-old boy fights for his life in hospital after plunging from a window.

Emergency services raced to the scene after the youngster fell from a property in Rochdale on Saturday afternoon.

An air ambulance was also scrambled and landed close to the area shortly after 4.15pm.

The toddler was rushed to hospital and remains in a critical condition.





Two women, aged 19 and 20, were arrested at a property in Blackburn earlier today.

They were held on suspicion of causing serious injury to a child.

Greater Manchester Police said officers responded to a concern for the welfare of a child at around 4.16pm yesterday.

A force spokesperson said: “Two women have been arrested in relation to an incident in Rochdale yesterday.



“The two women, aged 19 and 20, were arrested at a property in Blackburn earlier today (Sunday 23 August 2026) on suspicion of causing a serious injury to a child.

“Officers had responded to a concern for welfare of a child report yesterday (Saturday 22 August 2026) at around 4.16pm at Spotland Tops, Rochdale.

“Emergency services attended and the child was taken to hospital for treatment, where he remains in a critical condition.

“Enquiries into the full circumstances around this incident are ongoing.”

News.title: Bus strikes announced in row over extreme heat with commuters facing 4 days of chaos THIS WEEK – as more dates to follow
News.content:
TRAVEL CHAOS Bus strikes announced in row over extreme heat with commuters facing 4 days of chaos THIS WEEK – as more dates to follow

BUS strikes are set to hit London for four days this week as some 1,500 drivers walk out over extreme heat disputes.

Travel chaos is expected to break out after drivers rejected attempts to resolve a disagreement over working in hot weather.



The drivers are demanding more air-con in buses.

The strikes will affect 42 routes in the capital as 1,500 members of Unite in North London and Essex walk out.



Arriva North, their employer, had their latest offer to put an end to the strikes rejected.

The Unite members initially paused strikes which were meant to happen between August 19 to 21 after negotiations.



Workers voted on a new offer but said it didn’t go far enough to resolve the hot weather issues.

The union said its members balloted against an offer to resolve the row.

Strikes will restart on Tuesday for four days until Friday this week.

This action will then be followed by multiple dates in September and October.



All strike dates August – Tuesday 25 to Friday 28 September – Friday 4 to Saturday 5

– Monday 7 to Tuesday 8

– Friday 18 to Saturday 19

– Monday 21 to Tuesday 22 October – Friday 2 to Saturday 3

– Monday 5 to Tuesday 6

– Friday 16 to Saturday 17

– Monday 19 to Tuesday 20

A Unite spokesperson claimed most Arriva North London buses do not have air conditioning – but instead less effective air cooling systems.

The cooling systems only reduce temperatures by around two or three during heatwaves, unions say.

Buses can therefore reach around 40C on the worst days.

Unite says this extreme heat can put drivers at increased danger of fatigue.

It has also caused some drivers to suffer health problems including heat exhaustion, heat stroke and dehydration, the union says.



Drivers will walkout from Barking, Edmonton, Enfield, Grays, Palmers Green, Stamford Hill, Tottenham, and Wood Green garages.

Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said: “London bus drivers do a vital job, but are putting themselves at risk due to these appalling conditions. Arriva can fully afford to make meaningful changes our members can accept.

“Until that happens, strike action will continue and our members at Arriva North London will continue to have the full backing of Unite.”

Unite regional officer Steven Stockwell said: “There is still time for Arriva to stop this disruptive action, but it relies on it coming back to the table with a deal our members believe will solve the serious problems with conditions once and for all.”

All strikes will begin at 4am and finish at 4.30am on the final day of the action.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Many of the dates in August and September are set to coincide with closures of the Piccadilly line as new trains are tested.

This will further increase disruption across North London.

News.title: 6ft 5in lad, 12, becomes Britain’s tallest pre-teen – and has chance of claiming the world record
News.content:
A LAD of 12 has raised the bar by becoming Britain’s tallest pre-teen — at 6ft 5in.

Samuel Webb has a big chance of being the current world record holder and is already loftier than 99.9 per cent of adults.



On the downside, referees don’t believe he is 12 when he plays football with other children his age.

He often jokes his 6ft 2in dad James is short.



James told The Sun: “Samuel enjoys being tall. He plays tennis and football.

“He plays goalkeeper for his local club but sometimes the ref goes, ‘no chance you’re 12’, and he’s had to prove his age.



“Tennis is his main sport.

“It’s definitely an advantage ­having long arms.

“He wasn’t that big when he was born.

“He was long and thin but not huge.”



Samuel, whose mum is 5ft 11in, may start testosterone therapy to put a limit on what height he will reach.

His dad said: “Being tall is good, but being too tall isn’t great when you can’t fit in a plane seat.

“Samuel has grown five inches in a year — we don’t want him to be 7ft 5in.



“If he’s predicted to grow too much, he’ll get testosterone and his growth plates will fuse so he stops growing.”

Samuel, of Skelmanthorpe, West Yorks, is due to see a specialist who will X-ray the lad’s hands to predict when he will cease growing.

The family say his sister Freya, eight, and brother Joseph, 11, are tall — but nowhere near what Samuel is.

A typical 12-year-old in the UK is roughly 4ft 11in.

The previous record for ­Britain’s tallest pre-teen was held by Sophie Hollins, from Southampton, who measured 6ft 2in aged 12 in 2018.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

At the time, bosses at ­Guinness World Records believed she was the tallest ­pre-teen on the planet.

After being contacted by The Sun, Guinness said it will look into whether Samuel is the globe’s loftiest 12-year-old.

News.title: Burnham considering spending billions to store foreign natural gas to help protect Britain’s energy security
News.content:
PM ANDY Burnham is considering spending billions to store foreign natural gas to help protect Britain’s energy security.

Ministers are said to be looking at buying a huge ship to house liquefied gas or creating a Government stockpile for emergencies.



But critics argue the PM should prioritise drilling in the North Sea rather than relying on fuel from overseas.

The plans — published by the Net Zero department — are designed to protect against turmoil in global supply chains.



But the Government admitted they would require an unprecedented investment in the gas market and added no decision had been made.

David Whitehouse of OEUK — representing the North Sea sector — said: “It makes no sense to increase Britain’s dependence on imported gas.



“With pragmatic Government action the North Sea can continue to play a significant role in meeting Britain’s gas needs.”

We revealed earlier this month how the PM told US President Donald Trump that he will take a “pragmatic” approach to oil and gas exploration.

Jackdaw — a major gas project operated by Shell — is expected to be given the green light towards the end of summer.

But Labour MP Clive Lewis said there was “no legitimate reason” to push ahead with the drilling.



Another, Rachael Maskell, also hit out at the proposals.

But Scottish Labour MPs have been privately urging Mr ­Burnham to allow new drilling in the North Sea, to create jobs and revenue for the area.

News.title: Families of two police officers killed in crash say they were heroes
News.content:
Two police officers who died when a car travelling the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into their vehicle have been hailed as heroes by their families.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died when a Volkswagen Passat, which officers had been pursuing until seconds before, collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 near Middlesbrough on Saturday.

The Passat's occupants - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17 - also died.

In tributes released by Cleveland Police, PC Clough's family said he had been "willing to help anyone", while PC Blades' wife described him as "loved beyond words".

"No words will ever feel like the right words to honour our Matt," she said, adding that he had been a "beloved husband" and the "most devoted father" to their two young sons who would grow up knowing what an "incredible" dad he had been.

"He gave his life in the line of duty, protecting and serving others with courage, dedication and selflessness," she said.

"The pain of losing him is beyond words, and our lives will never be the same.

"Neither will the love he gave us ever fade.

"He may have left this world committed to the duty he believed in, but his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave to his family."

She ended the tribute to her husband: "Forever loved. Forever missed. Forever our superhero. Our Matt and Dad."

News.title: How easy is it to find an NHS dentist? It depends where you live
News.content:
Sykes says that none of his friends in his graduating class in dentistry still works in the NHS. "My friends have gone private, retired or teach - any pathway to avoid NHS dentistry."

Shiv Pabary, chair of the British Dental Association's General Dental Practice Committee, says the situation is "the direct result of choices made by successive governments". He warns that unless ministers "fix and fund NHS dentistry", more dentists could choose to reduce their NHS work or leave the service altogether.

Overall dentist practice numbers have risen in England over the last decade.

"This is not a shortage of dentistry but a shortage of NHS dentistry," says Dayan. "Practices will need to be incentivised back into NHS work in the places where the NHS footprint has thinned most."

While most parts of England recorded declines in practices offering NHS dental care, the reductions were smallest in North West London, the Black Country and North East London.

North East London was the only area to see any increase during the period, recording one additional practice offering NHS treatment compared with a decade ago.

Every other region of England saw the number of NHS dental practices fall.

Looking at the number of practices doing NHS work is not the same as looking at exactly how much health service capacity there is - practices can vary in size. But if you look at other measures such as the amount of treatment being done, the numbers are still down, although not as steep as the fall in practice numbers.

The government says that it is changing the dental contract and training more dentists in the areas most in need. The government says it will also make it a requirement for newly qualified dentists to practice in the NHS for a minimum period of at least three years.

Campaign group 38 degrees calls the current dental crisis "shameful", with people being "forced to pay money they can't afford or suffer with the pain, shame, and further complications that come from being denied vital NHS healthcare".

News.title: Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan
News.content:
Governor Abdullah Sarhadi gives money to treat a boy's broken arm and hands out funds for a local mosque - then, in his office in northern Afghanistan, an astonishing exchange unfolds.

A young woman tells the grey-bearded former Taliban commander that she wants to divorce her husband, who she accuses of months of abuse and beatings.

She will not take no for an answer.

In a country where girls are banned from secondary education, the 18-year-old argues her case calmly and confidently, her face completely hidden behind a full-face veil and sunglasses.

"If there was any chance to live together, I wouldn't be hereâ¦ I have taken my decision," she says.

After trying to persuade her to avoid divorce, the governor later comments that women are "mindless" and "deficient in intellect", to laughter from the male officials, bodyguards and elders around him.

The moment gives a rare glimpse into the day-to-day realities of the Taliban's rule, five years after they swept aside the US-backed government in 2021.

News.title: Reform says it will prioritise British-born young workers for social housing
News.content:
Reform previously announced it would evict foreign nationals from social housing - a plan criticised by housing charity Shelter which said building more homes is the solution, rather than "changing the order of the queue" and "stoking division".

Tice will set out how the Reform intends to pay for the 50,000 affordable homes during Monday's news conference, the party added.

"It is time for us to prioritise young British workers, and that is what our policy is about," Tice said on Sunday.

"I have spent my entire career in property development, as a private citizen I have led companies which delivered thousands of new homes. In government I will break down the barriers to getting generation rent onto the housing ladder."

He added it is "time to get Britain building" and give "our young people the homes they deserve".

UK or Irish nationals made up 88.5% of main social home householders in 2024/25, according to the English Housing Survey.

That means around 11.5% of main householders, the perÂ­son in whose name the social home is renÂ­ted, were non-UK or Irish nationÂ­als.

For its part, Reform estimates 540,000 social homes are currently occupied by foreign nationals.

Labour rubbished Reform's plans and insisted social housing is already "tightly controlled".

"Illegal migrants, asylum seekers and migrants on student or work visas are not eligible for social housing," the Labour spokesperson said.

Labour said the Reform plan would target long-term UK residents that have contributed to our country but are not British citizens, including NHS staff.

"It would leave more families at risk of homelessness and drive up use of temporary accommodation at the taxpayers' expense. It would also mean renegotiations with the EU, resulting in years of wrangling."

The Conservative Party, which also said it would revoke the right of foreign nationals to social housing, accused Reform of "trying to catch up" with its policies.

The Tories have said their plan, which would allow Irish citizens and some EU nationals to remain in social housing, would free up around 230,000 homes.

Sir James Cleverly, shadow housing secretary, added: "The Conservatives have already set out comprehensive plans to ensure British nationals are at the front of the queue for social housing. Now Reform are trying to catch up.

"We also believe in a home owning society and that those who work hard should be able to buy their own home, without unnecessary barriers standing in their way."

Liberal Democrat spokesperson Gideon Amos said that Reform's plan was a "cruel gimmick".

News.title: Review launched into how pub and hotel business rates calculated
News.content:
A review is being launched into the way business rates are calculated for pubs and hotels in England and Wales, and could lead to a reform of the system.

The Treasury says business rates expert Jerry Schurder will lead the review into rate valuations and report back in March 2027, with the government calling for the views of landlords, hoteliers and business owners to feed in to the process.

Last month, Andy Burnham announced a 20% cut in business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England, to come into effect in April.

Pub groups have argued they face disproportionately higher rates bills, but other businesses have called for a wider reform of the rates system.

According to the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA), 161 pubs closed in the first three months of this year across England, Scotland and Wales, equating to the loss of around 2,400 jobs.

Rising business rates are cited as one issue facing the sector, although there have also been complaints that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made staff costs more expensive.

James Murray, financial secretary to the Treasury, said the new review would look at "a rethink of valuations - so that we can build a fairer system for the future".

Emma McClarkin, chief executive of the BBPA, said: "For years pubs have paid a disproportionately higher business rates bill which has ground down their ability to keep the doors open, so this review is sorely needed and hugely welcome."

The BBPA says pubs are valued differently for rates than retail venues. Instead of being based just on floor area, they are judged by a measure called Fair Maintainable Trade - which means when a pub's turnover increases, so does its rates bill.

Schurder is a former business rates policy lead at advisory firm Newmark UK, and his review will feed into the next rates revaluation in 2029.

His appointment was welcomed by Craig Beaumont of the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) who said he would bring "crucial heavyweight business rates expertise into the Treasury".

However, Beaumont said the government needed to address the wider business rates system and exempt more smaller firms by increasing the rates relief threshold for small businesses.

Tom Ironside from the British Retail Consortium also welcomed the review but said it was "vitally important that the needs of retailers are not overlooked".

Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said the review was "far too late for a sector this Labour government has already done its best to kill off".

"Tax hikes on business premises and jobs, alongside job-destroying regulation in the Employment Rights Act, have left many hospitality businesses on the brink," he said.

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said reform of business rates was "long overdue", but also called for an emergency VAT cut and a reverse to jobs tax changes "which have hammered hospitality in particular".

News.title: Ex-cricket captains urge 'proper medical care' for Imran Khan
News.content:
A group of former cricket captains, including Indian batting legend Sunil Gavaskar and one of England's longest-serving skippers Sir Alastair Cook, have called on Pakistan to ensure its ex-PM Imran Khan be given proper care while in custody.

The cricketer-turned-politician has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges which he denies.

In a letter to Pakistan's current leader Shehbaz Sharif, the 21 former skippers aired concern that Khan, 73, was allowed "only a few hours" at a hospital last week where he was examined by a state-appointed team.

Khan's party has also filed a contempt petition against the government for not giving him access to his own doctors, as ordered by the top court.

The former cricket captains laid out three demands in their letter, the first of which is that Khan be assessed by a medical board directed by Pakistan's Supreme Court â which would include his personal physicians â particularly on the reported loss of vision in his right eye.

They also urged authorities to allow weekly visits by Khan's family, as ordered by the court, "without interruptions or administrative delays".

Finally, they asked that any treatment recommended by the medical board be "provided without delay".

"Imran Khan is 73 years old and has now spent more than three years in custody," read the letter initiated by former Australian captain Greg Chappell.

"Whatever the legal and political arguments surrounding his case, the basic decency of ensuring a court-ordered medical process is actually completed is not, in our view, a controversial request."

Among the other signatories were England's Michael Atherton, Michael Brearley, Nasser Hussain, Andrew Strauss and David Gower, India's Kapil Dev and Dilip Vengsarkar, and Australia's Belinda Clark, Adam Gilchrist, Steve Waugh and Kim Hughes.

Fourteen of the former skippers had also supported an earlier appeal for "humane treatment and proper medical care" for Khan which was submitted in February.

Khan's lawyer claimed at the time that his client had 15% vision left in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.

The signatories of both letters had described themselves as "former colleagues and rivals who share a bond forged on the cricket field", adding that the bond "transcends the borders and disputes that too often divide countries".

Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.

He was imprisoned in August 2023 and has faced charges in more than 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts, all of which he and his party Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf say are politically motivated.

His jailing sparked large-scale protests by supporters, which were met with a crackdown by authorities.

Pakistan's Supreme Court had on Tuesday directed the government to transfer Khan to a private hospital to be examined by physicians.

He was instead seen by doctors at a government-run hospital in Islamabad, who deemed him "medically fit", before he was moved back to prison.

News.title: CrossCountry to provide full service on Monday after major disruption
News.content:
Train operator CrossCountry will run a full train service on Monday following major disruption to services across the country.

The operator said it plans to run a "very limited number of trains" from around 18:00 BST on Sunday evening, and a full service on Monday.

It comes after a power outage affected its control centre in Birmingham, resulting in mass cancellations across the network on Sunday.

A CrossCountry spokesperson said: "Our key priority is now to restore as close to a normal service as possible for our customers tomorrow."

They added: "With most facilities now reinstated, we are planning to operate a very limited number of services from around 18:00 this evening, primarily on routes towards Leicester and Derby.

"Planning is underway to support a full train service on Monday and we are working closely with National Grid and industry partners as recovery efforts continue.

"We would like to thank our customers for their patience and understanding during today's disruption."

Customers have been strongly advised by the operator to check their journey before travelling.

Customers delayed by 30 minutes or more may be entitled to compensation, the operator said, adding: "While those who choose not to travel can claim a refund from their original point of purchase."

News.title: Trump waves green flag to start IndyCar race through Washington streets
News.content:
US President Donald Trump was among hundreds of people who gathered to see the IndyCar race through the streets of Washington DC on Sunday, marking the culmination of a series of summer events to celebrate the country's 250th birthday.

Driver Kyle Kirkwood won the race, earning his seventh career Indycar win.

Ahead of the race, the president and First Lady Melania Trump took a ceremonial lap of the 1.7-mile track in his presidential limousine, The Beast.

As they reached the finish line, Trump's new Air Force One completed a flyover above the capital.

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix is the first time professional road racing has been hosted in the capital.

News.title: Rain to return this week with chance of thunderstorms and flooding
News.content:
The weather is set to turn more unsettled this week as rain returns with a chance of thunderstorms and localised flooding.

Some places could see a return to showery conditions by Tuesday, but it is from Wednesday onwards that more widespread and persistent rain will arrive from the south.

The wet weather will be welcome for parched regions of the UK, but a lot more will be needed before drought conditions start to ease.

Temperatures will also be on the rise once more, as warmer air moving in could push midweek highs close to 30C (86F) in places.

News.title: CrossCountry cancels 'almost all' UK services after power cut
News.content:
Trains across the UK have been cancelled by rail operator CrossCountry after a power cut at its control centre.

The power outage started in Birmingham on Saturday and as a result, many of the systems used to manage the railway are unavailable, the operator said.

Cancellations are affecting most routes, from Glasgow to Penzance and Leeds to Manchester, until further notice because of "significant and unforeseen disruption", said CrossCountry, ranked Britain's worst rail operator, in June.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said she was "concerned to hear about a power outage" and had asked publicly owned operators to provide "extra services where possible".

"We've also sent Network Rail power teams who are onsite and working to restore power and systems as soon as possible," she added.

Passengers are venting their anger on social media, saying the situation is the "worst case scenario" at the weekend, with some taking coaches before continuing their train journey with another operator.

Major routes between Manchester and Birmingham, which passes through Stoke-on-Trent, Coventry and Wolverhampton, along with routes from Leeds to York, Cheltenham to Cardiff and Glasgow to Edinburgh, are all affected.

CrossCountry confirmed tickets for Sunday would remain valid until Wednesday.

One user on X asked the operator if the situation would be resolved on Monday.

It responded: "We would hope so, but at the moment we have no further updates."

News.title: Newcastle and Liverpool united in tribute to legend Keegan
News.content:
Kevin Keegan's family were in attendance as Newcastle United and Liverpool supporters came together to pay tribute to the former England captain.

Keegan, who played for both clubs, before going on to manage Newcastle, died at the age of 75 last month following a battle with cancer.

As the teams met for the first time since his death, in their Premier League season opener at St James' Park on Sunday, members of Keegan's family were present in the directors' box.

A number of Keegan's former players from this memorable first spell in charge of Newcastle, between 1992 and 1997, were also at the game.

News.title: Wicker Man director's sons complete their late father's film trilogy
News.content:
Robin Hardy always envisaged his iconic 1973 folk horror film The Wicker Man as the first part of a trilogy.

The Wicker Tree, released in 2011, brought him closer to that ambition, but his death in 2016 at the age of 86 left the project incomplete.

Now his sons, Justin and Dominic, have been able to complete their father's trilogy, after finding a script for the final film.

Wrath of the Gods has its premiere at the FrightFest horror festival in London, external on Friday, a family dream made possible thanks to the surprise discovery of some long-lost family archive.

"The person who bought Justin's old family home said they'd discovered six sacks of letters, scripts and other material pertaining to Robin Hardy and The Wicker Man in the attic," says Dominic, an art historian at the University of Quebec in Montreal.

"Justin's first instinct was to burn them, but we couldn't ignore this original source material. Although we left it unopened for six months or more."

News.title: Scammers increasingly using QR codes to steal money and data
News.content:
When Les Howard could not find change for parking during a trip to the coast, a quick response (QR) code on the meter seemed to be the answer.

But the next day, the 61-year-old realised he had become the victim of an increasingly common scam as criminals started taking money from his bank account in Â£60 chunks.

Reports of QR code-related scams have gone up by 700% in the past four years, figures by Report Fraud have revealed.

Experts say criminals are finding different ways to exploit the codes as they become a common part of everyday life.

This could be disguising suspicious links in emails, gaining access to victims' messaging apps or convincing people who are out and about to download fraudulent apps to steal their money and data.

That is what happened to Howard, from Widnes, who was visiting Caernarfon in North Wales with his wife.

"We went to the car park where we normally go," Howard told the BBC Scam Secrets podcast.

"I normally have change in the car to pay for the parking, but this time I didn't.

"So there was a QR code to download and get an app and pay via an app."

News.title: Mayors to get powers to overrule local councils on planning decisions
News.content:
Mayors across England will be given new powers to overrule local councils on some planning decisions.

The change would apply to proposals with more than 150 homes, more than 15,000 square metres of commercial space or buildings over 30 metres.

Mayors in 13 areas including Manchester, Liverpool, the West of England and the West Midlands will gain similar powers to Sir Sadiq Khan in London, who is already able to "call in" planning decisions.

Housing minister Matthew Pennycook said the powers were an "essential part of the toolkit that mayors need to effectively deliver new homes and regeneration".

The Conservatives questioned whether it was right for councils to lose the "ability to make planning decisions in their own communities".

The powers will also be available to mayors in the Combined Authorities in North East England, South Yorkshire, West Yorkshire, York and North Yorkshire, Hull and East Yorkshire, Greater Lincolnshire, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, East Midlands, and Tees Valley.

Paul Bristow, the Conservative mayor of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, told BBC Breakfast that if he had local powers, he would approve "tomorrow" a couple of blocked schemes that he said would "get new homes built that families could move into and charge economic growth".

Bristow said "it's not about overriding what local people want", but about developers and councils finding a compromise on projects instead of just saying no - which he believed the "perceived threat of intervention" would help.

In London, where Khan already has the power to review decisions on certain developments, external, housebuilding has fallen in recent years. But Pennycook insisted the "call in" powers had helped the mayor "unblock strategic growth sites" in the capital.

Bristow said if he had a similar local plan it would be "much more light touch" than London.

In the 2024 general election, the Labour government promised to build 1.5 million homes in England by the end of the decade, but housebuilders have warned the target could be missed.

Pennycook said the government was "absolutely determined to stick with that ambition".

He acknowledged the target was "really stretching" but said nearly 180,000 children were in temporary accommodation and "any smaller target wouldn't be commensurate with the scale of the challenge".

Bristow said the government has "no chance whatsoever" to meet its 1.5 million target.

"We need economic growth in this country, we need to get building and families need places to live, and at the moment, the planning system just isn't working."

In addition to gaining the new "call-in" powers, mayors are set to be able to grant "up-front permission", which the government says will allow building to begin "without a developer having to apply".

A consultation on how the powers will work is due to be published next week.

The government has sought to stress that local councils will continue to decide the majority of applications and that all decisions must still follow planning rules.

It has also said mayors will get a "bigger say" over how housing funding is spent in their area, with the government directing national agency Homes England to focus on local mayors' priorities.

New Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who served as mayor for Greater Manchester for nearly a decade, has repeatedly expressed his desire to transfer more powers to local mayors.

"Challenge does need to be made to local decision-making and actually it cuts both ways," he told the Sunday Times.

"Sometimes it's the other way round. It's the local authority putting forward something that's unacceptable in terms of the impact on the community. It's a two-way street."

Last month, Burnham promised to give all mayors a share of income tax revenue, saying he wanted to "bring power home" to "every postcode".

Earlier this week, he announced a secondment programme to send high-performing civil servants to work in mayoral offices.

The approach has faced criticism from some in his own party and the Liberal Democrats, who fear it could create a "two-tier system" that discriminates against those areas that do not have an elected mayor.

News.title: Restriction zone scheme for offenders to start in October
News.content:
A scheme that could see serious sexual and violent offenders confined to areas just a few miles wide after leaving prison will be launched in October, Justice Secretary Alex Norris has announced.

Government ministers say this is designed to give victims greater freedom and further reduce the possibility of unwanted contact

The intention to introduce "restriction zones" for violent offenders who leave prison and who are on probation was first announced by the government last year.

Probation officers will be able to limit where serious offenders can go for as long as it is deemed necessary. Those who breach their new boundaries could be recalled to prison.

This would go beyond the current practice of imposing "exclusion zones" which ban offenders from specific locations such as a victim's home or place of work.

Norris is expected to come up with proposals to further restrict the early release of some prisoners when Parliament resumes next month.

But the Conservatives say that the best thing Labour could do to protect victims is to bring forward emergency legislation which would stop the early release of thousands of criminals.

There is a risk that serious sexual and violent offenders and victims could encounter one another outside exclusion zones.

The new scheme will specify confined areas for offenders in plans tailored to them and developed in consultation with victims.

Norris said the scheme would use GPS technology monitored by probation officers so that "those who step outside the boundaries can be quickly identified and face being sent back to prison".

"Offenders should carry the consequences of their crimes, not their victims," he added.

Amy Glover, director of domestic abuse services at Advance, a charity supporting women and girls who have experienced domestic abuse, praised the "change in focus".

However, she also called for reform to the criminal justice system saying many survivors of abuse chose "not to pursue a criminal conviction, and for those that do only 5% reach conviction."

A domestic abuse survivor named only as Kristina called the restriction zones a "fantastic concept" but noted that a perpetrator had continuously breached her indefinite restraining order "without consequence".

"The biggest challenge would be to gain victims' confidence in authorities to follow through their promises of protection," she added.

The announcement of the restriction zone scheme's start date comes after a change to the government's early release scheme following a backlash.

Introduced to ease prison overcrowding, on 4 August the policy was updated so people sentenced for rape, serious child sex offences and grooming would not be eligible for early release.

The Prison Governors' association warned this change to plans at a "very late stage" put further pressure on prison staff.

The restriction zone scheme was criticised when it was announced last year for potentially putting pressure on probation staff, something the government says it hopes to alleviate with more staff and a greater use of technology.

If you are suffering from domestic abuse, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line

News.title: 'My skin makes me unique and I'm learning to embrace it'
News.content:
A woman born with a rare genetic skin condition that covers 98% of her body in birthmarks has spoken of how she is learning to embrace her appearance after years of trying to hide it.

Laura Kelly, 28, was born with congenital melanocytic naevus (CMN) and underwent 14 operations as a baby, with doctors fearing she may not live beyond the age of eight.

Laura said CMN made her self conscious about how strangers might react and that, growing up as a teenager, she often wore heavy makeup and planned outfits to cover her skin.

She said embracing how she looks and raising awareness of CMN has given her more confidence and hopes sharing her story will help others with a visible difference.

Andy Burnham has promised Britain is “100 per cent behind” Ukraine as he visits Kyiv on his first foreign trip to mark the country’s independence day.

The prime minister is to chair his first meeting of the coalition of the willing as he arrives in Kyiv on Monday morning to signal Britain’s continued support for Ukraine.

It comes as relations between the Kremlin and Downing Street continue to suffer amid Vladimir Putin’s ongoing war on Ukraine and threats from Moscow.

But Mr Burnham is set to assure Ukrainians of the UK’s backing and reiterate that Russia’s threats only strengthen British resolve.

“On Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes,” he said.

open image in gallery But Mr Burnham is set to assure Ukrainians of the UK’s backing and reiterate that Russia’s threats only strengthen British resolve ( AFP/Getty )

“I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine’s security is our security.”

Mr Burnham added: “The friendship between our two countries will long outlast Russia’s illegal war. In both the fight and in the rebuilding to come, we will stand with Ukraine and deliver opportunities for people across both our countries.

“Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace.”

Earlier this month, Russia’s embassy to the UK said reports that Ukrainian forces had used unmanned aircraft manufactured by two UK companies “confirm that London is deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis”.

It accused Britain of “seeking to contain Russia and inflict maximum damage on it by proxy” and warned that the deeper its involvement becomes, “the higher the price it will pay”.

“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” it said.

As well as chairing a meeting of the coalition of the willing, Mr Burnham will take part in Independence Day events and accept an award on behalf of the British people recognising the UK’s support.

open image in gallery Burnham welcomed President Volodymyr Zelensky to the UK during his first weeks in office. ( AFP/Getty )

The government has agreed to allow defence firm MBDA to release classified information on UK components for the long-range Scalp missile – the French-produced version of the UK’s Storm Shadow.

Both missiles use shared French and British technology, and Ukraine and France are looking to set up local assembly lines for Scalp missiles in Ukraine.

His visit marks his intention to continue Britain’s long-standing support for Ukraine, with every prime minister except Liz Truss having visited the country since the war with Russia broke out.

Sir Keir Starmer, who set up coalition of the willing, visited Ukraine on his final foreign visit as prime minister, where he said the UK’s “cast-iron” support of Ukraine will “always endure”.

Meanwhile, relations between Moscow and Downing Street remain sour, with Mr Burnham having hit back at the Kremlin’s threats.

open image in gallery The government has agreed to allow defence firm MBDA to release classified information on UK components for the long-range Scalp missile – the French-produced version of the UK’s Storm Shadow ( Reuters )

Asked what his message to Putin was after Russia accused the UK of escalating the war, Mr Burnham said: “This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100 per cent against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin.

“We are providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself, and that’s been the British position all the way through this conflict by previous prime ministers.

“It remains the case with me. We are not fair weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine’s hour of need, and that won’t change.”

The Kremlin is also yet to put forward a replacement candidate for its ambassador to the UK after Andrei Kelin left his post in London in recent weeks.

The charge d’affaires has taken the lead, an embassy spokesman told The Times, raising questions about whether Russia is seeking to downgrade its diplomatic relations with the UK.

The internet is obsessed with discussing Gen Z’s behaviour, and rightly so – we’ve become known for phenomena including “hustle culture” and dating “icks”.

When it comes to travel, we’re defining trends via TikTok. One minute we’re giving “quick trips” new meaning with one to two-day international getaways inspired by viral videos, and the next we’re embracing logging off and “touching grass”. It’s then no surprise that when it comes to solo travel, young adults are at the forefront – driving the boom. The latest Hostelworld report on the topic found that over two thirds of the solo travellers it surveyed were under the age of 30.

As a first-born daughter from a Caribbean background, travelling the world solo wasn’t something I thought was an option for me growing up. Raised in the mostly affluent Devon countryside, which has a predominantly white population, the images of solo travel I saw both around me and on social media were of privilege; often wealthy, young, white people who could afford to postpone university or getting a job in favour of extravagant gap years.

open image in gallery Aaliyah in Valencia, one of the 40 cities she has visited solo ( Aaliyah Harris )



I mainly saw men doing it – those who also had an invisible but very real “safety net” protecting them from the dangers many women experience. Dangers that women, like myself, just couldn’t be oblivious to. It seemed scary and depressingly lonely. Why would anyone choose that?

Fast-forward to 2026, and aged 28 – nine countries and 40 cities later, I’ve become addicted to solo travel. Though it wasn’t by choice, initially.

After the pandemic hit and lockdowns caused widespread feelings of loneliness, I signed up to the popular friend-making app Bumble in 2021, with hopes of connecting with like-minded girlfriends who wanted to make up for lost time by exploring new places.

I soon had a calendar filled with plans, from brunches to treetop zip-lining adventures, and after these mate dates – spent discussing whether we were Type A or Type B travellers – new friendships had formed that would grow in the years to come.

I met Shannon, 28, a reality TV expert and TikTok creator, around three years ago, after she packed up her nine to five job and opted for a freelance lifestyle. In 2024, we flew to the Canary Islands – and upon our return she left London permanently to become a nomad.

“Travelling solo is better because you have complete freedom to choose your own agenda and you're not constantly waiting for someone to show up,” Shannon told me.

We bonded through similar experiences shaped by race, as she shared that her Congolese upbringing didn’t encourage solo travelling.

Despite that, she’s been travelling the world full-time, backpacking and staying in all kinds of accommodations from hostels, to pet-sitting stays and with locals in their homes. One particular homestay in South Korea stood out.

open image in gallery Aaliyah and Shannon bonded after meeting on Bumble Friends and took a trip to the Canary Islands ( Aaliyah Harris )



“He was my first male host. He took me out to dinner every day, to a palace outside of Busan, and to a temple, and taught me about spiritual history. All stuff I wouldn't have done myself if I didn't have the knowledge of a local. He was 52, a dad with grown kids living elsewhere and he was lonely. He wanted a language exchange and to see other people's ways of life,” Shannon explained.

As well as my trip to the Canary Islands with Shannon, I’ve been to Spain, Mallorca, Turkey, Cyprus, Tunisia, Albania, Germany, Amsterdam and several UK city breaks with Bumble-made friends.

Not long after a beachside holiday to Antalya, I encountered my first major Bumble buddy hurdle. I was let down by someone who dropped out of a planned holiday last minute – and it felt like a huge knockback.

After several panicked phone calls to close friends and family, I had no luck trying to find someone who might be free for a spontaneous trip. Luckily nothing was paid for yet, but it was August and I couldn’t bear to waste my limited time off from work over summer.

So in under 48 hours, I had taken the plunge and booked my first solo trip. It cost double what I had planned, and I almost threw up from anxiety on the way to London Gatwick airport, but I was fortunate enough to have a dear friend accompany who helped calm me down.

A few hours later I landed in sunny Madrid, a deliberate choice that felt safe and wasn’t too far from home.

In the morning, I woke up to parrots chirping outside my window instead of a “shower rota alarm” (essential for avoiding shared house bathroom clashes). I was at The Social Hub, a modern hotel right in the city centre. Its community-focused layout – with co-working spaces, a bar and communal dining areas – was perfect for mingling with other travellers. Plus, its rooftop pool sat adjacent to the stunning Royal Palace of Madrid.

Here, I realised that being in control of where my feet take me next is an unmatched feeling. It was odd knowing I only had to think of my own wants and needs, but it was empowering. All of a sudden, there was no need to check whether someone else was happy with the planned activities. Instead, I was taking it easy with my time and relying on my own navigation skills at a pace that suited me.

open image in gallery Aaliyah Harris on her first solo trip in Madrid ( Aaliyah Harris )



It wasn’t half as daunting as I’d thought it would be – or embarrassing. I made connections with other travellers in the hotel and while exploring. At one point I got slightly lost and asked a stranger for directions who turned out to be another woman who was solo travelling from a much more impressive distance – she was from Sri Lanka. We got chatting and before I knew it we were swapping stories over an enormous seafood paella.

My confidence grew and I felt a real sense of accomplishment and pride about everything I was able to do independently.

I challenged myself further, train-hopping from Madrid to Barcelona, and spent a sweltering day wandering around historic landmarks like the Sagrada Familia, before cooling off in Barceloneta Beach’s salty sea. It was bliss.

Don’t get me wrong, I still get nervous travelling solo. I’m vigilant and I always check government travel advice on safety for women, as well as information on crime, sexism and racism for where I’m travelling. I’m cautious about who I tell I’m alone, and I often send my whereabouts to trusted friends or family back home. But in a lot of ways, I actually feel so much safer solo. Perhaps because I’m more diligent and aware of my surroundings when knowing that I'm the only person responsible for myself.

I find there’s something about the unknown that’s both nervewracking but equally exhilarating. And an unexpected benefit is that I have learned so much about who I am, from my interests to personal strengths.

Climbing Bali's Mount Batur, 1,717 metres above sea level, taught me just how resilient I can be. Staying with a family in rural Cambodia showed me that true comfort doesn't come from luxury wet rooms, western toilets or appliances, but from sharing experiences, such as cooking meals over an open fire.



Clubbing with locals in Mallorca led to partying alongside an incognito Charli xcx, proving you never know who you'll meet if you put yourself out there.

Then there was the time that even after getting caught in a crazy, snowstorm in Kanazawa, Japan, without a phone, Google Maps or anyone nearby who spoke English, I relied on my instincts to find my way home, reminding myself just how resourceful I can be.

Overcoming these challenges and fully immersing myself in different cultures has made my travel experiences feel unique. I’ve seen places through a totally new lens, and in turn I think I’ve become a better tourist.

Bumble BFF gave me long lasting friendships and memories I’ll never forget, but having my friend drop of out of our trip by chance taught me that I didn’t need other people to explore the world with – I just needed to take a leap of faith.

News.title: The Michael Carrick question sparked by Man United’s dismal Premier League start
News.content:

“They hire me to be kind and calm with the players, and then at the first sign of trouble along the way, that’s the very characteristic they point to as the problem.”

Carlo Ancelotti had only won three Champions Leagues when he argued he could be fired for the same qualities for which he was hired. Ancelotti could afford to be philosophical about it, which underlined his innate calmness, and Real Madrid, having sacked him once, rehired him and he won a further two Champions Leagues, before they sacked him again.

The words came in the Italian’s book ‘Quiet Leadership’. The title could serve as a two-word description of Michael Carrick’s approach.

open image in gallery Carrick doesn’t have the air of a ranter and raver, despite the influence of Sir Alex Ferguson and Jose Mourinho ( Getty )

He was the antidote to the more charismatic leadership of Ruben Amorim. As Manchester United’s season started at Hull on Saturday, one manager was hyperactive on the touchline: City’s Sergej Jakirovic. Carrick was a beard-stroking onlooker or, more often, impassive as his side lost 2-0.

His side felt similarly lifeless, though Carrick demurred. “That doesn't mean you're passive just because you get beat,” he argued.

It was nevertheless hard to shake off the impression that this was a team taking after their manager. United were too slow and sedate, lacking urgency or aggression. They started the season in a slumber, albeit lacking the precision in possession Carrick used to lend from the base of the midfield.

Carrick’s personality made him the right man at the right time last season, an answer to the drama. A question now is if he can be a galvanising force in the long term. A mild-mannered man suggested his public persona conceals what happens inside: both inside him and inside the dressing room. There nevertheless has rarely been the sense that Carrick inherited his former manager Sir Alex Ferguson’s infamous hairdryer. He doesn’t have the air of a ranter and raver.

“There's a difference in calmness, you know?” he said. “I'm talking to you quite calm, but I'm not exactly calm inside and enjoying the day. So there's a big difference. I played here for a long time. You don't get to play here for a long time without just going day by day, the results, the ups and downs, but you just carry on as normal.

“It's 100 per cent not that, and trust me, it's not that. It just doesn't mean that we all have to shout and scream and come out and create some chaos just because of it. Inside we're hurting, the boys know, and we need to get better. But the calmness doesn't mean that there's no emotion in it, for sure.”

open image in gallery Bruno Fernandes questioned why United made the 'same mistakes as we did last season, [in] every away game' ( Getty )

The reference to his playing career felt pertinent. Carrick lasted a dozen years at Old Trafford and played 464 games in part because of an emotional equilibrium which was reflected in a consistent level of performance. Others crashed and burned. Managers more noted for their explosions of temper, whether Ferguson or Jose Mourinho, valued him.

Carrick’s way is to give as little away as possible. The global obsession with United can bring calls for a response. His will not be performative. “There's a lot goes on outside of our football club,” he said. “I understand the responsibility I've got, but it doesn't make me do things differently just because of that.”

It nevertheless raises the issue of what he will do. His expensive new midfield were outmanoeuvred and outfought by a Hull duo who cost about £1m, or about £82m less than Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos. A side without an out-and-out striker did not look like scoring; Carrick can talk about the benefits of having versatile forwards but he had the wrong combination at Hull. United conceded twice from set-pieces and revived the theory they struggle to play against teams with a back five. Carrick offered few clues what he will do.

open image in gallery Carrick and United will face another newly promoted side in Ipswich in their first home game of the new season ( PA Wire )

That does not necessarily mean he will do nothing. One of the most impressive elements of his successful audition for the full-time job came in the way United reacted to setbacks. They only lost twice under Carrick last season. They then delivered two of their best results of the season. After going down 2-1 at Newcastle, they beat the eventual Europa League winners Aston Villa 3-1. After being beaten 2-1 by Leeds, they triumphed over Chelsea at Stamford Bridge.

Yet Hull’s status as relegation favourites, in their first top-flight game for nine years, made this much the worst result of Carrick’s time in charge. It came on a day that can set the tone for the season, when he could first unveil his signings, his vision. United were dismal. The game seemed to pass Carrick by.

But his subtlety was a strength as a player. It needs to be again. Ancelotti was often accused of doing nothing because he was not demonstrative. But he usually knew when to do something, and what. And that may be the test for Carrick. He is averse to overreacting. The key is when to react, and how.

It applies to almost every instance. Got a new job? Crying emoji. Ludicrous date? Crying emoji. Dog fell off the sofa? Crying emoji. That little yellow circle with tears streaming down its face has officially been named the most popular emoji worldwide, according to data from Google shared with The New York Times. Looking through my most frequented Whatsapp chat, in the last 72 hours, I’ve used it 15 times – 😭😭😭.

While the original cry-laughing face and its diagonal sibling have traditionally been used to convey joy digitally, their overuse has essentially rendered them a bit toe-curling. Want to show your age? Send one to anyone below the age of 30 and see them send a (dead from laughing) skull back. Honourable mentions also go to: the two beers emoji, the monkey covering its eyes and the sunglasses smiley. They can all get – unless used with irony – firmly in the digital bin.

Much like with new fashion drops or sought-after artwork, the appeal of an emoji in 2026 stems from its originality. So, it’s no surprise to find that, although young people are conveying the same emotions as everyone else using a smart phone, the images being used to express them have evolved: the wilting rose 🥀 (93rd most used) instead of the broken heart 💔, the praying hands 🙏 instead of thumbs up, And then we come to the Moai statue 🗿, which has become the 33rd most used emoji up from 482nd in 2021. This, The New York Times says, is used now instead of raised eyebrows 🤨 or the routine deadpan smiley 😐.

One of Apple’s newly released favourites among Gen Z includes the Face with Bags Under Eyes 🫩 , which can be used in times of stress or weariness – or joking distress. Eg. “Mum’s making stew again” – immediate Face with Bags Under Eyes. In March 2026, my pride and joy was introduced to the emoji keyboard: Distorted Face 🫪, whose eyes are so far an the periphery of its head, he’s perfect for conveying worry, embarrassment, terror or all-round dismay. Novelty is the thing.

open image in gallery Over it: The cry emoji has overtaken the original cry laughing icon ( Getty/iStock )

During research for this article, my editor told me she uses the maracas emoji 🪇 to convey joy. That is the type of emoji entrepreneurial spirit that’ll get you in with Gen Z – if you’re trying. Lest we forget when the person standing emoji became shorthand for “well, this is awkward”🧍.

While it’s easy to dismiss emoji use as irrelevant or childish, the symbols have become a language in their own right, with more and more people leaning on the icons to convey meaning.

Although emojis play increasingly critical communicative functions, studies have found that frequency of use decreases among older adults, who may struggle to adapt to new forms of non-verbal communication due to lack of confidence.

For the uninitiated, there’s Emojipedia, which offers a glossary of the icons. In 2015, even the Oxford English Dictionary made its word of the year the crying-laughing emoji, noting that it had cause the biggest linguistic shift that year.

In Adolescence, emojis like the red pill were used in incel subcultures, which police struggled to decode without a teen’s help, On the flip side, a recent study by researchers at Bournemouth University found that emojis can trigger similar neural response patterns to those involved in processing real human facial expressions 🙏.

“This suggests that emojis are not simply fun additions to digital communication but may be processed by the brain in ways comparable to genuine facial cues. In this sense, emojis can function as meaningful emotional signals during online interaction,” said the study’s lead, Madeline Molly Ely.

So, whether you’re perceiving this year’s most popular emoji as joy or sorrow, could actually be having an impact on your brain. “‘We use it all the time apart from when we’re actually crying, 😭😭😭” laughed one user on TikTok. Take from that what you will 🥀.

Walmart has announced a major change to the way you pay at stores.

Starting August 24, shoppers at certain Walmart and Sam’s Club stores will be able to buy groceries using tap to pay.

Previously, Walmart and Sam’s Club stores didn’t support tap-to-pay technology. Now, all U.S. stores and clubs will have tap to pay as an option by the end of 2026, with plans to expand to fuel stations by mid-2027, the company announced Friday. It wasn’t immediately made clear which stores will implement the technology first.

Axios reported that both Apple Pay and Google Pay will be supported as tap-to-pay options. Customers will also be able to add eligible Walmart, Sam's Club and OnePay cards to their digital wallets.

In a Friday press release announcing the change, Walmart said, “We want customers and members to have choice in how they pay, so they can check out in the way that works best for them.”

open image in gallery Walmart is changing how shoppers pay ( AFP/Getty )

“It all comes back to giving customers and members more choice and making everyday shopping a little easier — from how they manage their money to how they pay at checkout.”

Walmart is one of the last major retailers to implement tap-to-pay technology, as Axios reported that 85 percent of all retailers support Apple Pay. Previously, shoppers relied on physical cards or Walmart Pay, which required scanning a QR code.

Walmart has implemented several other changes in recent months.

Central Florida residents can now receive retail items in less than 30 minutes through a new drone delivery operation launched by Walmart and Alphabet-owned Wing in the Greater Orlando area.

The service currently operates out of Walmart stores in Apopka and Clermont, reaching more than 50,000 homes, apartments and local businesses.

open image in gallery The company is adding tap to pay as an option at certain stores ( Getty )

“We measure success in minutes saved and life made a little easier in Central Florida,” Heather Rivera, Wing’s chief business officer, said this week in a company news release. “Whether it’s helping a family grab a quick lunch without loading everyone into the car, or delivering sunscreen to a visitor at their vacation rental, we want drone delivery to be a simple, seamless part of daily routines.”

Earlier this year, Walmart shared plans to open around 20 new stores and remodel 650 existing locations from 2026 to 2027. The wide-ranging initiative is meant to “make shopping faster and more convenient for our customers,” the company said in a statement at the time, and grow the brand’s massive 4,611-store footprint in the United States.

Better integration of Walmart’s app into shoppers’ in-store experience is part of the remodeling plans, too, industry news and analysis site Retail Dive reported.

The company did not say where the 20 new stores are located but did note one future superstore location — Celina, Texas. Four super centers have already opened this year in Eastvale, California, and three Florida cities: Apollo Beach, Jacksonville and The Villages.

Moving tributes have been paid to two “hero” police officers who died in a collision near Middlesborough as their families described their “pain beyond words”.

PCs Tom Clough, 38, and Matthew Blades, 37, died after the police vehicle they were driving was struck by a Volkswagen Passat travelling on the wrong side of the A66 in Teesside on Saturday night.

In tributes released by Cleveland Police, the two officers’ families said they had died “in the line of duty” and that their lives will “never be the same”.

“He was our hero with a fantastic sense of humour,” PC Clough’s family said. “Jumped into action whenever needed, and willing to help anyone for any reason. Proudly fought for his country to make the world a better place. Always on public duty throughout his short life.”

In a separate tribute, PC Blades’ wife said he was a “devoted” father and her “best friend”.

open image in gallery PC Tom Clough (left) and PC Matthew Blades ( Cleveland Police )

"He was an adored son and brother, a perfect son-in-law, and the most fun uncle,” she said. “He was loved beyond words by all his family and friends, and his loss has left a space that can never be filled.

"He gave his life in the line of duty, protecting and serving others with courage, dedication and selflessness. The pain of losing him is beyond words, and our lives will never be the same. Neither will the love he gave us ever fade.”

She added: “Forever loved. Forever missed. Forever our superhero. Our Matt and Dad.”

Donations to a fundraiser set up by Cleveland Police to support the families of the two police officers have now reached over £230,000. Organisers said funds raised would be split equally between the two officers’ families and the federation would continue to provide support.

Five teenagers and young men who died driving on the wrong side of the road in the crash have also been named as Makai Saddington, 18, Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Theo Rae, 17, Cole Robert Worthy, 17, and Jakub Matusiak, 23. No-one survived the collision, which is being investigated by the police watchdog.

open image in gallery Jakub Matusiak, Theo Rae, Michael Robert Cahill, Makai Saddington and Cole Robert Worthy were killed in the crash ( Facebook )

Cleveland Police had launched a pursuit after spotting the VW acting “suspiciously”, the force said in the aftermath of the fatal crash.

Officers began following the car in South Bank, near Middlesbrough in Teesside, before it joined the A66 in the wrong direction.

Officers ended their pursuit, but just 10 seconds later the VW collided with an oncoming police armed response unit at 3.39am. The police car, which was travelling in the right direction, was not part of the pursuit.

Friends and family of the teenagers and young men have also spoken of their heartbreak.

In a post on Facebook, Sharon Morgan said she had lost her “beloved nephew” Makai Saddington, aged 18, from Middlesbrough.

“There are no words that can truly express the pain of losing someone so young, so loved, and so full of life,” she wrote.

“You brought so much love and happiness into our family, and your memory will stay with us forever. This loss has left a space in our hearts that can never be filled. Rest peacefully, my beautiful nephew. You will never be forgotten.”

open image in gallery Police officers at the scene of a fatal crash on the A66 ( PA )

Grieving mother, Kelly Cahill, paid tribute to Michael Robert Cahill, adding: “Fly high my boy forever 23 go and be at peace with ya dad keep me a place up there till will we meet again.”

Ellie Webster, who described herself as a close friend of Theo Rae, said watching his family’s hearts being broken was one of the hardest things she had ever done.

“Theo Rae you’ve left so many people broken,” she said.

“I’m gunna miss your daily checkins making sure we’re all okay. I wish I could take the pain away from your mam, how are we going to get her through this I’ll never know! It just doesn’t seem real. Rest in peace Theo.”

Channy Brown shared pictures of all five VW occupants as she called for their faces to “light up” social media.

Paying tribute, she said they were “top lads” with “kind hearts”. “Forever young forever going to be missed and loved by everyone who new them,” she added.

open image in gallery Flowers left near the scene on the A66 in South Bank ( PA )

Others posted details of balloon releases in the coming days in memory of some of the five.

Doorbell footage from nearby Lime Road appears to show multiple police vehicles chasing a car at speed. The footage was filmed at 3.36am, three minutes before the fatal crash.

Teesville resident Neil Hutchinson told the Mail on Sunday: “There were police cars tearing down the street at 3.30am with lights flashing and their sirens going, it woke me up.”

The police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), confirmed it had launched an investigation into the “tragic incident” following a mandatory referral from the local force.

In an update on Sunday, the watchdog revealed Cleveland officers had been chasing the Passat for seven minutes, but ended the pursuit when it entered the A66 in the wrong direction.

open image in gallery Balloons left near the scene on the A66 ( PA )

The force had received intelligence regarding numerous incidents linked to the car, which was suspected of having cloned number plates.

The Passat struck the oncoming police response vehicle just 10 seconds after the chase was abandoned. The officers who were killed had not been involved in the pursuit but were in the area to assist in the search for the car.

IOPC director of engagement Derrick Campbell said: “We recognise the devastating impact the incident has had on those in the force, and the wider policing community, and offer our condolences.

“We have obtained initial accounts of officers involved in the pursuit, the incident log and in-car footage of the incident. Work is ongoing to obtain additional material.”

The A66 has been closed in both directions between Normanby Road and Church Lane in Eston as investigators examine the wreckage. A large white tent was erected over the scene, with multiple emergency service vehicles around.

The closed section of the A66 is bordered by large industrial units to the north and is close to the major Teesworks site.

New Zealand was set to introduce legislation proposing a ban on social media for children under the age of 16, prime minister Christopher Luxon announced on Monday.

Under the plan, tech firms face penalties of up to 10 per cent of their global revenues if they fail to comply.

The proposed law would mandate that platforms implement reasonable age-verification measures, utilising digital identity documents, facial technology, and existing account data.

Mr Luxon emphasised the government's duty to protect young people. "We simply can’t accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children," he said in a statement.

"Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with and it's affecting their family life, mental health, sleep and education."

However, the bill faced an uncertain path through the parliament after New Zealand First, a coalition partner, confirmed its opposition.

"We’ve been concerned with the proposed legislation and the direction and slippery slope that legislation like this will inevitably take our country," the party’s leader and the country’s foreign minister Winston Peters said.

In December, Australia became the first country in the world to ban social media for under-16s, blocking access to services like TikTok, Alphabet's YouTube and Meta's Instagram and Facebook.

That law was a "colossal failure", Peters said, stating that keeping children off platforms was a parental responsibility.

Speaking at an event, Mr Luxon conceded the challenge ahead. "I won't pretend that it will be simple or that it will be perfect," he said. "We won't get every single child off social media. Some will always find ways around it, but frankly, it's just way too important not to at least try."
