World.title: Anti-vaccine mandate protests spread across the country, crippling Canada-U.S. trade
World.content:
Speaking to reporters at a press conference in Ottawa, Emergency Preparedness Minister Bill Blair said the blockade at Windsor’s Ambassador Bridge is particularly alarming because a quarter of all Canada-U.S. trade moves through that one crossing, which connects Canada with Detroit and points beyond.

Hundreds of millions of dollars worth of products have been held back for three days as 50 to 75 vehicles and about 100 anti-mandate protesters camp out on the main road that leads on and off the bridge.

The Canada Border Service Agency (CBSA) has closed the bridge to commercial traffic temporarily, diverting trucks to the Blue Water Bridge in Sarnia, Ont. instead. CBSA is reporting wait times in excess of four hours to make the short trip across to Port Huron, Mich.

We’ve seen the criminal acts, acts of thuggery and the obnoxiousness that they’ve inflicted on the people of Ottawa. Now they’re blocking the highways leading into our ports of entry. They’re putting their foot on the throats of all Canadians.

Labour unions representing auto workers have reported some idled Windsor plants have sent workers home while the trucker convoy holds up much-needed parts coming from the U.S.

Transport Minister Omar Alghabra said central Canada could soon see empty store shelves because so much of the region’s fresh food and produce comes into the country across that bridge.

To be honest, I find it ironic that the same people who were trying to sell Canadians fake stories about empty shelves are now causing those shelves to go empty, Alghabra said.

Windsor Mayor Drew Dilkens said the protesters appear to be determined to stay. They feel such a passion for this particular cause that they’re willing to die for it, he said.

Speaking briefly to reporters before question period, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said his government is working with Ontario and the City of Windsor to put an end to the blockade.

World.title: Excellent prospects for Mercosur beef exports, except Argentina
World.content:
The Argentine beef industry is optimistic about world meat production and global demand this year, with China again playing a leading market role. A report issued by Argentina’s Rosario Stock Exchange (BCR) and the Mercado Ganadero Department (Rosgan), world beef production will reach 58 million tons, representing a 1% increase over 2021.

This prospect would reverse the downward trend seen in 2021, mainly because of the recovery of the meat-packing industries in Brazil and Australia, the world’s first and third-largest meat exporters, respectively.

As for the global flow of imports, the expected average, according to analysts at BCR/Rosgan, is 10 million tons, which would imply an increase of 2.7% compared to last year.

China, which reduced the pace of international beef purchases in 2021 to 950,000 tons compared to more than 1.1 million tons in 2020 will once again represent 32% of global consumption. According to BCR/Rosgan, China accounted for 13% of global meat demand in 2017.

At that time, Argentina was in the top five beef exporters, having previously been in the top three. But Argentina has dropped out of the top ten beef exporters in recent years, owing to government restrictions on beef exports with the purpose of supporting the domestic market and helping with lower prices.

Nevertheless the Brazilian and Argentine beef markets had an unusual year in 2021. Traditional animal protein producers, the two countries witnessed declines in their exports, particularly in the last months of the year. Overall compared to 2020, Brazil beef sales dropped 9,92% while Argentine exports decreased 13,84%.

The reduction experienced by Brazil can be explained by the beef embargo imposed by China. In effect on September 2021, Brazil voluntarily suspended exports to China after the identification of two cases of mad cow disease in the country.

The World Organization for Animal Health (OIE) recognized that these were atypical episodes and that the risk to the national herd was negligible. Despite this, China insisted in freezing Brazilian beef exports for over three months until December 15.

The drop in Argentine beef shipments were motivated by the high price of the product in the domestic market, and thus the government suspended all exports in May 2021. ” As a consequence of sustained increases in the price of beef cuts in the domestic market, the national government decided to implement a set of emergency measures to better organize the sector, restricting speculative practices, improving the traceability of exports and avoiding tax evasion,” said the decree issued at the time.

Further measures were implemented, and given the deteriorating economic situation of Argentina and its impact on inflation, the country’s export ban on certain beef cuts was extended until the end of 2023.

As a result of this situation, Mercosur junior member Uruguay strongly benefitted and saw beef shipments increase 35%. The same can be said of the other Mercosur member, Paraguay, that also experienced a record year of beef exports in 2021.

World.title: Unemployment in Chile almost back at 2019 levels
World.content:
Chilean authorities have reported Monday that unemployment nationwide had fallen in 2021 to 7.2% while in the same period of 2020 it had hit 10.3%. In the middle of the social uprisings of 2019 it had been recorded at 7.1%.

“It is the eighth consecutive annual decrease in the unemployment rate,” said Leonardo González of the National Institute of Statistics (INE), which also reported the unemployment rate for women stood at 7.4%, and for men at 7.1%.

In the quarter of the year, 119,930 jobs were created compared to the previous quarter. With seasonal adjustment, González specified, the number of jobs recovered quarterly reached 49,625.

Around 1,436,000 jobs have been recovered, which represented 77.5% of all jobs lost during the worst part of the COVID-19 pandemic, with 81.8% accounting for jobs held by men and 73.1% for those carried out by women.

The INE also said 80.1% of formal jobs and 94.5% of informal jobs had been recovered.

“If we continue at this rate, we estimate that we will soon be able to recover all the jobs that were lost in the worst moment of the pandemic,” González stressed. He warned, however, that “we have been consistently seeing these rates rise, but we are not yet seeing pre-pandemic levels.”

Employment ended 2021 at 54.3%, while the labor force participation rate ended at 58.5%, an 8.1% yoy increase, driven by women (11.7%) and men (5.7%).

Jobs were boosted by construction (22.2%), commerce (8.5%) and the hotels and restaurants (30.9%).

Economy Minister Lucas Palacios said that during “2021 we met the goal of strongly recovering economic activity and also employment.”

“We have recovered 80% of the jobs that the pandemic and recession destroyed. It was necessary to create health, operational security and certainty conditions to reactivate the economy and especially investment, which is the main source of opportunities,” Palacios said.

Palacios also highlighted joint efforts by the public and private sectors. “Incentives from the State can be very relevant to promote investment and employment,” the minister explained.

Labor Minister Patricio Melero agreed the unemployment figures meant “great news” and praised “the measures adopted by the government, both in economic and health matters,” which were yielding “results which are very positive for the country.”

(Source: ANSA)

World.title: Argentina votes this week on the reform barring the central bank from funding the Treasury
World.content:
Argentina votes this week on the reform barring the central bank from funding the Treasury

23rd Sunday, August 2026 - 22:41 UTC Full article

The bill also prohibits the purchase of national, provincial or municipal government bonds on the primary market, the mechanism through which the central bank has historically financed the Treasury

Argentina's Chamber of Deputies will on Wednesday debate the reform of the central bank's charter promoted by Javier Milei's government, which bars the monetary authority from financing the fiscal deficit through money creation and restores preservation of the value of the currency as its sole objective.

The bill removes the five functions added to the institution's mandate by the 2012 reform — among them promoting employment and economic development with social equity — and replaces them with a single objective. It also prohibits the purchase of national, provincial or municipal government bonds on the primary market, the mechanism through which the central bank has historically financed the Treasury.

Central bank governor Santiago Bausili and deputy governor Vladimir Werning defended the initiative before the budget and finance committees. They argued the purpose is to shield the institution from the political pressures of successive administrations and to consolidate a structure aimed at preventing a return to high inflation.

The same session will take up the bill known as Fiscal Innocence II, which expands a simplified scheme designed to bring undeclared assets into the formal system, estimated by the government at some 170 billion dollars. It removes the annual income and asset ceilings that limited access to the scheme and cuts by 25% the penalties for individuals and small and medium-sized companies that sign up. Opposition lawmaker Victoria Tolosa Paz, of Unión por la Patria, has called for an article barring officials of all three branches of the state from accessing those benefits.

The special session was called for midday by La Libertad Avanza bloc leader Gabriel Bornoroni, with backing from nine parliamentary groups including PRO, the Unión Cívica Radical and blocs answering to provincial governors. The governing coalition believes it has the votes to secure approval in the lower house.

The debate comes against a backdrop of deteriorating financial indicators. In August the country risk premium passed 470 basis points and sovereign bonds gave up much of their first-half performance, in a move not mirrored in other emerging markets. Arrears on credit to individuals reached 17.5% of total lending in June, according to a study by Universidad Austral and the consultancy Eco Go. A recent survey puts the share of Argentines identifying as opponents of the government at 52%.

Milei will chair a cabinet meeting on Monday, the first since July 9, and will receive deputies and senators on Tuesday ahead of the vote.

World.title: The Mercosur-Singapore trade agreement reaches Argentina's Congress
World.content:
The Mercosur-Singapore trade agreement reaches Argentina's Congress

23rd Sunday, August 2026 - 22:32 UTC Full article

The request carried signatures from nine groups, among them PRO, the Unión Cívica Radical, Provincias Unidas, Innovación Federal, Por Santa Cruz, La Neuquinidad and Adelante Buenos Aires

Argentina's Chamber of Deputies will on Wednesday take up ratification of the free trade agreement between Mercosur and Singapore, signed in December 2023 and still awaiting parliamentary approval. It is the first trade treaty the bloc has concluded with a Southeast Asian country.

The text appears on the agenda of a special session called for midday by La Libertad Avanza bloc leader Gabriel Bornoroni, alongside a reform of the central bank's charter and an expansion of the scheme for regularising undeclared assets. The request carried signatures from nine parliamentary groups, among them PRO, the Unión Cívica Radical, Provincias Unidas, Innovación Federal, Por Santa Cruz, La Neuquinidad and Adelante Buenos Aires, suggesting sufficient backing to secure approval in the lower house.

The Singapore agreement was negotiated over several years and signed under Brazil's pro tempore presidency of Mercosur. It requires ratification by the parliaments of all four member states — Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay — to enter into force.

The same agenda includes Argentina's accession to the Patent Cooperation Treaty, an instrument administered by the World Intellectual Property Organization that allows protection for an invention to be sought simultaneously in multiple jurisdictions through a single filing. Argentina is one of the few countries in the region not yet part of the system.

The session also covers a series of domestic measures: a reduction in the value added tax rate on cassava starch, promoted by lawmakers from Misiones province; the creation of additional chambers in the federal appeals courts of Tucumán and Mar del Plata; and a dozen bills designating various towns as national capitals of different productive and cultural sectors.

Consideration of the Singapore agreement comes at a moment of tension within the bloc. Brazil on August 4 downgraded its diplomatic relations with Argentina to chargé d'affaires level, after President Javier Milei took part in a campaign event for Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro at which he referred to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in terms Brasília considered offensive. Paraguayan President Santiago Peña said on August 14 that the differences between the two leaders had not affected how Mercosur functions.

The bloc, made up of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, also has Bolivia's full accession process under way. Brazil's presidential elections on October 4 are the next political milestone bearing on the regional agenda.

World.title: Colombia's earthquake toll rises to 329 dead and more than 300,000 affected
World.content:
Colombia's earthquake toll rises to 329 dead and more than 300,000 affected

22nd Saturday, August 2026 - 08:47 UTC Full article

Records of material damage have also risen substantially: 171,273 homes damaged, 31,183 destroyed and 553 buildings collapsed, mainly in Cali and Pereira, the two worst-hit cities

The magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western and central Colombia on August 10 has left 329 dead, 4,600 injured and 247 missing, according to the National Disaster Risk Management Unit's assessment as of Friday. The number of people affected stands at 314,751, from 154,014 families, across 481 municipalities in 16 of the country's 32 departments.

Records of material damage have also risen substantially: 171,273 homes damaged, 31,183 destroyed and 553 buildings collapsed, mainly in Cali and Pereira, the two worst-hit cities. Damage has also been recorded at 367 health centres, 3,710 schools, 5,584 community centres and 427 roads. The number of people rescued alive remains at 364.

The figures have varied considerably between the agency's successive reports. On August 12 the toll stood at 239 dead and 49,214 people affected; on August 16, at 289 and 185,016; on Friday, at 329 and 314,751. The number of missing has fluctuated between 143 and 379 depending on the day, and collapsed buildings rose from 66 in the August 14 assessment to 553 on Friday.

The agency has attributed these variations to three factors. The first is the cross-checking of initial reports, mostly verbal, against official records held by the attorney general's office and the forensic service, in order to remove duplicates. The second is the progressive incorporation of surveys compiled by municipal governments: the jump recorded on August 16 was largely due to the integration of data from Pereira. The third is the on-site assessment of each building by engineering teams, which corrects the count of homes and structures in both directions.

The epicentre was located in San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, one of those with the highest poverty rates in the country. The worst-affected departments are Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, Caldas and Quindío. The Colombian Geological Service described it as the strongest seismic event recorded in Colombia this century and had counted 325 aftershocks one week after the quake.

Search operations gave way last weekend to body recovery and debris clearance, after several days without anyone being pulled out alive. President Abelardo de la Espriella declared an economic emergency on August 12, a constitutional mechanism subject to Constitutional Court review that empowers the executive to issue decrees with the force of law, and announced the creation of a fund to channel reconstruction resources.

World.title: Colombia's government objects to the law barring lower requirements for senior posts
World.content:
Colombia's government objects to the law barring lower requirements for senior posts

22nd Saturday, August 2026 - 08:40 UTC Full article

The presidency's legal secretary, Andrés Barreto, said the initiative “encroaches on exclusive powers of the national government, such as barring the government from organising public employment.”

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella this week objected to the first bill sent to him for signature since he took office on August 7: legislation prohibiting any reduction in the minimum education and experience requirements for senior positions in the public sector and in companies with state participation.

The text, registered as bill 056 of 2024 in the Chamber of Representatives, was promoted by Hernán Cadavid, now a senator for the Centro Democrático, a party within the coalition backing the government, and had been approved by both chambers. The executive returned it to Congress on grounds of unconstitutionality and inadvisability, and asked that it be shelved or revised.

The presidency's legal secretary, Andrés Barreto, said the initiative “encroaches on exclusive powers of the national government, such as barring the government from organising public employment.” He also argued that Decree Law 770 of 2005 already sets mandatory minimum thresholds for such posts, making the new rule redundant, and that requiring three prior stages before each appointment — studies by the entity, by the public administration department and a binding opinion from the Council of State — “will paralyse the formation of management teams, delaying by months the execution of projects that are a priority for the country.”

The decision drew objections from within the government's own camp. Cadavid called it “baffling” and said the bill sought to prevent governments from arbitrarily lowering requirements. Former official Rafael Nieto Loaiza pointed to the contradiction with the “National Talent Bank” announced by the government so that access to public service would depend on ability, and recalled that the governing bloc had criticised the previous administration for amending job manuals to the same effect.

The objection coincides with questions over the executive's first appointments. These include the president's first wife, lawyer Yoly Beatriz Illidge, as deputy superintendent for notaries and registries; a married couple heading the Victims' Unit and the tax and customs authority; and businessman Jaime Andrés Uribe, founder of a rum brand and without a professional degree, as manager of the fund planned to administer reconstruction after the August 10 earthquake, valued at some 30 trillion pesos, close to 10 billion dollars.

At least six people from the law firm the president founded now hold posts in the executive, among them Barreto himself. Senator Daniel Briceño, of the Centro Democrático, questioned the appointment to head the National Planning Department on grounds of inexperience. Congress must now decide whether to accept the objections or insist on the bill.

World.title: Progressive leaders gathered in Uruguay denounce US interference and acknowledge their own mistakes
World.content:
Progressive leaders gathered in Uruguay denounce US interference and acknowledge their own mistakes

22nd Saturday, August 2026 - 08:28 UTC Full article

Participants questioned Washington's conduct in the region, citing that intervention, strikes on vessels in the Caribbean and sanctions on Cuba, and called for greater regional autonomy

The opening session of the third Pan-American Congress, held on Friday at the Legislative Palace in Montevideo, combined criticism of United States policy towards Latin America with calls for self-criticism within progressive forces. More than 150 lawmakers, former presidents, ministers and political figures from fifteen countries are taking part, according to organisers.

Former Chilean president Gabriel Boric delivered the most widely noted speech, calling for consistency between political discourse and action. He criticised what he described as a “new imperialism” driven by Donald Trump and said the major powers “today do not speak of democracy, but directly of oil at the expense of a people.” He then turned a demand on his own allies: “We do not believe that violating international law is the way to intervene illegitimately in another people, but we also have to say very clearly that Maduro had stolen the elections and that his presidency at that time was also illegitimate.” He warned that if the left fails to acknowledge such distinctions, it will struggle to persuade its own electorates.

Nicolás Maduro was captured in Caracas on January 3 during a US military operation and remains in custody in the United States. Delcy Rodríguez has since served as Venezuela's acting president.

Participants questioned Washington's conduct in the region, citing that intervention, strikes on vessels in the Caribbean and sanctions on Cuba, and called for greater regional autonomy. Former Colombian president Ernesto Samper urged a revival of Latin American integration and closer ties with the Global South, arguing the region holds strategic water, food and mineral resources but lacks the political coordination to defend its interests.

US Representative Pramila Jayapal shifted the debate to her own country, saying opposition is growing to taxes being spent on military operations abroad rather than on health services and living standards. She defended a foreign policy based on dialogue and diplomacy as the only route to “a lasting peace.”

Uruguay's vice-president, Carolina Cosse, focused on disinformation and the contest for public attention. “Indifference to truth leads inexorably to totalitarianism,” she warned. Mexican Morena official Carolina Rangel proposed combining economic growth with social rights and called for an agenda covering care policies, energy transition, productive integration and digital sovereignty.

The forum, created in Bogotá in 2024 on the initiative of then Colombian president Gustavo Petro, is organised this year around four themes: peace, security and multilateralism; sustainable development and regional integration; digital sovereignty and artificial intelligence; and wellbeing and care. Sessions continue until Sunday and will conclude at the Parlasur headquarters.

World.title: Uruguay's president meets Kicillof and agrees to cooperate on food and scientific research
World.content:
Uruguay's president meets Kicillof and agrees to cooperate on food and scientific research

21st Friday, August 2026 - 22:41 UTC Full article

Kicillof, governor since 2019 and a former economy minister, described the meeting as an opportunity to hear the Uruguayan leader's reading of the international situation

Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi on Friday received the governor of Argentina's Buenos Aires province, Axel Kicillof, at the Torre Ejecutiva in Montevideo, where the two signed two cooperation agreements covering agrifood and scientific matters.

The first links Uruguay's Ministry of Livestock, Agriculture and Fisheries, its Buenos Aires provincial counterpart and the Metropolitan Agrifood Unit, the wholesale food market supplying greater Montevideo. It provides for exchanges of information on production methods, training and certification, support for family-run operations and small businesses, and joint policies to reduce food loss and waste at wholesale markets.

“It concerns the UAM, which would be like the Mercado Central in Argentine terms,” Kicillof told a press conference, referring to the Buenos Aires wholesale market. “In Buenos Aires we do similar work,” he added, noting that both jurisdictions share a farming and food production profile.

The second agreement was signed between the Scientific Research Commission of Buenos Aires province and the University of the Republic, Uruguay's main public university, with the aim of strengthening institutions linked to research, science and innovation. The governor attributed the initiative to what he described as the defunding of the scientific sector by Javier Milei's government.

It is not the first understanding between the two jurisdictions. The province has cooperation agreements already in operation with the Montevideo city government, signed in previous years.

Kicillof, governor since 2019 and a former economy minister, described the meeting as an opportunity to hear the Uruguayan leader's reading of the international situation. “The president has international contacts, he has been talking to presidents in the region and was able to give us an overview of the situation and his view,” he said.

The governor used his visit to Montevideo to criticise the Argentine government's foreign policy, and in particular Milei's participation in a campaign event for Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro on July 25. He said the president's conduct “was not good for Argentina” and had led to a situation of diplomatic fragility. Brazil downgraded relations with Buenos Aires to chargé d'affaires level on August 4, following Milei's insults directed at Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The Argentine government did not respond to the governor's remarks.

The visit coincided with the third Pan-American Congress, a forum of progressive forces held in Montevideo from Friday to Sunday with more than 150 participants from fifteen countries, according to organisers. Kicillof spoke at the opening event at the Teatro Solís, which also featured former Chilean president Gabriel Boric and US and Brazilian lawmakers.

World.title: FIFA sanctions Argentina over the final's brawl and the Falklands banner
World.content:
FIFA sanctions Argentina over the final's brawl and the Falklands banner

21st Friday, August 2026 - 21:52 UTC Full article

The heaviest penalty fell on midfielder Leandro Paredes, banned for ten international matches and fined 90,000 dollars for striking Spain's Eric García and Gavi

FIFA's Disciplinary Committee on Friday imposed financial and sporting sanctions on the Argentine Football Association and four members of its national squad over the confrontations at the end of the 2026 World Cup final and over breaches committed throughout the tournament, among them the display of a banner asserting a sovereignty claim over the Falklands.

The heaviest penalty fell on midfielder Leandro Paredes, banned for ten international matches and fined 90,000 dollars for striking Spain's Eric García and Gavi. Defender Nahuel Molina received seven matches and 90,000 dollars over his altercation with Rodri, and forward Thiago Almada one match and 30,000 dollars. Assistant coach Roberto Ayala was suspended for three matches and fined 30,000 dollars over an incident with Dani Olmo. On Spain's side, tournament winners, only Gavi was sanctioned, with one match and 30,000 dollars.

The incidents took place on July 19 at the New Jersey stadium, immediately after Spain won 1-0. As the Spanish players celebrated, Molina confronted Rodri; when Eric García intervened, Paredes joined in with a shove, and the sequence turned into a scuffle that also involved Almada.

Fines on the Argentine federation total 321,000 dollars, of which 100,000 is suspended. The breakdown released by the AFA itself shows the banner accounts for the smallest item: 10,000 dollars for using a sporting event for demonstrations of a non-sporting nature, plus 20,000 for improper conduct by spectators.

The bulk relates to racist, homophobic and discriminatory chanting and abuse by Argentine fans at five tournament matches, against Cape Verde, Egypt, Switzerland, England and Spain: a 100,000-dollar fine and a further 100,000 suspended for six months. Another 91,000 was imposed for objects thrown onto the pitch in the matches against Switzerland and England, a delayed kick-off and failures to comply with security protocol.

The sanction also includes closing 50% of the stands — mainly those behind the goals — at the men's national team's next official home match, with an equivalent measure suspended for a year. As an alternative, the federation may fill half those seats with community groups under anti-discrimination conditions. The AFA must also spend the fine within six months on an anti-discrimination plan approved by FIFA.

The banner, reading “Las Malvinas son argentinas” — “The Falklands are Argentine” — was unfurled by several players after the 2-1 win over England in the semi-final on July 15 in Atlanta. The British government and the Falkland Islands Government asked FIFA to investigate the episode. Argentina maintains a sovereignty claim over the archipelago, administered by the United Kingdom since 1833; in the 2013 referendum, residents voted overwhelmingly to retain their status as a British overseas territory.

The decisions can be appealed. The AFA said it will request the grounds for the rulings in order to appeal to FIFA's Appeal Committee and, ultimately, to the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

World.title: ECLAC trims its 2026 forecast for Latin America and the Caribbean to 2.2%
World.content:
ECLAC trims its 2026 forecast for Latin America and the Caribbean to 2.2%

21st Friday, August 2026 - 10:47 UTC Full article

If the projections hold, the region will complete five consecutive years of growth averaging close to 2.3%. The regional economy expanded 2.4% in 2025 and 2.3% in 2024

The Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean on Thursday lowered its regional growth projection for 2026 to 2.2%, one tenth below the estimate issued in December. The United Nations body expects a partial recovery to 2.5% in 2027 and warns that the current pace is insufficient to sustainably raise income per capita.

If the projections hold, the region will complete five consecutive years of growth averaging close to 2.3%. The regional economy expanded 2.4% in 2025 and 2.3% in 2024. “The projections show the region would preserve the gains made in macroeconomic stability, though with less economic dynamism,” said the commission, which is based in Santiago de Chile.

The revision reflects a more complex external environment than anticipated late last year, with heightened geopolitical tensions, restrictive financial conditions and global inflationary pressures. The figures were compiled using information available up to July 30.

Performance across subregions varies widely. South America would grow 2.5% in both 2026 and 2027. The Caribbean would advance 5.6% and 7.9% respectively, driven almost entirely by Guyana, whose oil expansion lifts its growth to 16.2% this year and 19.7% next; without that country, Caribbean rates would fall to 1.1% and 2.2%. Central America is listed at 1.6% for 2026, though the figure is shaped by the inclusion of Cuba and Haiti in that grouping: excluding both economies, the subregion would grow 4.0% this year and 4.2% next.

After Guyana, the projections are led by Venezuela at 6.5%, Nicaragua at 4.5%, Panama at 4.4%, Paraguay at 4.3%, and Guatemala and the Dominican Republic at 4.0%. The middle band includes El Salvador, Costa Rica and Honduras, followed by Argentina at 3.3%, Peru at 3.2%, Colombia at 2.6%, Ecuador at 2.4% and Brazil at 2.2%. Closing the positive range are Chile at 1.6%, Uruguay at 1.5%, Mexico at 1.3% and Bolivia at 0.5%. Cuba would contract 10.3% this year and 5.1% in 2027, while Haiti would fall 1.9% and Jamaica 1.2%.

The report attributes the sluggish performance to structural constraints: low investment, weak productivity growth, slowing formal job creation and high informality. “To overcome the low-growth-capacity trap, we need to raise investment and productivity,” said executive secretary José Manuel Salazar-Xirinachs, who called for progress towards productive formalisation that broadens social protection and generates quality formal employment.

World.title: The lessons on living a good life you learn in Mexico
World.content:
Moving to another country is exciting, but it’s also a highly effective way of discovering just how little control you actually have over your life.

I’ve lived in Mexico for almost six years now, and I arrived with plans, expectations and a fairly clear idea of what I thought my new life would look like. Mexico, as it turns out, had other ideas.

That’s probably the first thing living here taught me. There’s a big difference between knowing about a country and actually living in it.

I knew Mexico from holidays. I knew about the beaches, the food, the history and the colorful streets. I knew enough basic Spanish phrases to get by, or at least I thought I did.

What I didn’t know was what it feels like when the water suddenly stops working. Or when something that should take an hour takes three days. Or when you’re told something will happen mañana and eventually realize that “tomorrow” can be more of a concept than a date.

Expectation vs. reality

I’ve learned to laugh about those things. Not because they’re never frustrating. They are. But because getting angry doesn’t make the water come back or the paperwork move any faster.

Mexico has taught me that sometimes you simply have to adjust your expectations and get on with your day. That lesson alone has probably saved me quite a few pesos on negating the need for blood pressure medication.

It’s also taught me that there isn’t one Mexico. The country I know from Puerto Vallarta is very different from the one I experienced in Guanajuato. Mexico City has a completely different rhythm again, while Guadalajara seems to be constantly negotiating the space between its traditions and its rapid growth.

Travel around Mexico long enough and you start to realize how ridiculous it is when people talk about the country as though it’s one big, homogeneous place.

It isn’t.

Even the Spanish changes. I arrived with some vocabulary and considerably more confidence than I deserved. But Mexican Spanish is full of slang, expressions and regional differences that can leave you wondering whether you’ve misunderstood the entire conversation.

I have. Repeatedly.

Learning from mistakes

Some mistakes have been mildly embarrassing. Others have been memorable for all the wrong reasons. But there’s something useful about being forced to become comfortable with not being good at something. You make a mistake. Someone laughs. You laugh, too. You try again. And eventually, you get better.

That applies to more than just language.

Living in another country means accepting that you’re going to get things wrong. You’ll misunderstand how something works. You’ll make an assumption that turns out to be completely incorrect. You’ll occasionally find yourself standing in the wrong line, wondering why no one else seems to be getting anywhere.

The trick is learning from it without deciding that the entire country is doing it wrong, and that’s harder than it sounds.

Mexico has also changed the way I think about money. One of the biggest misconceptions about living here is that everything is cheap. It isn’t.

Puerto Vallarta can be surprisingly expensive. Parts of Mexico City are eye-wateringly costly. Guadalajara has changed considerably as demand and investment have grown. Imported goods can cost far more than you’d expect, while local products are often considerably better value.

I’ve learned to keep some money aside for the unexpected because, eventually, something unexpected will happen.

That’s life anywhere. Mexico just has a particularly effective way of reminding you.

Finding value in small things

Then there’s food. I knew Mexican food was delicious before I moved here. I didn’t understand, though, just how much variety there was: tacos al pastor, birria, mole, pozole, tamales, seafood, fresh fruit, regional specialties and an almost endless variety of salsas.

Travel around the country and the food changes with the geography, history and culture. Some of the best meals I’ve eaten have come from places that would never make it onto a tourist list, so I’ve learned not to judge a restaurant by its facade. And when in doubt, order the tacos.

But perhaps the biggest change has been in what I consider a good day.

It doesn’t necessarily involve doing anything remarkable. It might be a long lunch with friends. A neighbor stopping for a chat. Someone remembering your name. Fresh tortillas. A walk with nowhere particular to go. A sunset that makes you stop for a minute.

Those things aren’t uniquely Mexican, of course. But living here has made me notice them more.

There’s a tendency when moving abroad to think the big things will determine whether you made the right decision: the house, the job, the finances, the location and the lifestyle.

They matter, but after almost six years, I think the smaller things have mattered more.

A complex place to call home

The people you meet. The routines you develop. The places that become familiar. The shopkeeper who knows what you usually buy. The restaurant where they recognize you before you’ve even sat down.

That’s how a foreign country slowly stops feeling foreign.

None of this means Mexico is perfect. It isn’t. There are things that frustrate me. Things I disagree with. Things I think could be done better. Living here for years has made me more aware of those things, not less. But that, too, has been part of the lesson.

You can love a country without pretending it has no problems. You can be grateful to live somewhere while still questioning how things work. And you can recognize that moving abroad doesn’t magically make life easier. It simply gives you a different set of problems, experiences and perspectives.

If I could go back and talk to the woman who first packed her bags for Mexico, I wouldn’t tell her everything was going to be wonderful. I’d tell her it was going to be complicated.

I’d tell her plans would change, that she’d get things wrong and that there would be days when she wondered what on earth she had done.

And then I’d tell her that was all OK.

Because six years later, I’ve realized that the goal was never to create a perfect life in Mexico. It was to create a life that felt like mine.

And somewhere along the way, this place I once had to learn how to navigate became home.

Charlotte Smith is a writer and journalist based in Mexico. Her work focuses on travel, politics and community. You can follow along with her travel stories at www.salsaandserendipity.com.

World.title: The Jewish-Mexican food traditions hiding in plain sight
World.content:
My friend Jorge Fitz once told me a story about his childhood visits to the town where his grandfather grew up, Juliantla, just outside of Taxco, Mexico. He remembers many particular things about the way the town celebrated festivities and holidays, but one thing that stuck out in his memory was a special braided bread they made called pan de Juliantla.

As an adult, Jorge said he started making Jewish friends, and when he saw pan de Juliantla on their tables, he wondered how they knew about it.

“Jorge, that’s challah bread,” they would respond.

He later learned that Juliantla is believed to be the first Jewish settlement in the Americas, complete with a spiritual cleansing bath known as a mikveh that dates back to the 16th century.

As far as Jorge could tell, a majority of the townspeople didn’t realize where many of their customs and food came from. He and his parents definitely didn’t know about their Jewish ancestry until much later.

Hearing this story illuminated just how deeply rooted Jewish food is in Mexican culture, so much so that even when origins have been forgotten, they remain an integral part of community life.

Waves of migration and a culinary legacy

The first Jews to grace Mexican shores sailed in on the ships of Spanish conquistadors during the 1500s and 1600s. They were fleeing the Catholic Inquisition of the Iberian Peninsula, but found little solace in the New World as the Inquisition migrated across the ocean.

Many of these early Jews “converted” to Catholicism while continuing to practice their own religion in secret. In Spanish, they are called “conversos,” or the converted. In English, we often refer to them as Crypto Jews.

With these Sephardim came cinnamon, grapes, figs, dates, almonds, cherries, apricots, olives and olive oil, nutmeg, ginger, cardamom and mustard, as well as black pepper, thyme, basil, clove, fennel, oregano, cumin and other Mediterranean spices.

They also had a strong tradition of pickling what they brought to the New World. In northern Mexico, cabrito, slow-roasted baby goat, is a traditional dish among the Sephardic Jews of the Iberian Peninsula. Similarly, the region’s dessert bread known as pan de cemita and la capirotada, a kind of bread pudding, are also attributed to those early Iberian Jewish immigrants.

The second wave of Jewish immigrants to Mexico arrived at the end of the 1800s from the failing Ottoman Empire. Jews who were part of the diaspora from Spain and Portugal, now living in the countries of the Levant, came because of economic opportunities in Mexico. They arrived from what is today Lebanon, Syria and Turkey, and because they were not fleeing persecution, their culture, religion and food were much more visible.

Preserving culture in the neighborhood oven

A third wave of Jewish immigrants came to Mexico during and between the two world wars. Some had plans of continuing on to the United States but were turned away at Ellis Island because of the Immigration Act of 1924, which severely limited the numbers of Southern and European immigrants allowed into the country.

These immigrants brought the Ashkenazi dishes of Eastern European countries like Poland, Ukraine and Germany — hearty soups and stews made with root vegetables like borscht, matza ball soup, gefilte fish, schmaltz (rendered chicken fat), tzimmes, gribenes and braised meats like brisket.

Food is paramount for any immigrant community trying to preserve their identity. The Jewish community was no different.

When Syrian Jews moved into Colonia Roma at the beginning of the 20th century, they not only built one of the city’s oldest synagogues but also opened a community oven down the street where special traditional breads were baked and sold to worshipers coming from services. At the local market were kosher butchers, while elderly folks sat in neighborhood cafes sipping thick, Turkish-style coffee and eating the sweets of home.

Unlike some of the immigrant groups I have researched, the diverse Mexican-Jewish community not only preserved the traditional dishes of their culture, but also, over the generations, adapted and innovated with local ingredients and cooking methods, creating a distinct Judeo-Mexican cuisine.

The fusion kitchen and home recipes

“Sabor Judío,” published in 2024, is a recipe collection by two authors whose Jewish grandmothers passed down handwritten recipe books. They gathered together a comprehensive archive of recipes from kitchens across the Mexican-Jewish community. Among the book’s pages are traces of many cuisines — Mexican mestizo, Spanish, Sephardic-Iberian, Sephardic-Middle Eastern and Ashkenazi.

Yiddish blintzes with huitlacoche (Mexican corn smut considered a local delicacy), matza chilaquiles, a variation of shakshuka with poblano peppers and Mexican oregano, and brisket tacos with three-chile salsa are all included in the collection. Irma Appel’s stuffed poblano peppers with guacamole include a smattering of gribenes (often referred to as Jewish bacon), and Pati Jinich, of PBS’s “Pati’s Kitchen,” provided her recipe for jalapeño-mushroom matza ball soup.

Then there are traditional Mexican recipes that the Mexican-Jewish community has adopted as their own, cooking them for high holidays and other festivities. That includes nopal and tomato salad made in advance to eat cold during Shabbat, or ceviche with prepared horseradish on top, supposedly invented during a Passover Seder.

Not everything is kosher, but the community’s many identities are on full display.

Scanning through the menus of Jewish restaurants in Mexico City, however, it’s hard to find the fusion dishes represented in “Sabor Judío.” For whatever reason, these dishes hold sway in family kitchens, but haven’t yet made it to commercial dining rooms.

Where to find Jewish food in Mexico City

Maybe the world isn’t ready for spicy gefilte fish?

That’s not to say that you can’t get glimpses of them — the salami chilaquiles at Klein’s in Polanco is a delicious example. You’ll also find chiles making guest appearances in the Israeli dishes at Merkava, and kosher cafe Guacho Grill has al pastor tacos made with fish and chicken, as opposed to the traditional pork.

So maybe fusion is yet to take off in restaurants, but at places like Klein’s or Niddo, which once described itself in an interview as Jewish-Mexican-Canadian, diners will at least find Jewish and Mexican dishes coexisting on the table.

Plenty of other expressions of Jewish food can be encountered throughout the city — Mendl, for instance, has incredible U.S.-style deli sandwiches and bagels with lox. And at Pat Patz, chef Mijeal Seidel has a labneh recipe that he adds dill to as a shout-out to his Eastern European side, along with tons of other dishes worth exploring.

You may have to make some fusion dishes at home, but a taste of Jewish-Mexican heritage is definitely available across Mexico City.

Lydia Carey is a freelance writer and translator based in Mexico City. She has published extensively both online and in print, sharing her insights about Mexico for over a decade. She lives a double life as a local tour guide and is the author of “Mexico City Streets: La Roma.” Follow her urban adventures on Instagram and see more of her work at mexicocitystreets.com.

World.title: How the Middle East has shaped Mexico for almost 2,000 years
World.content:
I’m sitting in the courtyard of Guanajuato’s Museo Iconográfico del Quijote, admiring the stone arches and columns, waiting for a chamber music concert to begin. I probably walk through at least one courtyard a day in Guanajuato because they’re everywhere in town – not just in museums, but in restaurants, universities, government buildings and parks. Even the classic Mexican colonial home has a courtyard with a fountain in the center, surrounded by rooms.

Mexican courtyards reflect the influence of the Moors, the North African Islamic group that ruled Spain for 800 years and whose ornate tilework, intricate geometric patterns and decorative calligraphy influenced the art and architecture of Spain. After the fall of the Moors in 1492, Spain continued to use Islamic patterns in its designs, creating a unique style that blended Islamic and Christian elements known as mudéjar, which later made its way to Mexico.

But it’s not just courtyards that bear the mark of the Moors. From architecture and folk medicine to crafts and textiles, here’s a quick roundup of the Islamic group’s lasting impact on Mexican culture.

Alhambrismo

This is an architectural style in Spain and Latin America inspired by the decorative Islamic arts of the Alhambra, a palace and fortress complex in Granada, Spain, with Moorish elements such as horseshoe arches, intricate stucco and colorful tilework.

A well-known example of this is the Kiosk of Santa Maria la Ríbera, an ornate octagonal pavilion made of wrought iron with a glass cupola dome on the top, in Mexico City’s Alameda Park.

Churches

In many colonial Mexican churches, you can see echoes of the mudéjar architectural style, including azulejos, blue-glazed tiles that adorn domes, bell towers and facades; intricate geometric carved-wood ceilings resembling inverted ship hulls; and arches and doorways.

Oaxaca’s famous Templo de Santo Domingo de Guzmán, for example, displays these design elements in the intricate geometric arabesque patterns on the ceiling and the genealogical tree of the temple’s namesake saint.

Inward-facing living

I remember when my husband and I first saw the house we bought in Guanajuato. Although one of its assets was a close-up view of the dome atop one of the city’s signature churches, San Francisco, we could barely see it from the tiny window in one of the bedrooms.

Unlike in the U.S. and Canada, traditional Mexican houses face inward, revealing their Moorish and Andalusian roots, with walled enclosures and internal gathering spaces.

Urban layouts

While Spanish colonial urban planning in the Americas officially ordered a strict grid system, some historic Mexican towns like Guanajuato and Taxco have narrow, winding streets, reflecting the medieval and southern Andalusian urban layouts shaped by centuries of Moorish influence.

Tiles, pottery and ceramics

Moorish craftsmen influenced Iberian ceramic styles, including tin-glazed pottery, by integrating geometric patterns and calligraphic bands into their work. When the craft was established in Puebla during the colonial period, artisans carried over these traditional Iberian-Islamic design elements, including abstract script borders and traditional brushstroke motifs.

Puebla’s famous Talavera pottery also blends Indigenous styles with Spanish and Moorish glazed-tile traditions.

Crafts and textiles

Mudéjar geometric inlaid woodworking and carpentry techniques influenced traditional lacquerware and furniture crafts in regions like Michoacán and Guerrero. Precise interlaced framing merged with Indigenous wood-carving and pre-Hispanic lacquering, creating colonial furniture like desks with repetitive geometric paneling and floral touches.

As for weaving, the traditional Mexican sarape displays complex linear, diamond and star-centered layouts that show cross-cultural parallels to Middle Eastern flat-weave blanket traditions.

Curanderismo (folk medicine)

Moorish and Islamic medical practices influenced curanderismo, the herbal medicine still widely practiced in Mexico. Ritual cleansing, petitionary prayers and talismanic magic elements arrived via Spanish traditions that had absorbed Moorish folk customs.

For example, the belief that the “mal de ojo,” or “evil eye,” can cause physical discomfort like fever, crying and restlessness was brought to the New World via Spanish and Moorish folk magic.

Middle Eastern influences beyond the Moors

Influential as the Moors were, they are not the only Middle Eastern influence in modern Mexico.

Following the fall of the Moors, many Sephardic Jews fled from the Middle East to colonial Mexico to escape the Inquisition. Later waves of Sephardic Jews arrived from the crumbling Ottoman Empire in the early 20th century. These communities established synagogues, cultural institutions and social networks, primarily in Mexico City.

While Mexico has seen periods of antisemitism throughout its history, modern Mexico hosts one of the largest and most vibrant Jewish communities in Latin America, mostly in Mexico City.

Meanwhile, the Lebanese diaspora in Mexico — currently standing at more than 500,000 descendants — has shaped the nation’s culture, cuisine and commerce since the late 19th century.

In the 1890s, they left to escape political oppression, heavy taxes, religious conflict and military conscription. At the same time, Mexico’s then-president, Porfirio Díaz, encouraged foreign immigration and trade, offering a welcoming environment and growing business opportunities.

During the period between the 1890s and 1930s, more than 100,000 mostly Lebanese immigrants arrived from Arabic-speaking nations, settling predominantly in the Yucatán, but also in Veracruz, Puebla and Mexico City.

In the early 20th century, the Lebanese community contributed around 50% of the total immigrant input to Mexico’s economy, and it remains one of Mexico’s most successful immigrant groups.

I’ve known for years that words like ¡ojalá!, albañil, and azotea are Arabic in origin, but I had no idea about other enduring Middle Eastern influences. The next time I use the Talavera dish I bought in Puebla, I’ll appreciate its ancient Moorish history, going back almost 2,000 years.

Louisa Rogers and her husband Barry Evans divide their lives between Guanajuato and Eureka, on California’s North Coast. Louisa writes articles and essays about expat life, Mexico, travel, physical and psychological health, retirement and spirituality. Her recent articles are available on her website, authory.com/LouisaRogers.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Fugitive swaps, a strawberry spat and a stronger peso
World.content:
Mexico and the United States spent the week of Aug. 17 trading shows of security cooperation, from fugitive handovers to a new drone-technology pact, culminating Wednesday in a federal operation in Michoacán that saw nine alleged members of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel arrested and set off narco-blockades at more than 20 points across the state.

That cooperation ran alongside friction on other fronts. Mexico is contesting a proposed U.S. antidumping tariff on strawberry exports and objecting to Washington’s decision to deport some Mexicans to Central America rather than home, as trade uncertainty lingers more than a month after the U.S. declined to renew the USMCA free trade deal in its current form. Domestically, the fallout from the U.S. visa revocation of former president López Obrador’s son continued to shadow the government’s messaging on fuel-smuggling enforcement. Against that backdrop, the peso’s push below 17 to the dollar stood out as a rare point of good economic news, as the central bank held its interest rate steady on lingering inflation concerns.

The week also brought a new Mexico-made electric vehicle, a national debate over kids and social media, and a presidential sick day. Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Fugitive returns and a new drone pact mark security cooperation

Mexico and the United States kept up a steady drumbeat of security announcements this week. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said U.S. authorities returned three wanted fugitives to Mexico in a single day — one linked to the CJNG, one wanted for murder in Zacatecas and one for fraud — while separately handing over six more fugitives wanted for crimes including murder and firearms offenses. Jalisco police also captured Antoni Covarrubias, wanted for second-degree murder in California, in Puerto Vallarta, which Johnson called the ninth high-profile U.S.-targeted arrest in the state in recent weeks. At the same time, the U.S. and Mexico conducted a joint security exercise along the El Paso-Ciudad Juárez border, and the two countries signed a declaration of intent on drone technology that will let Mexico’s Defense Ministry access the U.S. Army’s marketplace for unmanned aircraft systems, though no models, quantities or purchases have been agreed.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch drew public praise from DEA Administrator Terry Cole at the 40th International Drug Enforcement Conference in Buenos Aires, where García Harfuch said U.S. agencies are processing 155 arrest warrants tied to Mexican investigations and reported that Mexico’s Financial Intelligence Unit has frozen more than 8.6 billion pesos in assets. He also cited a more than 50% drop in daily homicides, from 86 to 42, over the past two years, a figure attributed to his ministry’s own count of arrests and seizures.

The Michoacán operation capped the week’s security news: Soldiers and National Guard troops arrested nine people, including two women identified as relatives of CJNG plaza boss Heraclio “Tío Lako” Guerrero Martínez, who evaded capture as the operation set off blockades that were largely cleared by Wednesday afternoon.

That flow of cooperation announcements ran alongside a separate dispute over fuel smuggling and politics. Sheinbaum said at Tuesday’s mañanera that fuel smuggling, or huachicol fiscal, is “practically over” in Mexico thanks to customs interventions and arrests — a claim she offered in the context of defending her government against opposition criticism. That criticism stems partly from the U.S. revocation of the visa of Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, son of former President López Obrador, which Sheinbaum has called a political matter, saying he “was not” ever on authorities’ radar for criminal involvement. The fuel-trafficking case itself advanced this week when Rear Admiral Fernando Farías Laguna, accused of leading a Pemex-linked smuggling ring, was extradited from Argentina and jailed at the Altiplano maximum security prison. The case has damaged the Navy’s reputation and drawn indirect allegations, which Sheinbaum has rejected, involving López Beltrán.

Strawberries, Vietnam imports and a Canada call test trade ties

Mexico is contesting a U.S. Commerce Department finding that could impose antidumping tariffs on Mexican strawberries, which supplies 98% of U.S. strawberry imports. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard called the U.S. criteria “arbitrarily applied” and inconsistent with USMCA provisions; a final ITC ruling isn’t expected until early 2027, and the case could affect roughly 5,000 Mexican producers and 151,000 jobs if it proceeds. Sheinbaum has warned the case could set a precedent for challenging other Mexican agricultural exports.

Separately, Mexico’s imports from Vietnam more than doubled in the first half of 2026 to $18.4 billion, a jump that has raised suspicions — flagged in a recent White House report naming Mexico a “Tier 1” transshipment risk — that Chinese goods are being routed through Vietnam to dodge Mexico’s tariffs on non-free-trade-agreement countries. Mexico has denied being a transshipment hub for Chinese goods bound for the U.S.

Against that backdrop, President Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney discussed North American trade by phone on Thursday. Carney’s office said the two underscored the importance of renewing the USMCA pact soon, and separately thanked Mexico for deploying more than 400 firefighters to help combat wildfires in British Columbia. The call came as Trump-imposed tariffs on Canadian goods, delayed this week, loomed for Saturday absent a deal. (The U.S. tariffs on Canada ultimately went into effect after trade talks collapsed late Friday night.)

Peso strength collides with a cautious Banxico

The peso dropped below 17 to the U.S. dollar this week, dropping below 16.9 on Friday, largely on dollar weakness following a U.S. Treasury bond buyback announcement. The currency has appreciated nearly 6% in 2026, a gain Banxico credits with helping cool inflation.

Even so, the central bank held its benchmark rate at 6.5% earlier this month. In meeting minutes released this week, four of five board members cited persistent services inflation as a driver of that decision. Headline inflation slowed to 3.12% in July, but Banxico now doesn’t expect it to reach its 3% target until the fourth quarter of 2027. The bank also flagged Middle East tensions as an upside risk to oil prices. Separately, INEGI’s preliminary July data showed the economy growing 2.7% annually, which Rodríguez called “another piece of good news” following 2.1% growth in the second quarter.

Other business and finance news this week:

Mañanera themes: EVs, phone lines and a presidential sick day

On Monday, Sheinbaum said she opposes a social-media ban for minors like Australia’s, calling the idea “very problematic” and noting enforcement challenges, while Education Minister Mario Delgado announced a nationwide teacher consultation on classroom device rules ahead of the Aug. 31 school year.

At Thursday’s press conference, Sheinbaum unveiled a prototype of Olinia Carga, the government’s second domestically developed electric vehicle, a light-cargo EV that can carry 650 kilograms and will sell for around 150,000 pesos starting in late 2027. The same day brought a new arrest in the 2024 kidnapping case of Sinaloa Cartel figure “El Mayo” Zambada.

On Friday, Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez, standing in for an ill Sheinbaum, told U.S. Ambassador Johnson that Mexico disagrees with Washington’s decision to deport some Mexicans to Guatemala, Honduras and Costa Rica rather than to Mexico.

Elsewhere, millions of Mexican cell phone lines were suspended after an Aug. 15 mandatory registration deadline passed, though regulators say most affected users can still recover service. Mexico also abstained from an OAS vote, which passed 29-1, to convene an emergency session on Nicaragua’s move to bar opposition candidates, with representative Alejandro Encinas citing Mexico’s non-intervention principle. Friday’s mañanera, run by Rodríguez after Sheinbaum announced she had the flu, also touched on new archaeological finds in a Chiapas cave tied to Zoque ritual traditions.

Regional news roundup:

And some good news to close out the week:

Looking ahead

Several threads left open this week are likely to develop further: Security cooperation with the U.S. continues to strengthen, while trade friction between the two countries shows no sign of easing. On a practical note, cell phone users facing the next registration deadlines — Aug. 31 for numbers ending in “1” — should act before their lines are suspended.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: From the archive: How to whistle like a true Mexican
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in January 2025 — is a perfect example, offering humorous insight into the fine art of whistling.

I have known no jealousy like the jealousy I feel when I hear Mexicans’ elaborate category of effortless whistles.

Okay fine, they’re not effortless. They just sound that way because they learned how to do it when they were kids. You know, like speaking Spanish.

Indeed, whistling is part of the language in some meaningful ways. There are specific whistles used for getting people’s attention. There are whistles for saying “Hey buddy, what’s up?” from across the street. There are whistles for saying, “But of course, my horse” — okay, maybe not exactly that, but a kind of “You know it!” with that adorable tone. There are whistles to say, “Wowza, nice butt, strange woman I don’t know!” Some whistles say, “Okay, back up your car now, a little more, a little more, a little more, stop!” There are even whistles to tell people where they can stuff it. Careful with those.

And I am going to learn them all.

A realistic goal

Well, I’m going to try. Forget turning my health or finances around; it’s too big a task. I need something I actually stand a chance at being able to bite off. Even though the prospect of practicing them takes me back to the deep humiliation I felt trying to string a four-word sentence together in Spanish while the three-year-old next to me rattled off deep, complex sentence after deep, complete sentence, I’m committed. I did it once, and I can do it again!

I won’t necessarily use them all, or use them frequently. In fact, I’m fairly certain that men whistle much more than women around here, anyway. Like cursing, it falls into a decidedly “male” category of behavior, and is seen as somewhat crass and unladylike.

I’ve also noticed that whistling is more prevalent among lower socio-economic classes than among the more well-to-do. Part of this is simply cultural habit, growing out of the need to communicate at great distances. It’s more pleasant sounding, and clearer, than shouting. If you’re willing to do some digging, there are actually some fascinating examples of whistles-as-language. There’s a cool short video about this below.

But I don’t need to be communicating over great distances in the Oaxaca countryside. I just want to have some fun.

Indigenous Whistle Language In Mexico

Watch this video on YouTube

And I don’t want to go too fast, but I’m also an eager learner. This video is pretty cute, by the way, as an introduction to the meanings of different whistles.

Here are the specific ones that I want to learn:

Learning how to whistle in Mexico (in different styles, for different purposes)

The whistle to get someone’s attention

Say you’re walking along a busy street and you need to get someone’s attention. Maybe it’s a vendor, or maybe a taxi that didn’t notice you! This whistle is perfect for it. It’s also important for me personally, because my voice does not carry at all. My loudest is not very loud, and the strain on my voice physically hurts! This can either be a quick low-high sound, or the more universally recognized high-low-slightly higher.

The ‘you can count on me, buddy’ whistle

I mostly want to learn this one because I think it’s both hilarious and adorable. My partner does this one sometimes, and even though it’s kind of a joke, I am 100% charmed.

‘Hey, friend on the other side of the street!’

Finally, I’ve just got to learn this whistle. It’s short and sweet, and I don’t care that I’ve hardly ever heard it from a woman’s lips.

So those are the three goals. Three distinct whistles — I can kind of do a “pucker” whistle now, but not very well — should be manageable in a year, right?

In the meantime, I’m dying to know: can you whistle? Can you do any specifically Mexican whistles? I especially want to know how many women out there can — please let me know in the comments!

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Guadalajara residents turn to citizen science as water crisis deepens
World.content:
On a Saturday morning in Guadalajara’s historic Analco neighborhood, residents arrived at the Casa Bandera community center carrying bottles and jars filled with water from their homes.

At folding tables, researchers from ITESO, Guadalajara’s Jesuit university, showed them how to dip inexpensive reactive strips into the samples, wait for the colors to change and compare the results against a chart measuring pH, chlorine, lead, mercury and other indicators. Samples showing signs of possible bacterial contamination could undergo additional testing for E. coli.

It was the latest workshop in an expanding citizen water-monitoring network that has grown out of Guadalajara’s months-long water crisis — and out of residents’ frustration with what they see as inadequate information and action from the authorities responsible for providing safe water.

“We don’t claim to be scientific specialists or water experts,” Héctor Morales, one of the workshop presenters, told participants. “We are citizens contributing evidence from what we are observing and living through, and that is equally valid.”

“We’re not trying to compete with science,” he continued. “We’re trying to generate knowledge that comes from everyday life. That’s the approach of citizen science.”

Sunday: Mega March + Agua KK Fest

Guadalajara’s water activists will be having some fun with the theme at Sunday’s festival — without losing sight of the very serious problem behind it.

When: Sunday, Aug. 23

10 a.m.: Gather at Parque Rojo

11 a.m.: Mega March for Water departs along Av. Juárez

Noon: Agua KK Fest at Plaza Liberación

The workshops will feature home water filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets and water testing, plus children’s activities, music, decorated water jugs, costumes and karaoke. The cheeky Agua KK name is a play on the word caca — a pointed joke about the dirty water that residents say has been coming from their taps.

From complaints to citizen evidence

The network brings together neighborhood residents, scientists from ITESO University, the Mexican Institute for Community Development (IMDEC) and the citizen campaign #ElSiapaQueQueremos, or The SIAPA We Want — SIAPA being the city water utility.

The idea is not simply to tell residents what might be in their water. María González of IMDEC said the testing has two purposes: helping families take care of themselves, and creating a body of evidence that can be used to press authorities for action.

“This helps us protect ourselves. You are going to know what is in the water in your homes,” González told the group. But the results, she said, are also “our citizen evidence for legal action, for institutional action, for mobilization.”

Before Saturday’s workshop, the network had analyzed roughly 184 samples from 90 neighborhoods in five municipalities. Organizers said residual chlorine was found in only 12 of the 184 samples. That’s a problem, they pointed out. Chlorine is added during water treatment, and a small amount should remain as water travels through the distribution network to help protect it from bacterial contamination.

The monitoring also detected lead in 20 samples, fluoride in 52 and mercury in an unspecified number, according to Morales. Four of the 184 samples tested positive for E. coli, a form of fecal coliform bacteria.

The citizen findings are not a statistically representative survey of Guadalajara’s water supply, a limitation organizers repeatedly emphasized. The low-cost tests do not measure all of the dozens of parameters required under Mexico’s drinking-water standard.

“What does this analysis tell us?” Morales asked. “It tells us when the water is not safe. What doesn’t it tell us? It doesn’t tell us when the water is good.”

Certifying water as safe, he said, requires much more extensive laboratory testing.

Still, official testing has now documented some of the same warning signs.

In late July, Jalisco health authorities confirmed that E. coli had been detected in 18 of 297 samples analyzed between March and June in neighborhoods affected by water-quality problems. Officials also acknowledged insufficient chlorination in some areas.

The findings came after months of complaints about yellow, brown or foul-smelling water, as well as sediment and service interruptions across the Guadalajara metropolitan area. González said the #ElSiapaQueQueremos campaign has now received nearly 1,500 complaints, with water quality by far the most common problem, followed by outages and high rates.

A multibillion-peso response

The Jalisco government and SIAPA, the metropolitan water utility, have acknowledged serious problems in the aging system and announced a long-term overhaul requiring more than 20 billion pesos in investment.

Among the major projects are the replacement of the aging Chapala-Guadalajara aqueduct and the modernization and expansion of Potabilizadora No. 1 in Miravalle. Governor Pablo Lemus said this month that the federal government had agreed to support both projects.

But for the citizen coalition, repairing infrastructure is only part of the solution.

The movement is increasingly focusing on who participates in decisions about the water system, how information is shared and whether communities themselves can have a formal role in monitoring and oversight.

That shift will be on display Sunday, when the same groups organizing the monitoring workshops will hold a “Mega March for Water.” Participants will gather at Parque Rojo at 10 a.m. and march along Avenida Juárez to Plaza Liberación, where the deliberately scatological “Agua KK Fest” — a play on caca, or “poop,” in reference to residents’ complaints about dirty water — will begin at noon.

The festival will combine protest with workshops on household filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets, urban gardens, community water systems and water-quality monitoring. Organizers describe the event as peaceful, family-oriented and nonpartisan.

Beyond fixing SIAPA

The coalition’s demands now extend beyond cleaner water. Its latest statement calls for greater transparency, citizen participation in decisions over water quality, distribution and infrastructure, formal recognition of community monitoring and protection of the watersheds that supply the metropolitan area.

It also proposes “public-community agreements” that would bring SIAPA, universities, neighborhood organizations, workers and other sectors together to share knowledge and participate in water governance.

The organizers explicitly reject privatization as the answer to SIAPA’s failures.

“The alternative to an inefficient SIAPA is not a privatized SIAPA,” their statement says, calling instead for a public utility that is transparent, efficient and subject to democratic social oversight.

González said the campaign is also pushing for a permanent working group focused specifically on water quality, health and sanitary risks. Authorities have not yet agreed to participate.

But organizers do not intend to wait indefinitely.

The group, González said, “is going to be established with authorities or without authorities,” functioning independently if necessary to prevent health risks.

That determination reflects how far the movement has come since residents first began showing up at public meetings with bottles of discolored water.

Morales said citizen monitoring allows residents to reach places government agencies may not sample and to turn individual experiences into systematic evidence. He has watched workshop participants take what they learn back to their neighborhoods — and then into the streets.

“It’s beautiful to see people who come to the workshops later at demonstrations with signs saying, ‘There are nitrates and nitrites in our water,’” he said.

“The authorities never expected that.”

World.title: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — August 23, 2026
World.content:

São Paulo · Nightlife

São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — August 23, 2026

If You Only Go to One Place Elba Ramalho — Free at Caixa Cultural A perfect Sunday note: one of Brazil’s great forró-and-MPB voices closes a three-night run in the centre, and it’s free. The show starts at 7 pm, early enough for a Sunday, and joyful enough to carry the weekend out on a high. It’s free and capacity is limited, so arrive well ahead and plan a rideshare home from the centre.

Tonight at a Glance —Elba Ramalho · Caixa Cultural A free show by the forró-and-MPB star, 7 pm in the centre — arrive early. —Roberto Carlos · Espaço Unimed (sold out) The legend plays an extra Sunday date, 8:30 pm — sold out, and both box offices are shut on Sundays. —CCBB & the museums · Centro / Paulista Sunday is the city’s culture day — MASP and the Pinacoteca are open; CCBB is between exhibitions. —Sunday wind-down Feijoada and samba by day, easy bars in Vila Madalena by night. —Quiet night: The big electronic rooms rest on Sundays — but Canto da Ema runs forró from 7 pm if you want a floor.

Tonight, Sunday 23 August 2026, São Paulo winds the weekend down gently. It’s the quietest night of the week — the big electronic rooms sit it out — but the pick is a lovely one: Elba Ramalho playing free in the centre, the last of three nights. Add a day among the museums, forró at Canto da Ema if you want to dance, and the easy bars of Vila Madalena, and Sunday has just enough without asking too much.

São Paulo after dark. Sunday is the city’s quietest night, and its best one for a free show. (Photo: Diego3336, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr)
