World.title: Dancing House Marks 30 Years With a Free Weekend of Dance in Prague
World.content:
Prague’s Dancing House will celebrate its 30th anniversary with a free two-day program of dance classes, performances and workshops on August 29 and 30.

Jiráskovo náměstí, next to the landmark on the Vltava embankment, will host a temporary stage and dance floor throughout the weekend.



The program will run from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both Saturday and Sunday.

Visitors can join professional instructors for classes in bachata, street dance and Latin American dance. There will also be sessions for children, dance demonstrations and opportunities to meet and talk with instructors.

The event is open to all levels, with participants able to watch performances or take part in the classes.

Weekend program

The schedule is the same on both days until the evening finale.

11:00 a.m. – Opening

11:05 a.m. – Children’s dance class

11:50 a.m. – Talk with the instructor

12:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

12:05 p.m. – Bachata class

12:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

1:00 p.m. – Street dance demonstration

1:05 p.m. – Street dance class

1:50 p.m. – Talk with the street dance instructor

2:00 p.m. – Latin American dance demonstration

2:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

2:50 p.m. – Talk with instructors

3:00 p.m. – Hat Jazz performance

3:05 p.m. – Children’s dance class

3:50 p.m. – Talk with the instructor

4:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

4:05 p.m. – Bachata class

4:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

5:00 p.m. – Street dance demonstration

5:05 p.m. – Street dance class

5:50 p.m. – Talk with the street dance instructor

6:00 p.m. – Latin American dance demonstration

6:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

6:50 p.m. – Talk with instructors

7:00 p.m. – Acrobatic performance

7:05 p.m. – Hula Hoops performance

The closing acrobatic performance will differ each day. Saturday will feature a handstand performance, while Sunday will bring Duo ReAct.

Admission is free. Organizers will also provide light refreshments.

Completed in 1996, the Dancing House is one of Prague’s best-known examples of modern architecture. It stands at the corner of Rašínovo nábřeží and Jiráskovo náměstí, overlooking the Vltava.

The building was designed by Croatian-Czech architect Vlado Milunić in collaboration with Canadian-American architect Frank Gehry. Its curved forms and leaning towers give the impression of a dancing couple, which inspired its Czech name, Tančící dům.

The building is also known by the nickname “Ginger and Fred,” referring to American dancers Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire.

World.title: Bolt Launches App-Free Ride Kiosks in the Czech Republic
World.content:
Bolt has introduced self-service kiosks in the Czech Republic that allow customers to order a ride without a smartphone, mobile data or the Bolt app.

The first kiosk is now operating at Westfield Chodov in Prague. A second will open at Westfield Černý Most on September 1. The company says it plans to consider other high-traffic locations in the future.



The kiosks use TapBox technology and provide access to the same Bolt driver network, pricing and safety standards available through the app.

Customers can place an order directly at the screen, making the service available to people who do not use smartphones or cannot access their phones at the time.

Both shopping centres have also introduced dedicated parking spaces for Bolt drivers collecting passengers. Customers are directed to these designated areas rather than having to meet drivers at potentially unsafe stopping points such as bus stops.

How Bolt kiosks work

Ordering a ride takes several steps. Customers enter their destination, select a ride category and provide their phone number. The available categories are Standard, Comfort, Premium and XL.

Payment is made by card. Once the booking is completed, the kiosk prints a confirmation and sends an SMS containing the vehicle details, estimated arrival time and instructions for finding the driver.

The kiosks operate around the clock and support Czech, English, German, French and Ukrainian.

Each ride booked through a kiosk carries an additional CZK 25 fee.

Bolt says the system could also benefit drivers by connecting them with customers who might otherwise be unable to use the app. The company expects the kiosks to reduce waiting times between rides at busy shopping centres and create additional opportunities for drivers.

The Czech launch follows the introduction of similar kiosks in Slovakia earlier this summer, including at airports.

World.title: Prague Adds 18 Kilometers of Cycle Routes but Cycling Numbers Barely Rise
World.content:
Prague is continuing to expand its cycling infrastructure, but the number of recorded bicycle journeys across the city has remained largely unchanged.

Automatic counters installed on major cycling routes recorded about 5.6 million passages in 2025, roughly 1 percent fewer than the previous year.

After adjusting for counter failures and temporary route closures, however, the Technical Road Administration (TSK) calculated a 0.4 percent increase in cycling traffic.



Prague Adds 18 Kilometers of Routes Away From Traffic

The city added 18 kilometers of two-way cycle paths and other cycling routes separated from motor traffic during the year. The total length of marked cycling routes increased by one kilometer to approximately 550 kilometers.

Routes separated from car traffic now account for 263 kilometers of the network, an increase of seven kilometers compared with the previous year.

TSK operates automatic counters at 31 locations on Prague’s main cycling routes. The devices use induction loops or radar to record cyclists and can determine their direction of travel.

The largest increase in two-way cycling routes came over the past year. Their combined length grew from 63 to 81 kilometers. These routes allow cyclists to travel in both directions on streets that are otherwise one-way for motor vehicles.

New two-way routes were added mainly in Prague 7 around Letná, in Prague 5 in Barrandov, and in Prague 6 around Na Petynce, Rozdělovská and Podbaba.

Modřany Remains Prague’s Busiest Cycling Route

The highest number of cyclists was recorded in Modřany, at the intersection of Vltavanů and U Kino streets. The counter registered 578,016 passages during the year.

Another 540,656 cycling journeys were recorded on Povltavská Street south of Troja Castle.

The largest year-on-year increase was recorded on the Barrandov Bridge, where cycling traffic rose following the completion of its more than two-year reconstruction.

World.title: “Upcycling” Prague: Old Offices and Industrial Sites Find New Life as Apartments
World.content:
Former offices, commercial properties and industrial sites in Prague are being converted into apartments rather than demolished, giving developers another option in a city struggling to build enough new homes.

The approach is sometimes described as “upcycling” — adapting ageing buildings for a new purpose while making use of structures and land that are already developed.

One recent example is in Pankrác, near Vyšehrad, where an office building has been converted into the Mo-cha HOME residential complex.



Developed by Cimex, the project opened this spring with 91 fully equipped apartments, most of them in the Czech 2+kk layout, consisting of a living room with a kitchenette and one separate bedroom.

Existing buildings offer valuable locations

Owners of older properties increasingly have to decide whether to renovate them, change their use or demolish them. Many were built for different needs and standards than those expected from buildings today.

Their locations, however, can be a major advantage. Older properties are often close to public transport, shops and other services, making them attractive for residential conversion.

Transforming an existing building can also be faster to prepare than developing a completely new project on a brownfield, although each property must be assessed individually.

The approach can preserve existing structures, reduce demolition and make better use of land that is already developed.

More former offices are becoming homes

Pankrác is not the only part of Prague where old buildings are being converted into housing.

In Holešovice, the former Tesla complex, once used for light-bulb production, has been transformed into a residential project with 149 apartments. The building had stood unused for years, but its main structure remained in relatively good condition.

In Prague 7, another former administrative building near Urania has also been adapted for residential use.

In Prague 3, PSN is preparing the reconstruction of a former telecommunications exchange on Fibichova Street. Built in 1926 and designed by architect Bohumír Kozák, the building is expected to become a rental housing project with 116 units.

One of the largest transformations is planned in Žižkov, where the functionalist former General Pension Institute will be converted into an apartment building with smaller units. The project received a building permit last year.

Not every older building is suitable for conversion. Technical condition, layout, location, project costs and future use all determine whether redevelopment makes economic and practical sense.

World.title: More Czech Companies Test Four-Day Work Weeks Despite Political Resistance
World.content:
A growing number of companies in the Czech Republic are experimenting with a four-day working week, with some reporting higher productivity and greater employee satisfaction.

But politicians remain reluctant to make the arrangement a standard option across the country.

Under the model, employees work four days instead of five while keeping their full salaries. Companies that have introduced the system say workers can maintain their output while having more time to rest.



At Trinity Group, the arrangement has been in place for five years. Jan Hanulík, the company’s product and marketing director, said productivity had risen despite employees working one day less each week.

“Although we have one working day less, productivity has increased,” Hanulík said, adding that the company’s results have roughly doubled since the system was introduced.

A survey cited in the report found that around 70 percent of employees in the Czech Republic would welcome a four-day working week.

Politicians remain cautious

The idea has already been adopted in different forms elsewhere in Europe. In Belgium, for example, employees can request to work their weekly hours over four days rather than five. The system therefore does not necessarily mean fewer working hours.

Czech politicians, however, argue that a single system would not work across all sectors.

Labor and Social Affairs Minister Aleš Juchelka of ANO said a legally mandated four-day week could create problems in areas already facing staff shortages, including social services and health care.

SPD lawmaker Lucie Šafránková also said the working week should reflect the conditions of individual professions and employers rather than follow one nationwide rule.

Czech companies are already experimenting

Several companies have introduced or tested four-day schedules, including SAB Finance, Phonexia, Sherpas, Digiskills and Café Eternity.

Not every experiment has lasted. The Cognito agency eventually returned to a traditional five-day working week after testing the shorter schedule.

World.title: Foreign Workers Now Make Up 22% of Czech Employees
World.content:
Foreign workers accounted for around 22% of all employees in the Czech Republic at the end of 2025, according to data from the Czech National Bank (ČNB).

Their number has nearly tripled over the past decade, rising from about 323,000 in 2015 to 935,000 last year.

The increase has significantly changed the makeup of the Czech labor market. Foreign workers represented roughly 8% of all employees in 2015. By the end of 2025, their share had reached 22%.

Ukrainians made up the largest group of foreign employees, with approximately 358,000 working in Czechia at the end of last year. Slovaks were the second-largest group, numbering almost 230,000.



The Czech labor market has also seen increasing numbers of workers from other countries outside the European Union, including the Philippines and India.

Foreign workers are particularly important in several sectors, including manufacturing, construction, retail, transport and hospitality.

Their presence is most pronounced in accommodation, food services and hospitality. Foreign nationals accounted for more than half of all employees in the sector at the end of 2025.

The figures should, however, be interpreted with some caution when comparing individual industries. The CNB notes that employment agencies can distort the sectoral breakdown.

Workers employed through agencies are recorded in official statistics under administrative and support services, even when their actual jobs are in manufacturing, construction, logistics or other industries.

World.title: Tesco Teams Up With Wolt. Can Express Delivery Save Its Czech Business?
World.content:
Tesco will launch a new express delivery service in Prague in September, working with Wolt to deliver orders within 40 minutes.

The service, called Tesco Hned, will initially be available from selected Tesco stores in the Czech capital.

The launch comes as speculation continues over a possible sale of Tesco’s Central European operations and the British retailer’s future in the Czech Republic.



Tesco Hned is designed for customers who need groceries and other everyday products quickly rather than as part of a larger planned shop. Orders will include food, drinks, cosmetics, household products, pet supplies and other goods.

The company says its standard online shopping service will continue to focus on larger orders, while the new option is aimed at customers who need a few items immediately.

Tesco has already tested the service at six Prague stores. It plans to extend Tesco Hned to another 22 locations in the coming weeks.

Delivery will be provided through Wolt, giving customers access to Tesco products through the courier company’s platform.

Tesco faces questions over its future

The new service comes at a difficult time for Tesco in Central Europe.

According to the Financial Times, Tesco’s British owners are considering selling their operations in the region, including the Czech Republic. The Schwarz Group, which owns Lidl and Kaufland, and Polish retailer Biedronka have reportedly been mentioned among potential buyers.

Tesco has not announced plans to leave the Czech market, and the launch of Tesco Hned suggests the company continues to invest in its services.

World.title: New Budget Airline to Launch Direct Flights from Prague to Santiago de Compostela
World.content:
A new budget airline is set to launch direct flights between Prague and Santiago de Compostela in Spain, giving travellers from the Czech capital a new low-cost option for visiting Galicia and the famous Camino de Santiago.

Fly2Galicia plans to begin operating flights from Santiago–Rosalía de Castro Airport to eight European destinations from December 1, 2026.



Prague is among the international destinations, alongside Brussels, Munich, Venice and Milan.

Tickets are already on sale, with fares from Prague to Santiago de Compostela starting at €51.

The new route could be particularly attractive in 2027, when Santiago de Compostela will celebrate a Holy Year. The occasion is expected to bring increased numbers of pilgrims completing the Camino de Santiago, one of Europe’s best-known pilgrimage routes.

There is, however, one detail to note: Fly2Galicia will not operate the initial flights itself. The airline says the routes will be operated by another European carrier, which has not yet been named.

The new service comes as airlines continue to expand connections between Central Europe and Spain. Wizz Air has also announced new flights to Santiago from Rome and Warsaw starting this December.

What to see in Santiago de Compostela

For travellers arriving from Prague, Santiago’s historic centre is the main attraction. Its UNESCO-listed Old Town combines Romanesque, Gothic, Baroque and Neoclassical architecture, with the Cathedral of Santiago at the heart of the city.

The Mercado de Abastos is another popular stop, offering fresh seafood and local produce. Galicia is also known for Albariño, a white wine that pairs particularly well with the region’s seafood.

Santiago can also serve as a base for exploring Galicia, with trips to A Coruña, Vigo and the Rías Baixas wine region, as well as the area’s beaches and islands.

World.title: Sunshine, storms and then scorching heat: Hungary braces for a sweltering end to August
World.content:
The final week of August will begin with moderately warm, pleasant summer weather, with daytime temperatures around 30°C and refreshing mornings. However, the heatwave will return in the second half of the week. Showers and thunderstorms may occur in several parts of Hungary on Tuesday, but most of the week is expected to be sunny and dry, according to a forecast from HungaroMet Zrt. sent to MTI on Sunday.

The beginning of the week

On Monday, cloudier areas will gradually clear and become more broken, followed by plenty of sunshine alongside high and developing cumulus clouds. The northern parts of the country may remain cloudier at times, with a chance of light rain or showers. Northerly winds may occasionally produce stronger gusts. Daytime temperatures will generally range from 26 to 32°C.

On Tuesday, cloud cover will increase significantly from the south-west and west. Showers and thunderstorms may occur in several parts of Transdanubia, with rain potentially spreading further east from the evening onwards. Southerly and south-easterly winds will occasionally strengthen in Transdanubia, while easterly and north-easterly winds will pick up elsewhere. Temperatures will rise from 9–19°C in the early morning to 26–33°C in the afternoon.

Wednesday and Thursday

By Wednesday morning, patches of fog and low cloud may form in western and south-western Hungary. Once these clear, sunny weather is expected across the country, with only a few cumulus and high clouds. A few showers may still occur in the morning, but no further rainfall is expected later in the day. Winds will generally remain moderate. Morning temperatures will range from 11 to 21°C, while afternoon highs will reach 27–32°C.

Thursday will be mostly clear and sunny, with only a few high and cumulus clouds and no rainfall expected. Winds will turn south-easterly and southerly and strengthen. Overnight lows will range from 9 to 19°C, while afternoon temperatures will reach 29–34°C.

The weekend

Friday is expected to be sunny with only a few clouds. No rain is expected during the day, although showers and thunderstorms may develop overnight in northern and north-western areas. South-westerly and southerly winds will strengthen across much of the country. Temperatures will range from 14–22°C in the morning to a scorching 32–38°C in the afternoon.

On Saturday, cloud cover will temporarily increase significantly, with scattered showers and thunderstorms likely. Winds will turn north-westerly and may become strong across large parts of the country. Early morning temperatures will range from 18 to 24°C, while afternoon highs will generally reach 28–34°C.

Sunday is expected to be mostly sunny, with no significant rainfall. North-westerly winds may bring occasional stronger gusts. Temperatures will range from 11–19°C in the morning to 25–30°C in the afternoon, according to HungaroMet (met.hu).

World.title: Former House Speaker Kövér accused of refusing handshake from Tisza deputy speaker at memorial ceremony
World.content:
A dispute has erupted over an alleged handshake snub involving former parliamentary speaker László Kövér and Krisztián Kőszegi, a Tisza Party MP and deputy speaker, at a memorial ceremony in Báta on Sunday.

Kőszegi said Kövér refused to shake his hand during the event commemorating the 500th anniversary of the national assembly held in Báta before the Battle of Mohács. He shared a photograph appearing to show himself extending his hand while Kövér keeps his hands in his lap.

The photograph does not establish whether Kövér ultimately refused the handshake or whether the two politicians shook hands at another point during the ceremony.

‘We would expect more dignity from a former speaker’

Kőszegi criticised the alleged gesture, saying: “We would expect more dignity from a former speaker.” He argued that the history of the Battle of Mohács should serve as a reminder of the consequences of division replacing cooperation in a country.

The Tisza politician said Kövér’s “deliberate turning away” only deepened the social divisions he believes Fidesz had deliberately created over the past 16 years. Kövér served as Speaker of the Hungarian Parliament from 2010 until 2026, when Fidesz lost power following the parliamentary election.

Current Speaker: ‘It is simply inhumane’

Ágnes Forsthoffer, the current Speaker of Parliament, also reacted to the incident in a Facebook post, describing the photograph as “shocking”. “There is no way to sugar-coat it, this is simply inhumane to me. Humiliating,” Forsthoffer wrote.

She said a handshake should not be treated as an ideological issue, but as a basic human gesture. “A handshake is not about party affiliation, but about seeing the person in the other person first,” she wrote.

Forsthoffer also claimed that Kövér left the parliamentary office without meeting her. According to her account, he did not consider it important to say a few words of appreciation to the office staff he had worked with for 16 years.

She said Kövér came to Parliament to say goodbye to the staff while she was still undergoing her preparation for the role of Speaker, and that she had been advised to leave the building during his visit. Forsthoffer thanked Kőszegi for representing Parliament at the memorial ceremony and added: “Thank you for extending your hand on my behalf as well.”

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

Fidesz does not deny the alleged snub

Fidesz communications director Bertalan Havasi was asked by Telex whether Kövér had indeed refused Kőszegi’s handshake and, if so, why. Havasi did not confirm the incident, but neither did he deny it. “I don’t know, I wasn’t there, and for that reason I wouldn’t disturb our party’s national council chairman on Sunday evening,” he said.

However, he went on to argue that, if the incident had happened, Kőszegi was a representative of the Tisza Party, which Fidesz accuses of undermining the democratic rule of law.

Havasi referred to Fidesz’s July “Declaration of Resistance”, in which the party declared its total opposition to what it described as Tisza’s “anti-democratic system”. He said Fidesz members and all Hungarians had the right to freely express their opposition to the Tisza Party and its representatives.

The exchange highlights the increasingly bitter political divide between Fidesz and Tisza, which has been in government since winning the April 2026 parliamentary election.

World.title: Hungary’s Kossuth Radio to relaunch on Monday with new ‘everyone’s radio’ slogan
World.content:
Hungary’s Kossuth Radio is set to relaunch on Monday with a completely revamped programme structure, new presenters and a new slogan promising that the public broadcaster will once again be “everyone’s”.

The renewed station will officially return on 24 August, with the Rákóczi March marking the start of its new public-service programming at 4.30 AM. The station’s new slogan will be “Kossuth Radio – everyone’s again”, according to a statement from Hungary’s public media operator, MTVA.

The broadcaster said the station had spent the past month and a half broadcasting radio plays and “timeless, emblematic” interviews around the clock while its new programming was being prepared. Channel director György Kerényi said the station would preserve what was worth keeping while saying goodbye to programmes and formats that had become tired.

News and current affairs to be revamped

News programmes and several key time slots will undergo major changes. The station says its new approach will focus on reliable reporting, credible stories and knowledgeable guests, promising that its “news will be true, our stories will be authentic and our guests will be knowledgeable.”

Several new programmes will also be available as podcasts, while the station says some of its content will even be broadcast through traditional Sokol radios. Zsolt Bogár and Péter Magyari will serve as the station’s two deputy editors-in-chief.

Magyari, who previously worked for Válasz Online, will launch Nyílt titok (Open Secret) on Saturday mornings. The programme will examine controversial cases from Hungary’s past 16 years – and, according to the station, the past 36 years – with investigative reporters Róbert Báthory and Áron Kovács.

Magyari will also host Világrend (World Order), a foreign affairs analysis programme due to launch on 29 August.

The morning news and information programme Felkelő, the Krónikák news bulletins and daily current affairs programmes will be presented by Rita Benyó, Erika Hatvani Tóth, Tímea Tatár and Nóra Teszári.

György Farkas, László Illisz, István Dániel Király and Gábor Kiss will work as editors, while Dávid Dercsényi, Mátyás Fórizs, Anna Kovács, Roland Papp and Ildikó Sipos will work on the news programmes. Pálma Fazekas will head the news department.

If you missed it: Hungary’s revamped public broadcaster launches new flagship news bulletin with a surprising shift

New programmes focus on different perspectives

The revamped station will also introduce programmes covering current affairs from different perspectives. Necces, an afternoon live programme hosted by Csilla Orosz and Zsófia Sashegyi, will examine public affairs through a female perspective.

Sunday mornings will feature two new programmes focusing on Hungarians living beyond the country’s borders and religious affairs.

Anyanyelve még mindig magyar (Hungarian Is Still Their Mother Tongue) will air from 7 AM and will be hosted by Vince Rácz, a journalist at Pátria Radio, the Slovak public broadcaster’s Hungarian-language service in Bratislava.

Hetedik nap (Seventh Day) will focus on religious and church-related issues and will be hosted by journalist Dóra Laborczi. The station also plans to significantly expand its cultural programming and radio plays.

Anita Bödő will head the revamped cultural department, while new daily programmes will include Doktor Kossuth, focusing on health, and A Föld marad (The Earth Remains), dedicated to sustainability and environmental issues.

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

Kossuth Radio seeks a new identity

The relaunch comes after years in which Kossuth Radio and Hungary’s wider public media system were heavily criticised by opposition figures and independent media for serving as a vehicle for the former Fidesz government’s political messaging.

Former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was a regular guest on the station’s Friday morning Jó reggelt, Magyarország! programme, where his appearances were frequently described as interviews despite rarely involving challenging follow-up questions.

The public media system itself underwent a turbulent transition earlier this summer. On 7 July, Hungary’s public media broadcasts were temporarily interrupted as an interim management team took over, with the M1 television channel displaying an apology message for an extended period.

World.title: Rare ‘water devil’ filmed on the Danube in Hungary – video
World.content:
A remarkable weather phenomenon was captured on video near Ráckeve after a swirling dust devil moved from the riverbank over the Danube and briefly transformed into a spectacular ‘water devil’.

The unusual scene was filmed by Péter Tóth, a member of the Pilis Park Forest team, who had originally gone to the Danube to document the river’s exceptionally low water level. Instead, he ended up recording a rare and striking atmospheric phenomenon.

Dust devil turns into water vortex

Tóth was working in the Ráckeve area when he noticed a small swirling column of air and dust on the riverbank. At first, he was unsure whether the phenomenon was worth filming. But when he realised that the rotating vortex was moving directly towards the Danube, he reached for his phone.

As the vortex reached the water, it began lifting droplets from the river, creating a spectacular swirling column above the surface. Tóth later described the sound of the falling water droplets as resembling a fountain operating in the middle of the river.

Although the phenomenon itself was relatively small and disappeared within a short time, it left behind a clearly visible disturbance on the Danube. According to Tóth, the vortex created waves similar to those produced by a small boat passing through the water.

What is a water devil?

The term “water devil” is commonly used to describe a short-lived rotating column of air over a body of water. However, such phenomena should not automatically be confused with a tornado or a classic waterspout.

Small vortices can form close to the surface when local heating, rising air and particular wind conditions combine. A dust devil developing over land can also move over water, as appears to have happened near Ráckeve.

Humidity, air movement, surface temperatures and local wind conditions can all influence the development of these vortices. Their appearance can be spectacular despite their typically short lifespan.

Can a water devil be dangerous?

According to Kemma, a small, short-lived water vortex is generally much weaker than a conventional tornado, but it can still pose a risk to people nearby. For small boats and kayaks in particular, sudden rotating winds, waves and disturbed water can create dangerous conditions.

The precise meteorological classification of the phenomenon filmed near Ráckeve cannot be established from the footage alone. What is clear, however, is that the vortex was strong enough to lift water from the Danube and create noticeable waves that remained visible even after the swirling column disappeared.

The extraordinary footage also provided an unexpected glimpse of nature at work during a period when the Danube has been making headlines for a very different reason: its exceptionally low water level.

World.title: Motorcyclist saves choking boy on Hungarian road after dozens of cars drive past
World.content:
A young motorcyclist has been praised for saving a choking child on Hungary’s Route 4 after reportedly being the only person to stop and help as around 30 cars passed the distressed family.

The incident happened on Friday on the stretch of Route 4 between Nyíregyháza and Kisvárda, according to the National Ambulance Service. The boy had been travelling in the back seat of his family’s car when he suddenly choked on food and began struggling to breathe.

His mother pulled over and got out of the vehicle with her son, but said she completely froze in the stressful situation. Then a motorcyclist stopped.

Motorcyclist immediately stepped in

The motorcyclist took the choking child and began providing first aid. He continued until the obstruction was cleared and the boy was able to breathe again. The whole incident happened so quickly that the family did not even manage to ask the motorcyclist his name before he left.

The National Ambulance Service subsequently shared the family’s account and praised the unknown passer-by for stepping in when help was urgently needed. The service said it was proud of members of the public who have the courage to act and provide assistance in an emergency.

The motorcyclist was later identified as Attila Horváth, who came forward in a Facebook video and confirmed that he was the person who had helped the boy.

“I’m not a hero”

Horváth said he had asked the boy’s mother to remove the appeal looking for him because he did not want the incident to become a sensation. According to the motorcyclist, helping someone in danger should be an everyday and natural thing to do.

He said he regularly travels between 20,000 and 40,000 kilometres a year and often encounters broken-down cars or people lying on the roadside while other motorists simply continue driving.

“This time, around 30 cars went past us, and nobody stopped to help,” he said.

Horváth also pointed out that basic first aid, including the Heimlich manoeuvre, is taught as part of obtaining a driving licence. He urged people not to automatically assume that someone lying by the roadside is drunk. The person could have suffered a head injury, a stroke or a heart attack, and the intervention of a passer-by could save their life.

“This doesn’t make anyone a hero. I’m not a hero either,”

Horváth said, arguing that paramedics, firefighters and police officers who risk their own lives to save others are the real heroes. Simply being in the right place at the right time and offering assistance, he said, should not be treated as extraordinary.

“If one person listens, we’ve succeeded”

Horváth asked people not to simply like his video, but to share it so that its message about helping others reaches as many people as possible. “If just one person takes this to heart and we save another life, then we’ve ended the day successfully,” he said.

The National Ambulance Service also said it wanted to find the motorcyclist after hearing the family’s story. What began as a search for an unknown passer-by has now ended with the family learning the identity of the person who intervened when their young son was unable to breathe. The incident is also a reminder that in an emergency, stopping to help can make the difference between life and death.

World.title: Best shopping malls in Budapest: Where to shop in 2026
World.content:
Looking for the best shopping mall in Budapest? The Hungarian capital has everything from huge shopping centres packed with international brands to modern malls with cinemas, restaurants and supermarkets. Whether you are visiting Budapest, living here as an expat or simply looking for the widest choice of shops, this guide compares the best shopping malls in Budapest, where to find them and which one to choose.

Budapest may be famous for its historic boulevards, markets and elegant shopping streets, but shopping malls remain an important part of everyday life in the Hungarian capital. They are particularly useful when the weather turns cold or rainy – or when you simply want fashion, electronics, food, entertainment and everyday essentials under one roof.

But which shopping mall in Budapest is best for you?

Best shopping malls in Budapest at a glance

If you do not have time to compare them all, here is the short answer:

Westend – best for a central location and huge selection

Arena Mall – best for fashion and a large modern shopping experience

Etele Plaza – best modern mall in Buda

Allee – best all-round choice in Buda

ÁRKÁD Budapest – excellent for everyday shopping and a broad selection

Mammut – best if you are around Széll Kálmán tér

All of them are accessible by public transport, so tourists generally do not need a car.

Westend City Centre – Best central shopping mall in Budapest

Shopping mall Budapest guide: Best places for shops, restaurants and city convenience. Photo: WestEnd

If location matters most, Westend is difficult to beat.

The shopping centre stands directly beside Nyugati railway station and is easily accessible by Metro M3, tram 4/6 and numerous buses and trolleybuses. Its location on the edge of central Budapest makes it particularly convenient for tourists.

Westend offers a very large selection of fashion, beauty, electronics, services, restaurants and cafés. According to the shopping centre’s official information, Westend has nearly 400 shops and more than 50 food and beverage outlets.

There is also a cinema and a rooftop garden, providing a break from the indoor shopping environment. For visitors staying in central Pest, Westend is often the easiest major mall to reach.

Best for: tourists, central location, large selection

Location: Váci út 1–3, District 6

Shopping centre: daily 08:00–22:00

Shops: Monday–Saturday 10:00–20:00; Sunday 10:00–18:00

Shopping mall Budapest guide: Best places for shops, restaurants and city convenience. Photo: WestEnd Shopping mall Budapest guide: Best places for shops, restaurants and city convenience. Photo: WestEnd

Aréna Mall – Best for fashion and a large selection of shops

Arena Mall is another strong contender for the title of best shopping mall in Budapest, especially if fashion is your priority.

Located near Keleti railway station, the complex combines a large retail area with restaurants, cafés, a supermarket and Cinema City. It is particularly useful if you want to compare a large number of fashion and lifestyle stores without travelling between different parts of Budapest.

According to Arena Mall’s official opening hours, the shopping mall is open from 10:00 to 21:00 from Monday to Saturday and from 10:00 to 19:00 on Sunday. Restaurants, cafés, the cinema and other businesses may operate different hours.

Best for: fashion, international brands, cinema

Location: Kerepesi út 9, District 8

Shops: Monday–Saturday 10:00–21:00; Sunday 10:00–19:00

Shopping mall Budapest guide: Best places for shops, restaurants and city convenience. Photo: Aréna Mall

Allee Bevásárlóközpont – One of the best shopping malls in Buda

Allee is another excellent option on the Buda side of the Danube and arguably one of the most convenient all-round malls for people living in District 11. Located close to Móricz Zsigmond körtér and Újbuda-központ, it is served by Metro M4 as well as numerous trams and buses.

Allee combines fashion and lifestyle stores with restaurants, cafés, a cinema and an Interspar supermarket. It is generally a better choice than travelling across Budapest if you are already staying in southern Buda.

Best for: Buda, everyday shopping, dining

Location: Október huszonharmadika utca 8–10, District 11

Shops: Monday–Saturday 10:00–21:00; Sunday 10:00–19:00

Shopping mall Budapest guide: Best places for shops, restaurants and city convenience. Photo: Allee Shopping mall Budapest guide: Best places for shops, restaurants and city convenience. Photo: Allee

Etele Plaza – One of Budapest’s most modern shopping malls

Shopping mall Budapest guide: Best places for shops, restaurants and city convenience. Photo: Etele Plaza

Opened in 2021, Etele Plaza is one of the newest major shopping centres in Budapest. It sits next to Kelenföld railway station and the M4 metro terminus, making it exceptionally easy to reach from central Budapest as well as from western Hungary.

The modern complex includes fashion and lifestyle stores, restaurants, cafés, a supermarket, cinema and fitness facilities. This makes Etele particularly useful for visitors staying on the Buda side or travellers passing through Kelenföld.

The plaza itself is accessible from 06:00 to 22:00, but this should not be confused with individual shop opening hours, which may vary.

Best for: modern design, Buda, Kelenföld travellers

Location: Hadak útja 1, District 11

Shopping mall Budapest guide: Best places for shops, restaurants and city convenience. Photo: Etele Plaza

ÁRKÁD Budapest – A major shopping centre in eastern Budapest

ÁRKÁD deserves a place on the list because it serves a different part of the city from Westend, Arena, Allee and Etele. Located at Örs vezér tere, the terminus of Metro M2, it offers a broad range of fashion, beauty, electronics, services and dining options. The neighbouring Sugár shopping centre adds even more options within the same area.

ÁRKÁD is particularly convenient if you live or stay in the eastern part of Budapest.

According to ÁRKÁD Budapest’s official opening information, the centre is open from 10:00 to 21:00 Monday to Saturday and from 10:00 to 19:00 on Sunday. Individual restaurants, supermarkets and services can have different opening hours.

Best for: eastern Budapest, everyday shopping, broad selection

Location: Örs vezér tere 25/A, District 10

Shops: Monday–Saturday 10:00–21:00; Sunday 10:00–19:00

Mammut – Best shopping mall near Széll Kálmán tér

Mammut is one of the best-known shopping centres on the Buda side and is particularly convenient for anyone staying around Széll Kálmán tér, the Castle District or northern Buda.

The complex contains shops, restaurants, services, a supermarket and cinemas. Its greatest advantage for visitors is location: Széll Kálmán tér is one of Buda’s most important public transport hubs and is served by Metro M2 and several major tram lines.

According to Mammut’s official information, stores are open from 10:00 to 21:00 Monday to Saturday and from 10:00 to 18:00 on Sunday. Restaurants generally stay open later.

Best for: central Buda, Széll Kálmán tér, cinema and everyday shopping

Location: Lövőház utca 2–6, District 2

Shops: Monday–Saturday 10:00–21:00; Sunday 10:00–18:00

Which is the biggest shopping mall in Budapest?

For visitors, the more useful question is often not simply which mall has the largest floor area, but which offers the best combination of shops, location and accessibility. Westend and Arena Mall are among the city’s major shopping destinations and both provide extensive retail and dining options.

If you are staying in central Pest, Westend will usually be the most convenient. If your priority is fashion and spending several hours shopping, Arena Mall is another strong choice. On the Buda side, Etele Plaza and Allee are usually more practical.

What is the best shopping mall in Budapest for tourists?

For most tourists, we would choose Westend. Its biggest advantage is location. It sits beside Nyugati railway station and close to the Grand Boulevard, with excellent public transport connections to other parts of Budapest.

You do not need to dedicate half a day to reaching it, and you can easily combine shopping there with sightseeing in central Pest. However, the answer changes depending on where you are staying:

Central Pest: Westend

Near Keleti station: Arena Mall

Southern Buda: Allee or Etele Plaza

Central/northern Buda: Mammut

Eastern Budapest: ÁRKÁD

Where to find luxury shopping in Budapest

Shopping malls are not necessarily the best answer if you are looking specifically for luxury brands. For upscale shopping, central Budapest – particularly the area around Andrássy Avenue and Deák Ferenc Street/Fashion Street – may be more suitable than a conventional shopping centre.

For mainstream international fashion, however, Budapest’s major malls generally provide a much wider selection in one place.

Are shopping malls in Budapest open on Sundays?

Yes. Major Budapest shopping malls are generally open on Sundays, although Sunday opening hours are often shorter. For example, Arena Mall and ÁRKÁD currently list regular Sunday shop hours of 10:00–19:00, while Mammut’s stores close at 18:00.

Individual supermarkets, restaurants, cinemas and other services can have different schedules.

Are Budapest shopping malls open on public holidays?

Do not assume they are. On Hungarian public holidays, retail stores can be closed even when restaurants, cinemas or other entertainment businesses in the same complex operate.

For example, Arena Mall announced that its commercial units would be closed on 24 and 25 May 2026, while the restrictions did not apply to hospitality and entertainment establishments. If you plan to go shopping on a Hungarian public holiday, always check the mall’s official opening information before travelling.

When is the best time to visit a Budapest shopping mall?

Weekday mornings and early afternoons are generally the easiest times if you want to avoid the busiest periods. Late afternoons, Friday evenings and weekends tend to attract more shoppers. During the Christmas period and major sales, central malls can become considerably busier.

Shopping centres are also useful alternatives on extremely hot, cold or rainy days, particularly for travellers looking for an indoor programme.

Shopping malls or shopping streets: Which is better in Budapest?

It depends on what you are looking for. Choose a shopping mall if you want many stores, restaurants, a supermarket and entertainment in one building. They are also convenient when the weather is poor.

Choose central shopping streets if shopping is part of your sightseeing experience. Váci Street, Fashion Street and Andrássy Avenue put you closer to Budapest’s historic centre, cafés and major attractions. For practical shopping rather than sightseeing, the major malls are usually easier.

Best shopping malls in Budapest: The bottom line

There is no single best shopping mall in Budapest for every visitor. Westend is our pick for tourists who want a large mall in a central location. Arena Mall is a strong choice for fashion and a broad retail selection, while Etele Plaza offers one of the city’s most modern shopping environments. On the Buda side, Allee is an excellent all-round option, while Mammut is particularly convenient around Széll Kálmán tér. In eastern Budapest, ÁRKÁD provides another major shopping hub.

The most important consideration is location. Budapest has an extensive public transport network, so choosing the best-connected mall from your hotel or accommodation will often save more time than travelling across the city for one particular shopping centre.

If you missed it: New shopping centre to be built next to one of Hungary’s busiest motorways

The bottom line

Whether you are looking for fashion, gifts or simply a comfortable place to eat, a shopping mall in Budapest offers a stress-free alternative to busy high streets. With long hours, varied shops and plenty of restaurants, these modern retail destinations make city shopping easy for both tourists and residents.

World.title: “The defence minister’s smile is not sincere!”: PM Magyar jokes as ministers’ boat loses power on the Danube
World.content:
A boat carrying Hungary’s defence and economy ministers was briefly left drifting on the Danube after its engine broke down during a live-broadcast inspection of the Paks nuclear power plant’s emergency river works.

The unusual incident occurred on Sunday morning as Prime Minister Péter Magyar and his ministers were inspecting the construction of a bottom sill designed to raise the Danube’s water level near the Paks Nuclear Power Plant.

Magyar and his ministers had earlier held a press conference about the progress of the river works and the gradual restart of the plant’s turbines. Afterwards, the prime minister invited journalists to join him on a boat tour of the construction site.

Ministers’ boat falls behind

Magyar travelled in one boat, while journalists followed in another. Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi and Economy Minister István Kapitány were travelling together in a separate boat behind the prime minister.

During the live broadcast, it soon became apparent that the ministers’ boat was falling behind. The reason was rather less dramatic than the footage initially suggested: its engine had broken down, leaving the boat drifting on the river.

Magyar, who briefly took over the camera from his operator during the tour and provided a running commentary, eventually noticed the problem. He asked whether it was normal for the defence minister to be drifting away on the Danube with nobody apparently coming to his rescue.

An army colonel at the scene responded: “Reporting, they have been rescued.”

The two ministers were subsequently brought safely to shore aboard another boat. As Ruszin-Szendi stepped ashore, Magyar could not resist a joke about the incident.

“The defence minister’s smile isn’t sincere!” the prime minister quipped.

Magyar welcoming Ruszin-Szendi to the shore. Screenshot: Facebook/Péter Magyar

Magyar welcoming Kapitány to the shore. Screenshot: Facebook/Péter Magyar

New 1956 memorial planned for 70th anniversary

During the same press conference at Paks, Magyar also announced plans for a new, larger memorial site dedicated to the 1956 Revolution ahead of its 70th anniversary in 2026. The prime minister said he wanted Hungary to have a more substantial and dignified memorial than the existing sites in Budapest.

He said he would ask Hungarian companies to contribute voluntarily to the project, drawing a comparison with the private donations made by wealthy French individuals and companies following the 2019 Notre-Dame fire in Paris.

According to Magyar, Hungarian businesses are now also beginning to take greater responsibility for national causes. He argued that the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Revolution should provide an opportunity for companies of all sizes to contribute to a shared national commemoration.

He said there should be a culture in which the private sector feels that the country is also “its own”, adding that joint celebrations could carry an important symbolic message.

Government funding criticised

Magyar also criticised the previous government over spending on national commemorations. He claimed that despite large amounts being spent on national events, the planned renovation of the memorial park for the 500th anniversary of the Battle of Mohács had not been completed.

He also said only a few hundred million forints remained in the budget for this year’s 23 October commemorations and that no plan had been prepared for a new 1956 memorial.

In Magyar’s view, Budapest currently lacks a sufficiently suitable monument to the 1956 Revolution. He said neither the steel columns at Ötvenhatosok Square nor the House of Terror adequately fulfils that role.

The prime minister said he would therefore write to major Hungarian businesses and ask them to contribute to the construction costs of a new, large-scale memorial ahead of the revolution’s 70th anniversary.

World.title: Budapest spoiled you: why the Airport you land at won’t work like the one you left
World.content:
There is a small piece of civilization at Budapest Airport that most Hungarian travelers never think about until they leave the country: the taxi rank. One contracted provider, a city-regulated tariff, a printed receipt at a marked queue. You land, you join the line, you pay what the meter says, and the number is the same for you as for the businessman ahead of you. It is so orderly that it becomes invisible.

Collaborative content

And that is precisely the problem. Travelers from Budapest step off long-haul flights in New York, Miami or Punta Cana carrying an assumption they don’t know they’re carrying: that every airport works like BUD. Almost none of them do.

What the rest of the world actually looks like

Land at a large American airport and there is no single contracted provider waiting in a tidy line. There are ride-hailing apps whose prices surge exactly when flights bunch together — the same ride costing double at nine in the evening that it costs at nine in the morning. There are taxi queues that stretch past an hour at peak times. At some terminals, app-based pickups have been moved to garages or remote lots a signposted walk away, arrangements that shift with construction. And hovering around the arrivals hall of many airports in the Americas is a figure that simply does not exist at Budapest: the tout, offering a “taxi” at a price he will decide later.

At beach destinations popular with Hungarian travelers, the picture has its own flavor. Arrive in the Caribbean at the peak of charter season and transport demand spikes with every landing wave; the traveler who planned nothing negotiates tired, in the sun, in a currency they haven’t used before, with their luggage as a visible signal that they have no alternative.

None of this is a reason to stay home. It is a reason to plan the one leg of the trip that Budapest never taught you to plan.

The thirty kilometers nobody budgets for

A Hungarian traveler will compare long-haul fares across three booking sites, track them for weeks, and celebrate saving fifteen thousand forints. Then they land after twelve hours of flying and hand back that entire saving — sometimes several times over — at the airport curb, because the ground leg was never part of the plan. The flight was optimized; the last thirty kilometers were improvised.

The fix that has emerged across the travel industry is simple: book the ground transfer the way you book the flight — in advance, at a fixed price, from your sofa in Budapest. Transpovia, an airport transfer platform covering airports across the United States, the Caribbean and Latin America — including JFK and Newark in New York, Miami, Orlando, Punta Cana and Bogotá — is built on exactly this model: the price is fixed at booking, the driver tracks your flight number and adjusts to delays automatically, and instead of hunting for a pickup zone, you walk out to a driver holding a sign with your name.

For anyone raised on Budapest’s orderly system, the appeal is easy to explain: it recreates abroad the thing you took for granted at home — a known price and a predictable process — at airports that offer neither by default.

Three habits worth packing

Book the arrival transfer with the flight, not after landing. The planning-phase version of you compares calmly; the arrivals-hall version of you accepts whatever is in front of you. Every trick of the airport curb — surge pricing, touts, “special price for you” — works only on the second version.

Check the total, not the headline. Wherever you book, confirm the quoted price includes tolls, airport fees and waiting time after landing. A fixed price that quietly excludes the toll road into the city is not fixed.

Keep the Budapest rule with you everywhere: legitimate transport never comes looking for you. At BUD, the real taxis wait at the rank. Abroad, the real drivers wait at a marked zone or hold a name sign in arrivals. Anyone approaching you inside a terminal — on any continent — is not the official option.

The souvenir worth bringing home

There is a quiet irony in all of this. Hungarian travelers often come back from the Americas with stories about the chaos of getting out of the airport — the queue, the surge price, the driver who appeared from nowhere. The travelers who pre-book come back without that story, which is exactly the point. The best arrival is the one you don’t remember, because nothing happened: a sign with your name, a fixed price you already paid in forints’ worth of certainty, and a car door closing on the noise.

Budapest spoiled you. The trick is refusing to be unspoiled the moment you fly somewhere else.

World.title: Less than half of Romanians manage to save regularly, survey finds
World.content:
Roughly 48% of Romanians are able to put away money every month or most months, while a quarter manage to put money aside only occasionally, when they have funds left, according to a survey conducted at the initiative of tbi bank on a sample of 1,223 employees nationwide.

The survey, published on Friday, August 21, shows that Romanians’ real savings capacity remains limited and vulnerable to increasing pressures on the monthly budget.

Roughly 22% of respondents currently do not save at all or are forced to draw on previously accumulated reserves. Moreover, about 46% manage to save no more than RON 500 in a typical month, and 16% are unable to set aside any money at all.

The ability to save remains moderate even among those who manage to put money aside: almost 22% save between 11% and 20% of income, and just over 22% manage to keep between 6% and 10%.

“For many Romanians, saving remains the result of a fragile balance at the end of the month rather than a consistent financial plan. The increase in essential costs limits the amounts available, and this makes financial discipline, access to simple and safe products and the formation of savings habits increasingly important,” said Gergana Staykova, Market Leader, tbi bank Romania.

The ability to save has deteriorated for an important part of Romanians in the last period. Almost 42% say they save less than last year, and over 9% managed to put money aside previously, but currently they can no longer do so. At the same time, more than 29% save primarily for unforeseen situations or emergencies, and about 20% aim to build more security and financial independence.

Over 36% say they save only what they have left after covering expenses, while only about 15% set aside a fixed percentage of their monthly income. At the same time, almost 23% could cover their expenses for less than a month if they lost their main source of income, and about 22% could cover their expenses for between one and three months.

Romanians keep their savings mainly in forms perceived as safe and easy to access. Over 23% keep most of their savings in their current account, and almost 22% choose bank deposits. At the same time, more than 26% point to the increase in the price of food and basic products as the main obstacle to saving, and almost 25% say that income is too low in relation to expenses.

Savings are used both for planned experiences and needs, and as a reserve for unforeseen expenses. Almost 19% of Romanians have used or would have liked to use their savings for vacations and personal experiences, and over 14% for home or car repairs. The financial targets for 2026 are mainly geared towards strengthening reserves and protecting personal stability, amid fears related in particular to health and income. Almost 20% of Romanians aim to save more than last year, and almost 15% want to protect their existing savings. At the same time, more than 30% point to health problems as their biggest financial fear, and 21% primarily fear losing their job.

The tbi bank survey on how Romanians manage their money in 2026 was conducted online in July this year, on a total sample of 1,223 internet users in Romania, of which over 53% are men, 68% work in the private sector, and over 31% have a net income of over RON 6,000.

World.title: Romania’s real estate investment volume falls to EUR 300 million in H1 2026 - report
World.content:
Romania’s real estate investment market recorded transactions worth approximately EUR 300 million in the first half of 2026, down from around EUR 400 million in the same period last year, according to a Colliers report. The consultancy estimates that the full-year volume could approach EUR 1 billion if several large transactions currently underway are completed.

Romania accounted for roughly 5% of the EUR 5.8 billion invested across the six largest Central and Eastern European economies: Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Romania, and Slovakia.

Regional investment increased by 7% year-on-year and exceeded both the five-year average of EUR 4.6 billion and the ten-year average of EUR 5.1 billion. Colliers expects the regional total to reach EUR 12.5-13 billion in 2026, compared with EUR 11.6 billion last year.

“The decline in transaction volumes in Romania during the period under review should be seen in a broader context,” said Robert Miklo, partner and head of capital markets at Colliers.

He noted that several deals are in progress, while the sale of a MAS retail portfolio to AFI Europe was completed shortly after the end of the reporting period, shifting the transaction into the third quarter.

“If other large transactions currently in progress are also completed, 2026 has the potential to close with investment volumes of close to EUR 1 billion, which would make it only the second year since 2007 in which the market has reached this threshold,” Miklo said.

Office properties generated approximately 60% of Romania’s transaction volume during the first half, their highest share since 2022. Colliers expects that percentage to decline as major deals in other sectors are completed during the remainder of the year.

“Influenced by the limited supply of properties available for sale, investment volumes remain below the level suggested by both investor appetite and the size of the local economy. In the first half of the year, Romania attracted just 5.4% of the investment volume recorded across the six largest economies in the region, despite accounting for almost 18% of their combined GDP. This gap shows that the local market still has substantial room for growth,” added Robert Miklo.

In Bucharest, prime yields stood at approximately 7.5% for offices, 7.75% for industrial and logistics properties, and 7.25% for shopping centers. These levels remained above those recorded in Warsaw, Prague, and Bratislava.

Colliers said investors are increasingly prioritizing assets with stable income, good energy performance, and clear long-term value prospects. Properties with weaker energy performance face tighter lending standards and lower demand.

“Financing conditions are favorable, but the advantage lies with high-quality properties with stable income, credible sponsors, and clear sustainability strategies,” Miklo said.

Across Central and Eastern Europe, Poland led the market with more than EUR 3 billion in transactions, representing 52% of the regional total. The Czech Republic followed with more than EUR 1.4 billion, while Hungary recorded close to EUR 600 million.

Offices accounted for 29% of regional investment, followed by retail at 27%, residential at 19%, and industrial and logistics assets at 17%.

World.title: Romanian animated short film selected in UK’s Official Encounters Competition
World.content:
Happy New Year, the Romanian animated short film directed by Radu Gaciu and produced by Adriana Bumbeș through Ariadna Films, has been selected for the Official Competition of the Encounters Film Festival. The film will have its world premiere on September 23, 2026, at Watershed in Bristol.

The film, set in 2009 in Romania, follows a woman who returns home on her birthday to the isolated cabin in the mountains where she spent part of her youth with her twin sister. She rediscovers a space where memory and dreams intertwine and where echoes of the past speak of the pain of separation.

With a running time of 25 minutes, Happy New Year is a fantasy drama made using a mixed 2D digital animation technique.

Encounters is a qualifying festival for the BAFTA, BIFA and European Film Awards and also gives filmmakers the chance to enter the race for the Academy Awards, in the Best Animated Short Film category. The film is eligible for the Animated Encounters Grand Prix and the Audience Award.

The movie was built over five years of work, two years of pre-production and three years of production. The animation was based on more than 60,000 reference photographs, used to build the characters and backgrounds. The project brought together a team of more than 25 people, from actresses and screenwriters to production, sound and image specialists. The film’s visual universe was created from several thousand digitally made elements, characters and backgrounds, complemented by almost 100 unique watercolor paintings.

“The film’s animation technique is mixed, a combination of digital drawing, rotoscoping and collage, in which both the characters and the settings are stylistically rendered realistically. The characters are predominantly digital drawings that were later animated or, in a few cases, rotoscoped, also digitally. The backgrounds are complex collages of adjusted photographs composed with the help of additional graphic elements,” director Radu Gaciu said.

The lead role is voiced by Ana Ularu, one of the Romanian actresses with the most solid and visible international career. The voice cast is completed by Ana-Maria Guran, Clara Angela Roman and Oana Rotaru.

The project’s journey began at the Animest International Festival, where Happy New Year won the 2020 edition of the Pitch, Please! competition. The award took the project to the CEE Animation Forum 2021. The project continued its development and production in Romania, received production support from the National Cinematography Center, and was completed on January 31, 2026.

The film is produced by Ariadna Films. The screenplay is by Radu Gaciu and Nicoleta Colopelnic, while the producer is Adriana Bumbeș.

The film’s original music was specially composed by Matei Vasilache.

World.title: President Nicușor Dan to lead Romania’s delegation to UN General Assembly
World.content:
President Nicușor Dan will lead Romania’s delegation to the high-level segment of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, which will take place in New York next month, according to an announcement from the Presidential Administration.

The central theme of the next UN session is 'Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all.'

The head of state will deliver the national statement in the plenary session of the UN General Assembly on September 23. He will highlight Romania’s efforts to support the organization’s reform process and the country’s contribution to ensuring peace, security and an international order based on rules and norms, according to the same source.

This is the first time president Nicușor Dan will attend the UN General Assembly. Last year, Romania was represented by foreign minister Oana Țoiu. Dan explained at the time that he did not go to New York because he considered it “more useful” to be present in the country.

At the next UN assembly, the president will also participate in New York in events organized on the sidelines of the high-level segment. He will hold bilateral meetings with other heads of state or government, including to support Romania’s candidacy for the leadership of the International Organisation of La Francophonie.

Former European Commissioner Dacian Cioloș is supported by Romania for the position of Secretary General of the OIF.

radu@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: presidency.ro)

World.title: Environment Ministry says Romania exceeded PNRR target with over 5,000 recycling islands completed
World.content:
Romania has completed 5,091 digitized recycling islands nationwide, exceeding its target of 5,000 under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), the Environment Ministry announced. The investment’s total budget is EUR 72.75 million.

The waste collection systems have been installed across 36 counties, with Bacău, Bihor, Arad, Cluj, and Constanța among those hosting the largest numbers.

“The commissioning of these thousands of islands contributes to modernizing Romania’s waste management infrastructure,” interim environment minister Diana Buzoianu said. “Through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, we managed to exceed the target of 5,000 islands and help Romanians make the transition to a circular economy more easily.”

The systems allow waste to be separated into five categories: paper and cardboard, plastic and metal, glass, biodegradable waste, and residual waste.

“Beyond projects and financing, the circular economy is built through cooperation between authorities, the private sector, and citizens,” minister Buzoianu also said. “These islands will contribute to a cleaner environment in the communities where they operate.”

Three types of collection systems were financed through the program: enclosed above-ground islands, above-ground islands with individual containers, and underground islands with individual containers. According to the ministry, the underground systems are intended in part for urban and tourist areas where available space is limited.

The investment also includes the development of a software platform for operating the recycling islands and managing the data they generate. It further covers measures to promote the “pay-as-you-throw” principle.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Facebook/Ministerul Mediului - România)

World.title: Animation film festival Animest returns to Bucharest in October with nature-themed edition
World.content:
The Animest International Animation Film Festival will hold its 21st edition in Bucharest from October 2 to 11, with a program exploring the relationship between people and the natural environment. Screenings and events will take place at Cinema Muzeul Țăranului, Cinemateca Eforie, Instituto Cervantes, and CINETic.

The thematic section will comprise three short-film programs titled Living with Nature, Human Nature, and Nature, curated by Animest artistic director Mihai Mitrică and French film journalist and historian Alexis Hunot.

“We propose three directions for observing how animated film approaches vital topics: questioning our relationship with the environment, reflecting on human nature, and imagining nature in our absence,” Hunot said.

The selection includes Karni Arieli and Saul Freed’s Wild Summon, which presents the life cycle of wild salmon through human figures, and Mark Baker’s The Village, a black comedy about the inhabitants of an isolated community. Other titles include Chris Landreth’s Ryan, which explores the life of Canadian animator Ryan Larkin, and Vergine Keaton’s Je criais contre la vie. Ou pour elle, in which a herd of deer begins hunting the dogs that pursued it.

The festival’s 2026 visual identity was created by Brazilian-Welsh illustrator and animation director Luiz Stockler. It depicts nature entering an urban apartment and transforming the interior into a plant-filled space.

Animest is also accepting applications for two programs aimed at Romanian animation creators. TOON SCRIPTS is a competition for animated series concepts and scripts, while PITCH, PLEASE! is a development workshop for animated short-film projects. Applications for both programs remain open until September 7 through the festival’s official website.

Limited Ten Stops and Full Trip passes for Animest.21 are available through Eventbook. Further details can be found here.

World.title: Romanian startup launches tool to assess websites’ visibility in AI search
World.content:
Romanian company Human AI Labs has launched Blind Spot, a platform that assesses whether websites can be understood, cited, and recommended by generative AI systems. The tool evaluates sites against 70 technical and content-related criteria and generates an AI visibility score.

Blind Spot analyzes factors including access for AI crawlers, structured data, semantic clarity, quotable content, digital authority, and trust signals. It then identifies issues that could make a website difficult for generative systems to interpret or cite and provides recommendations for addressing them.

The platform is designed for services such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, and Google AI Overviews, which can extract and synthesize information rather than only display lists of links.

“For years, companies optimized for Google: keywords, backlinks, titles, and meta tags. All of these remain important, but AI search works differently,” said Human AI Labs founder Andrei Mihnea Răileanu. “It needs structure, clarity, coherent data, easily quotable content, and authority signals that it can verify. A website can be excellent for people and still be difficult for AI to read.”

Unlike tools that monitor how brands appear in AI-generated answers, Blind Spot focuses on a website’s underlying infrastructure. Its score is calculated using deterministic criteria without AI participating in the evaluation, according to the company. For some technical issues, the generated report can also include code examples or implementation guidance.

During its beta stage, Blind Spot audited several Romanian websites and recorded an average AI visibility score of 48 out of 100. The most common issues included incomplete structured data, content that was difficult to cite, unclear authority signals, and an inconsistent presence in sources that AI systems could treat as references.

Human AI Labs filed a patent application with Romania’s State Office for Inventions and Trademarks (OSIM) in June 2026 covering elements of the platform’s architecture, including its normalized extraction methodology, deterministic scoring, and semantic gap analysis.

Blind Spot is available online, with a free audit covering the first pages of a website. The platform also offers six months of free access to eligible nongovernmental organizations and a free diagnostic audit for startups.

World.title: Western Romania: Thick smoke covers city of Timişoara for second day as wildfires rage in Serbia
World.content:
A thick layer of smoke covered Timişoara on Friday, August 21, for the second consecutive day, following recent out-of-control wildfires in Serbia. In response, authorities recommended that residents stay indoors.

Thousands of hectares of forests and grassland have burned in the neighboring country in recent days, and smoke easily crossed into Romania. A day earlier, on Thursday, August 20, dozens of calls to the 112 emergency number from Timişoara and the county reported a strong smell of smoke, according to News.ro.

Sent to verify the surroundings, Romanian firefighters said that no fires were identified. “Based on the information available, the smoke observed in Timiş County could most likely originate from the large-scale dry vegetation fires in the Dubovac area, Serbia. Depending on weather conditions and wind direction, the smoke may also be felt in our county,” ISU Timiş said.

In recent days, no fewer than 45 vegetation fires have been recorded, with the most intense one in the sandy Deliblato area of Serbia, a nature reserve in the northeast of the country, where flames have burned approximately 3,500 hectares of vegetation.

Two other major active fires are in the Stolovi mountain area (Serbia), where approximately 200 hectares of forest and low vegetation have burned, and further south of it, where around 60 hectares of forest have burned.

Serbia has appealed to Russia for help in fighting forest fires due to the lack of aircraft available from the European Union, the country’s Interior Ministry announced. Serbia is not an EU member, but has access to EU emergency assistance through the European bloc’s Civil Protection Mechanism. This summer, Belgrade sent a firefighting helicopter and an emergency response team to help Spain fight forest fires under this mechanism, but forest fires across Europe have depleted EU resources.

Until the fires are extinguished, the Timiş Public Health Directorate recommended that the population close their windows and refrain from outdoor activities. “This situation may lead to an aggravation of respiratory symptoms, especially among vulnerable people with chronic respiratory conditions (bronchial asthma, etc.) and cardiovascular conditions,” DSP Timiş said.

Lead consultant in pulmonology in Timişoara, Cristian Oancea, provided further recommendations, noting that smoke from vegetation fires contains a mixture of fine particles and toxic gases that can affect the respiratory system, including in healthy people.

“One of the main dangers is represented by fine PM2.5 particles. Due to their very small size, they can penetrate deep into the respiratory tract and reach the level of the pulmonary alveoli. Even short-term exposure to high concentrations of smoke can irritate the eyes, nose and throat, cause coughing, runny nose, wheezing, a feeling of pressure in the chest or shortness of breath,” he said on Facebook.

Moreover, according to the doctor, smoke produced by fires can also contain carbon monoxide, a toxic gas that, at high concentrations, prevents the normal transport of oxygen in the body. “For people diagnosed with asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, emphysema, pulmonary fibrosis or other chronic respiratory diseases, exposure to smoke can lead to worsening symptoms or the occurrence of an exacerbation. In severe cases, going to the emergency room or even hospitalization may be necessary,” he added.

Timiş County Council vice-president Alexandru Iovescu commented on the situation and said that Serbia has not yet requested the help of firefighters from Timiş County to extinguish the vegetation fires.

The official noted that the Environmental Guard has activated the sensors for monitoring air quality. “There is no reason to panic, but it is good to be careful and follow the recommendations of specialists. We are in contact with the responsible institutions and will communicate any important information,” Iovescu said.
