The ten-year horizon indicates an intention to create a more predictable environment for exporters. Government support should help companies become more competitive in international markets. However, over the longer term, the foundation of their competitiveness should be productivity, quality, innovation and efficient logistics rather than subsidies.

Part of a broader strategy

Transportation cost compensation should not be viewed separately from other support measures adopted in June for non-oil and gas exports. Another presidential decree signed on June 16 provides for state compensation of certain customs clearance costs for exporters that are micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. This mechanism will also take effect on September 1, 2026, and will apply to export operations carried out through September 30, 2031.

The government's approach is therefore expanding beyond the production stage to support different parts of the export chain, including financing, customs clearance, logistics and market access. This approach is particularly relevant for an economy such as Azerbaijan, which has a strategically important geographical position and significant transit potential but also faces distance and logistics-cost challenges when accessing many foreign markets.

Overall, the new transportation support mechanism could become an important tool in Azerbaijan's non-oil and gas export policy. Its greatest potential lies not simply in reducing exporters' costs, but in making it economically more viable for Azerbaijani products to reach foreign markets. The fact that non-oil and gas exports stood at $3.63 billion in 2025 shows that there remains significant room for expansion. The new support mechanism could ease one of the financial barriers to realizing that potential.

Ultimately, however, the success of the mechanism will be measured not by the amount of subsidies provided, but by the additional exports generated. If state spending on logistics helps open new markets, encourages more companies to become exporters and improves the global competitiveness of Azerbaijani products, the mechanism will have achieved its objective. Otherwise, it could simply result in part of the existing export volume being transported at a lower cost at the expense of the state.

World.title: Kazakhstan increases rail freight transportation in 7M2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 24. The volume of freight transportation across the network of Kazakhstan's Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ) JSC reached 184.4 million tons in January-July 2026, increasing by 3.2% compared to the same period of 2025, the company's press service said.

"Domestic transportation reached 97.2 million tons, while the volume of export transportation increased by 6.5% compared to the same period of last year, reaching 53.4 million tons," the company said.

During the reporting period, 60.4 million tons of hard coal were transported across the KTZ network, up 3.5% compared to January-July 2025. Of the total volume, 40.9 million tons were delivered to Kazakh consumers, 3% more than a year earlier. Coal exports amounted to 18.8 million tons, increasing by 3.1%.

Positive dynamics were also recorded in grain transportation. In the first seven months of 2026, 8.1 million tons of grain were transported, 10% more than in the same period of 2025. Grain exports increased by 10.4% to 6.3 million tons, while 1.8 million tons were transported within Kazakhstan, up 8.6% year-on-year.

The volume of transportation of milling products in export traffic amounted to 1.3 million tons, increasing by 14%.

KTZ also reported that 12.5 million tons of non-ferrous ores and 11.3 million tons of construction materials were transported across its network in January-July 2026.

Growth was recorded across several key cargo categories. Iron ore transportation amounted to 13.8 million tons, up 16.6%; petroleum products - 15.2 million tons, up 1.5%; crude oil - 1.2 million tons, up 3%; and other cargoes - 36.9 million tons, up 4.2%.

The growth in rail freight transportation comes amid the continued expansion of Kazakhstan's role in regional transit and logistics, particularly along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor.

Kazakhstan's Vice Minister of Trade and Integration Aset Nusupov told Trend that the route has become one of the country's key strategic assets over the past decade.

"The figures speak for themselves. Over three years, from 2022 to 2025, the volume of transportation along the route increased more than fivefold. By the end of 2025, total cargo traffic reached 4.5–4.7 million tonnes, of which container transportation accounted for 76,900 TEUs, 36% more than a year earlier," Nusupov said.

World.title: Azerbaijan sheds light on heavy fuel oil production
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 24. A total of 74,200 tons of heavy fuel oil were produced in Azerbaijan from January through July 2026.

This was announced in the report by the State Statistics Committee.

According to the report, this figure rose by 17,600 tons, or 31.1%, compared to the same period of 2025.

As of August 1 this year, stocks of finished heavy fuel oil at the warehouses of the country’s industrial enterprises stood at 5,100 tons.

During the reporting period, the total production value in Azerbaijan’s petroleum products sector amounted to 3.46 billion manat ($2.03 billion), down 4.9% compared to the first 7 months of last year.

In an interview with Trend, Jihad Azour, director of the International Monetary Fund's Middle East and Central Asia Department, said revenues generated by the energy sector should be managed efficiently to strengthen long-term economic resilience.

According to Azour, effective management of revenues from the oil and petroleum products sector is particularly important given the high volatility in global energy markets.

"We live in an environment of highly volatile oil and gas prices, and it is therefore important to plan ahead to avoid excessive dependence on periods of peak prices," Azour told Trend.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan sees strong surge in fixed capital investment in 7M2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 24. Investment in fixed capital in Kyrgyzstan increased by 59% from January through July 2026.

This was reported by the press service of the Cabinet of Ministers of Kyrgyzstan, citing a statement by Chairman Adylbek Kasymaliev made during the official opening ceremony of the renovated A.S. Pushkin Park in Karakol.

"Investment in fixed capital increased by 59%, reaching 238 billion soms ($2.72 billion). The construction sector is growing particularly rapidly, with growth reaching 60.6%," Kasymaliev said.

Adylbek Kasymaliev noted that Karakol has undergone significant development in recent years, including the renovation of road infrastructure, construction of new residential facilities, and modernization of water supply and sewerage systems.

He added that the city’s tourism and transport infrastructure is also reaching a new level.

According to Trend’s analysis, the sharp increase in fixed capital investment highlights the strengthening of investment activity in Kyrgyzstan and the growing contribution of capital spending to economic expansion.

The 59% increase in investment to 238 billion soms ($2.72 billion) indicates a significant expansion in spending on infrastructure, construction and other fixed assets during the first seven months of 2026.

The construction sector’s 60.6% growth stands out as a key driver of this trend. Rising construction activity, alongside investment in roads, residential facilities and utilities, points to continued development of physical infrastructure across the country.

Karakol provides a regional example of this process, with ongoing projects covering road infrastructure, housing, water supply and sewerage, as well as tourism and transport facilities.

Looking ahead, sustained investment growth could support broader economic activity, improve infrastructure capacity and create additional opportunities for businesses. At the same time, maintaining investment momentum will depend on the availability of financing, efficient project implementation and continued development of the country’s infrastructure.

World.title: China accounts for nearly 30% of Uzbekistan's foreign-invested firms
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 24. China accounted for nearly 30% of all enterprises with foreign investment operating in Uzbekistan as of August 1, 2026, making it the country's largest source of foreign-invested businesses amid rapidly expanding economic ties between the two countries.

This was reflected in data published by Uzbekistan's National Statistics Committee.

A total of 20,973 enterprises with foreign investment were operating in Uzbekistan as of August 1, including 6,241 with Chinese participation. Of the overall total, 4,685 were joint ventures and 16,288 were foreign-owned enterprises.

Russia ranked second with 3,512 enterprises, followed by Türkiye with 2,327. Kazakhstan accounted for 1,321 enterprises, South Korea for 730 and Afghanistan for 706. Azerbaijan ranked seventh with 492 enterprises.

Kazakhstan accounted for 1,321 enterprises, South Korea for 730 and Afghanistan for 706. Azerbaijan ranked seventh with 492 enterprises, followed by Tajikistan with 467, the UAE with 453 and India with 439.

Trend's analysis shows that Uzbekistan's foreign-invested enterprise base remains concentrated among its largest economic partners. China, Russia and Turkey together accounted for 12,080 enterprises, or about 57.6% of the total.

China alone represented approximately 29.8% of all foreign-invested enterprises in Uzbekistan, meaning that nearly three out of every 10 such companies had Chinese participation.

The scale of Chinese business activity reflects the broader acceleration in economic ties between the two countries. Bilateral trade reached $17.8 billion in 2025, up 34% year on year, while Chinese direct investment in Uzbekistan increased fivefold to $17 billion, according to Uzbekistan's Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade. More than 6,000 enterprises with Chinese capital were operating in the country as of July 2026.

Trend's calculations show that the 6,241 Chinese-invested enterprises recorded by the National Statistics Committee account for about 29.8% of Uzbekistan's entire foreign-invested enterprise base. The figure is also substantially higher than the 4,731 Chinese-invested enterprises reported as of November 2025, indicating continued rapid expansion of Chinese business presence.

The growth extends beyond the number of companies. According to the Eurasian Development Bank, China's FDI stock in Uzbekistan rose from just $284 million in 2016 to $10.7 billion in the first half of 2025. Energy accounted for about 51% of that stock, while manufacturing represented another 31%, pointing to a growing focus on industrial and energy projects rather than purely trade-related activity.

The structure of Chinese investment is particularly relevant to Uzbekistan's industrial development. The concentration of Chinese capital in energy and manufacturing links the bilateral relationship directly to the country's efforts to expand production capacity, modernize infrastructure and develop new industrial value chains.

Recent cooperation has also broadened into green energy, agriculture, technology, logistics and export-oriented manufacturing. At a July 2026 Uzbekistan-China business forum in Tashkent, companies discussed projects in mining, green energy, agriculture, health care, advanced technologies and industrial cooperation. Moreover, the two countries have also been expanding cooperation in digital infrastructure and irrigation modernization. Uzbek and Chinese officials agreed in April to accelerate projects under the "Digital Silk Road" and discussed Chinese financing for the modernization of Uzbekistan's irrigation infrastructure.

Trend's assessment is that China's position as Uzbekistan's largest source of foreign-invested enterprises is part of a much broader transformation in bilateral economic relations. The relationship has evolved from primarily trade-based ties toward deeper investment cooperation spanning energy, manufacturing, infrastructure, technology and agriculture.

For Uzbekistan, the growing Chinese presence provides access to capital, technology and industrial partnerships, while the diversification of projects could support the country's efforts to expand its manufacturing base and integrate more deeply into regional and global supply chains. At the same time, the concentration of foreign-invested enterprises among a handful of countries underscores the importance of continuing to diversify Uzbekistan's investor base.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s renewable energy share rises fourfold to nearly 8%
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 24. Kazakhstan’s renewable energy sector is expanding rapidly, with the share of renewables in the country’s electricity mix approaching 8% as new wind and solar capacity comes online and grid infrastructure is upgraded.

This was stated by the Ministry of Energy of the Republic of Kazakhstan.

According to the Ministry, over the past six years, the share of electricity generated from renewable energy sources (RES) has increased fourfold, from around 2% to nearly 8%.

The Ministry notes that RES accounted for 7% of total electricity generation at the end of 2025, producing 8.6 billion kWh out of approximately 123.1 billion kWh generated nationwide. With additional capacity commissioned in 2026, the current share is approaching 8%.

The expansion has been supported by government policy measures, renewable energy auctions, investment attraction, and the commissioning of new generating capacity. Kazakhstan currently has 172 RES facilities with a combined capacity of more than 3.8 GW. The portfolio includes 71 wind farms, 54 solar power plants, 44 hydropower plants and three biogas facilities.

In 2025, renewable facilities generated 8.6 billion kWh, equivalent to approximately 8.6 TWh and around 7% of Kazakhstan’s total electricity generation. During the year, nine new RES facilities with a combined capacity of 503.5 MW were commissioned. These included five wind farms totaling 387 MW, three solar plants totaling 90 MW, and one hydropower plant of 26 MW. The expansion has continued in 2026. Another 10 RES facilities with a total capacity of 245 MW are planned for launch, including four wind farms, five solar plants and one hydropower plant.

As of mid-August, seven facilities totaling 212 MW had already been commissioned, meaning approximately 87% of the planned 2026 capacity has entered operation. Renewable electricity generation is expected to reach 8.8 billion kWh by the end of the year.

The project pipeline extends considerably beyond these additions. Approximately 100 projects with a combined capacity of 3.6 GW are planned for implementation, while another 4 GW of large-scale RES projects are under development, including 1 GW of projects with energy storage systems. The growing volume of variable renewable generation is also increasing the importance of transmission infrastructure and energy storage.

In an exclusive interview with Trend, EBRD Director and Head of Energy Eurasia Sule Kılıc said the bank has mobilized 4.2 billion euros for Central Asia’s energy sector and financed more than 6.5 GW of installed renewable energy capacity in the region.

"We are the largest investors in renewable energy in Central Asia, having financed more than 6.5 gigawatts of installed renewable capacity to date and mobilised 4.2 billion euros for the region’s energy sector," Kılıc said.

According to her, the EBRD’s involvement goes beyond renewable generation to include modernization of electricity grids, which is necessary to integrate growing volumes of solar and wind power into national systems.

For Kazakhstan, the bank’s key partners include national grid operator KEGOC. Since the 1990s, the EBRD has supported seven KEGOC projects, most recently the Integration of the West Zone Project, which connects the previously isolated western power zone with the rest of the country through more than 600 kilometres of high-voltage transmission lines. Kılıc also said the EBRD is considering projects under Kazakhstan’s National Project for Modernisation of Electricity and Municipal Infrastructure.

A major new investment platform was launched in April 2026, when the EBRD and Kazakhstan signed a memorandum of understanding on the Just Energy Transition Investment Platform (QaJET). The platform is expected to mobilize up to 20 billion euros to deploy 10 GW of renewable capacity by 2035.

The first project under the platform is the 1-GW Mirny Wind project, developed by TotalEnergies and local partners. The project includes a 300-MW battery energy storage system with 600 MWh capacity. "The Bank mobilised around $550 million for the project. The inclusion of the battery storage component is a critical element in ensuring the sustainable integration of the project into Kazakhstan’s energy system," Kılıc said.

International companies are already playing a significant role in Kazakhstan’s renewable energy expansion, including TotalEnergies, China Power, Masdar and China Energy. Their participation is bringing additional capital and technologies into a sector where the development of generation capacity increasingly needs to be accompanied by investment in grids and storage.

Trend’s calculations show that the 212 MW of renewable capacity already commissioned in 2026 represents approximately 87% of the 245 MW planned for the full year. At the same time, the projected 8.8 billion kWh of renewable generation in 2026 would be about 2.3% higher than the 8.6 billion kWh generated in 2025. The combination of new generation, transmission upgrades, and storage is important for Kazakhstan’s longer-term energy targets. The country aims to increase the share of renewable energy to 15% by 2030 and up to 50% by 2050, including alternative energy sources.

The EBRD’s regional approach indicates that achieving these targets will depend not only on adding wind and solar capacity, but also on expanding the infrastructure needed to move and balance that electricity. For Kazakhstan, the parallel development of generation, high-voltage transmission and battery storage is therefore becoming a central part of the transition toward a more diversified power system.

World.title: People’s Artist of Azerbaijan Tofig Bakikhanov dies
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 24. People’s Artist of Azerbaijan Tofig Bakikhanov has died at the age of 96.

Tofig Bakikhanov was born on December 8, 1930, into the family of renowned tar player and People’s Artist Ahmad Bakikhanov. He received his first musical education at the ten-year music school (now the Bulbul Secondary Specialized Music School) affiliated with the Uzeyir Hajibeyli Azerbaijan State Conservatory (Baku Music Academy). In 1990, he was awarded the title of People’s Artist.

For his contributions to the development of Azerbaijan’s musical culture, he was awarded the Shohrat (Glory), Sharaf (Honor), and Labor orders, including the Order of Labor, 1st Class.

For more than half a century, Tofig Bakikhanov taught at the Baku Music Academy.

He was the author of three ballets, three musical comedies, 25 concertos, 20 sonatas, five symphonic mughams, eight symphonies, six symphonic poems, numerous chamber works, as well as more than 100 songs and romances.

World.title: "New Tashkent" project is a unique achievement of modern urban development - President Ilham Aliyev
World.content:
TASHKENT, Uzbekistan, August 24. Of course, every time I visit Uzbekistan, I visit different places and see how Tashkent is becoming more beautiful, how its buildings, streets and infrastructure are being transformed, and how everything is being done with greater taste, care and quality, said President Ilham Aliyev at the award ceremony held in the presence of President of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev, Trend's special correspondent reports.

The head of state noted: "The project of my dear brother, “New Tashkent,” is a unique achievement of modern urban development and the result of his vision for the future development of the capital of Uzbekistan.”

World.title: Let your oven do the hard work with four of our favourite roast recipes
World.content:
Few dinners fill bellies and nourish souls as effortlessly as a good old-fashioned roast, so we thought we'd share four of our favourites.

From a slow-roasted lamb shoulder to upside-down roast chicken and pork with perfect crackling, these dishes make the oven do the heavy lifting.

Roasting the chicken upside down helps get the skin crispy skin and stops the breast from overcooking. (ABC News: David Sier)

This easy recipe turns the traditional roast chook on its head.

Placing the bird in a roasting tin, breast side down, protects the delicate meat and also exposes the parson's nose — the fleshy tail stump — to give it a golden, crunchy texture.

It's topped off with a delicious, creamy, herb and garlic-infused lemon gravy.

The secrets to a crispy crackling are scoring and adding spices to the pork, then leaving in the fridge for at least six hours to dry the skin out. (ABC TV)

One of the biggest challenges when trying to make the perfect pork roast is nailing the crackling.

For this recipe, chef and cookbook author Hayden Quinn teamed up with comedian Matt Okine to share some tips about how to get it just right.

It takes a few hours of prep, but it’s worth it – and it pairs perfectly with the green apple slaw, which is quite tart and cuts through the fat.

Rub the seasoning into your lamb before searing the fat to help release the flavours. (ABC TV: Wesley Mitton)

This is another recipe that requires a little pre-planning, as it needs a few hours in the oven.

However, it is simple to prepare, and the result is a tender, succulent, fall-apart lamb roast that’s bursting with flavour — and the oven does all the heavy lifting.

This whole roasted cauliflower with turmeric coconut sauce is an impressive vegetarian and vegan main that's perfect a special event or Sunday roast. (ABC News: Hetty Lui McKinnon)

Whole roasted cauliflower is versatile if you're looking for a meat-free option for the dinner table and there are plenty of flavour possibilities in this recipe from Hetty Lui McKinnon.

Hetty suggests smothering it under a lemony tahini sauce and topping with black olives, balsamic-soaked raisins and parsley, or serving on a bed of romesco sauce, scattered with roasted chickpeas and baby spinach.

World.title: Zak Butters informs Port Adelaide he will depart club
World.content:
Port Adelaide's three-time best and fairest winner Zak Butters has requested to leave the club via free agency and return home to Victoria.

The 25-year-old dual All-Australian's future has dominated headlines all season with reports of offers of up to $18 million over eight years from Richmond, Geelong, Collingwood and the Western Bulldogs.

"I've made a decision to head home. It's obviously been one that I've wrestled with for a while now," he said.

"It's been a tough decision and one that I haven't taken lightly.

"Although I've loved my time in Adelaide … I'm probably at a stage in my life where I'd like to get back around some family and friends and enjoy some more time with them.

"There are so many special memories I'll take with me and hold with me forever … I'll be forever in debt to the football club for drafting a skinny club from Darley."

Butters said he would "always be a Port Adelaide person" and would "always value this club and what it's done for me".

"The supporters have been everything, they've always got around since day one of being drafted, even this year they've been awesome and showed nothing but love and support," he said.

"I feel like I've always tried to repay them in the right way and play football in the right way."

Zak Butters has told Port Adelaide he plans to head to Victoria. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

In a club statement, the Power said they would now work to facilitate his request whilst securing the best outcome for the club.

"Port Adelaide has been informed by Zak Butters and his management that he intends to exercise his rights as a restricted free agent and explore a return home to Victoria," the statement said.

"Zak has been an outstanding servant to the football club since debuting in 2019.

"He is a three-time John Cahill Medallist and dual All-Australian and we thank him for everything he has given to Port Adelaide."

ABC Sport reported Zak Butters had informed some teammates in July of his decision to move to Victoria; a story that was denied by the club at the time.

Butters played 17 games this season before a syndesmosis injury in Round 18 prematurely ended his campaign, with coach Josh Carr admitting the star midfielder was likely departing after their 10-point win over Essendon on the weekend.

Port Adelaide has been adamant all season they would match any bid on Butters and force a trade to try maximise their draft capital.

Speaking to ABC Sport in April, chief executive Matthew Richardson said the club would focus on their best interests.

"There will be offers that we can match and we will match. It does give the club a fair bit of control in what happens," he said.

World.title: Business leaders urge governments to act as smelter power deadline looms
World.content:
Rio Tinto's deadline for a new power deal for its Bell Bay Aluminium smelter in Tasmania's north is just one week away, as business leaders step up pressure on the state and federal governments to help secure the smelter's future.

The smelter, which directly employs about 550 people, is one of the biggest companies connected to Tasmania's power grid.

Last year Rio Tinto signed a one-year power deal with Hydro Tasmania. That deal is due to expire at the end of the year.

Green energy funding snub for renewable-powered aluminium smelter Further doubt has been cast over the future of an aluminium smelter in Tasmania's north-east after a federal MP said it would not be eligible for a green energy scheme.

Last month, federal Bass MP Jess Teesdale said she understood Rio Tinto had set a deadline for the end of this month to secure a new power deal, with a "very high risk the smelter would close" if the deadline is not met.

State-owned power company Hydro Tasmania has continued to negotiate a power deal with Rio Tinto, which was offering $60 million less than what Hydro Tasmania was asking for.

Uncertainty over the deal and the smelter's future has prompted 13 northern Tasmanian industry and community leaders to write open letters to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Premier Jeremy Rockliff, calling for urgent federal and state action to secure the smelter's future.

Bell Bay Aluminium is one of the biggest power users connected to the Tasmanian grid. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

Industry, community leaders demand action

Among the signatories were Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone chief executive Susie Bower and Tasmanian Minerals, Manufacturing and Energy Council chief executive Ray Mostogl.

The letter to Mr Rockliff urged a new 10-year power agreement be signed as soon as possible.

"In 2025, the smelter paid almost $76 million in salaries, invested $40 million in capital works and spent approximately $262 million with around 180 Tasmanian suppliers," the letter reads.

Speaking at Bell Bay this morning, Ms Bower said the outcome of negotiations was critical to Tasmania's future.

"We want to have the voices here of industry, unions and community, come together with business to say to our governments, 'this is critically important that you work together, you get a solution, and you get it done now'," Ms Bower said.

"Hydro [Tasmania] is owned by the state government, so that is the critical negotiation that needs to occur.

"But if there is a gap then the state government needs to be putting that on the table for the federal government to be able to come to a solution together."

Susie Bower says community and business stakeholders have come together to call on the state and federal governments to act. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

George Town Mayor Greg Kieser said if the smelter were to close, the impact on the George Town community, and Tasmania more broadly, would be "huge".

"Both from the personal side and families who rely on that income, to the supply chain who rely on the business that keeps them viable," Councillor Kieser said.

"You really just can't understate the impact that [Bell Bay's closure] will have on this immediate community.

"So if you just looked at rateable revenue, the hole that it would leave in my community's finances would be massive," he said.

Government minister Jo Palmer said Hydro Tasmania had put a "very good" power deal on the table for Rio Tinto to consider.

"Now we need the federal government to step in, just as it's done in New South Wales and in Queensland to actually bridge that gap between what Rio is saying it needs and what Hydro Tasmania is able to put on the table," Ms Palmer said.

Jo Palmer says Hydro Tasmania has put a "very good" offer on the table. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Asked if Hydro Tasmania would be willing to bridge the $60 million gap to secure a deal, Ms Palmer said that was not Hydro Tasmania's responsibility.

A spokesperson for federal Industry Minister Tim Ayres said the Tasmanian government had "complete control" over the "supply of low-cost, renewable electricity for Tasmanian industry".

"We encourage the Tasmanian government to use all the levers at its disposal to support its industrial base," the spokesperson said.

Deputy Tasmanian Labor leader Janie Finlay said the state government needed to secure a fair and competitive deal.

"Once that deal is done, Premier Rockliff needs to take a clear package to Canberra and seek Commonwealth support," Ms Finlay said.

According to its website, the Bell Bay Aluminium smelter produces roughly 190,000 tonnes of aluminium annually.

World.title: Melbourne's social cohesion 'fraying', antisemitism inquiry hears
World.content:
There has been a "fraying" of social cohesion in Melbourne since the start of the war in Gaza, the city's lord mayor has told the antisemitism royal commission.

The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion has entered its final week of public hearings, with a final report due before the first anniversary of the Bondi Beach terror attack.

City of Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece appeared at the inquiry on Monday to discuss the challenges the local government had faced in addressing division in the community since the outbreak of war in 2023.

"We saw a significant rise of protest in Melbourne and … some fraying of cohesion in our city," he said.

" I've found it to be one of the most challenging issues I've had to face as lord mayor of Melbourne. "

Melbourne has the largest population of Jewish Australians in the country.

Synagogues spray-painted with 'threatening' graffiti

Mr Reece said synagogues in Melbourne had been graffitied on a near weekly basis since the start of the war in Gaza.

He said a targeted initiative aimed at removing "menacing" and "threatening" graffiti within one hour of reporting had cleaned more than 3,000 hateful items.

Mr Reece said of those, between 800 and 1,000 items of graffiti were antisemitic in nature.

"One of the things that has been most upsetting to me over the last two-and-a-half years is people telling me they are afraid to come into the city," he said.

"That was particularly focused around some of the protest activity we were seeing, but it was also focused around some of the awful materials we were seeing being put up around the city."

Graffiti at the Melbourne Hebrew Congregation in South Yarra last year. (Facebook: Australian Jewish Association)

The commission heard one of the incidents which occurred in January 2026 required the removal of 40 posters which depicted one of the Bondi Beach shooters behind the word "Aussie".

Mr Reece said the city was working with other inner-city local governments to expand the rapid response initiative, which was resource intensive.

"It's very expensive," he said.

"One recommendation I would make to the commission is that you do give consideration to some sort of funding program from the Commonwealth or another level of government that would allow local governments who want to implement policies like this to do so," he said.

NSW premier open to extension call

Meanwhile, NSW Premier Chris Minns has weighed in on discussions about the length of the royal commission.

Last week, Liberal MP Julian Leeser made a bid to extend the inquiry and to call government ministers and the prime minister to give evidence.

Mr Minns on Monday said he had spoken to witnesses who had been "satisfied" with the royal commission so far.

"But, you know, if we need to go a couple of weeks longer, given that most of the expense was spent setting it up, that would seem to be money well spent because both the federal and the and the state government are relying on these recommendations to shape some of our policy," he said.

The royal commission previously said Commissioner Virginia Bell SC was "committed to completing the final report within the timeframe set in the Letters Patent".

"The Royal Commission is currently holding its ninth and final hearing block which concludes late August 2026," a spokesperson said in a statement.

"We've heard from more than 200 witnesses and received over 20,000 submissions as part of our inquiry."

World.title: Another case of acute liver damage in counterfeit peptide user
World.content:
Another black market peptide user has suffered a severe liver injury, with doctors concerned a possible "contaminated batch" might be to blame.

The latest case means seven Victorian patients have now been hospitalised for acute liver toxicity, after using a counterfeit of the weight loss peptide retatrutide.

Liver transplant specialist Marie Sinclair, who has treated liver failure patients in Victoria, said another patient had recently become seriously unwell after taking an unapproved peptide labelled as retatrutide.

"We have seen a recent case again, fairly similar to previous cases, where after a second dose of unregulated retatrutide there was severe liver injury," Dr Sinclair said.

"It's uncertain as to why this has happened, but one possibility is that there could be a contaminated batch of [counterfeit] retatrutide that is in Victoria.

Doctors warn use of any black-market peptides could cause serious harm. (Supplied)

"It's one possible explanation … we don't have any testing results to support that, it's purely a hypothesis at this stage."

Dr Sinclair said she had commissioned testing of counterfeit peptides used by liver failure patients.

"This is something I think we are going to continue to see with peptides if the unregulated market continues," she said.

Dr Sinclair said the affected patients sustained liver injuries "within a few weeks" of taking the black market retatrutide.

"They may become yellow or jaundiced, which is very frightening for patients, and they can become very unwell," she said.

Marie Sinclair says the retatrutide being sold is not currently the same one in clinical trials. (ABC News)

The Therapeutic Goods Administration's (TGA) chief medical advisor Robyn Langham told the ABC "the localised nature" of the liver issues in Victoria suggested "a batch problem".

"We are seeing reports of acute liver failure which might be related to some batch issues certainly from Victoria," Professor Langham said.

Patients in liver failure after using knock-off weight loss drug Megan Hancocks bought a drug labelled as the peptide compound retatrutide in cash from a beautician. Within a week of her second dose, she was in acute liver failure.

She said the cluster of liver harm cases did not appear to be happening elsewhere in Australia.

Professor Langham warned consumers black market retatrutide was a "counterfeit product" and taking it was a risk.

"The retatrutide that's being sold is not the retatrutide that's currently in clinical trials," she said.

Professor Langham said her comments were not the result of an investigation.

Robyn Langham says the localised nature of the hospitalisations suggests a "batch problem". (Four Corners: Keana Naughton)

Peptides are small chains of amino acids which act as signalling agents in the body, telling it to carry out certain processes such as hormone release or tissue repair.

There are regulated peptide medications including insulin and GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic.

This year there has been a boom in social media promotion of counterfeit, unapproved peptides, which are not safe for human use.

Victoria's health department has been contacted for comment.

Do these wellness treatments actually work? Wellness and anti-aging clinics are popping up across Australia. But do their treatments work and are they safe?

It previously warned products labelled "retatrutide" may contain contaminants that could have "toxic effects".

The ABC contacted all other state and territory health departments to ask if there had been any cases of liver toxicity associated with unapproved peptide use.

Canberra Health Services confirmed it had detected liver damage from products sold as retatrutide, but would not say how many "due to the low numbers involved".

US-based pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly is the sole owner of the patent for retatrutide and is currently running clinical trials.

"Lilly continues to warn the public about the potential dangers of fake medicines," Manny Simons, general manager of Lilly Australia, said.

"Any retatrutide available online is unapproved, unverified and simply not worth the risk."

Adolescents 'injecting' counterfeit peptides

Professor Langham said it was important to note there were no good batches or safe unapproved peptides — the risk of serious harm applied to all the products.

"There are hospital admissions happening across the country because of the use of unapproved peptides," she said.

"The risks are real, they are not theoretical."

What's the point of peptides? We want to hear your stories Have you come across injectable peptides yet? They're everywhere on social media right now and we want to know why people are using them, and what their experience has been like.

Professor Langham said the TGA was particularly worried about young people using unapproved peptides being promoted on social media.

"What concerns us most is that adolescents, young children are buying these and injecting them into themselves, so goodness knows what is happening," she said.

"[The counterfeit products] have not been tested in clinical trials, they have not been tested in terms of their manufacturing, and they've not been tested for their safety and people are injecting these into their body."

The TGA said more than 94,500 unapproved peptide products had been destroyed this year, in collaboration with Australian Border Force.

Last week, the TGA and New South Wales Police seized more than $120,000 of "illicit peptide and anabolic steroid products" from premises allegedly linked to a social media influencers.

In April, authorities seized $2 million worth of steroids and peptides.

World.title: Court hears public at risk from bus driver for months before deadly crash
World.content:
A court has heard a bus company linked to a fatal Hunter Valley bus crash exposed the public to risk the entire time the driver involved was employed.

Linq Buslines and two of its directors, Christopher Fogg and Anthony Royle, are awaiting sentencing after pleading guilty to heavy-vehicle law breaches.

Christopher Terrence Fogg (left) and Anthony John Royle pleaded guilty to breaching their duty of care. (ABC News)

Brett Andrew Button, 61, was driving the Linq Buslines coach carrying wedding guests when he crashed at a roundabout in June 2023.

Ten people were killed and 25 injured.

Today, National Heavy Vehicle Regulator prosecutor Georgia Lewer told Gosford Local Court the company's recruitment policies put the public at risk.

"It is important that your honour is sentencing [Linq] for the seven months he [Brett Button] was employed to drive buses and the public was put at risk during that period," she said.

"It would not have happened had he not been employed.

"He drove as a casual bus driver for seven months and there was a continuing offence over a period."

The driver

Brett Button's driving career came to a shocking end on a tragic night in Greta.

Brett Button will spend at least 24 years in jail over the crash that killed 10 people in 2023. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

Button would later admit he was drug impaired, using the opioid Tramadol in excessive amounts at the time.

He was also speeding when he entered the roundabout and tipped the bus onto its side.

In September 2024, Button was sentenced to 32 years in jail, with a 24-year non-parole period.

He appealed against the severity of that sentence but it was unsuccessful.

Families face company directors

Families and survivors came face to face with company directors today during a sentencing hearing for the heavy vehicle breaches.

At least four of them are hoping to deliver victim impact statements, but the presiding judge is yet to rule if they can.

Jason and Sharyn Junkeer arrive at Gosford Local Court. (ABC News)

Survivors Jason and Sharyn Junkeer travelled from Victoria.

They had been among the passengers who pleaded with Button to slow down.

Matt and Leanne Mullen travelled to Gosford Courthouse from Singleton.

Their daughter Rebecca, a young doctor, was one of the passengers who died.

Since the crash, they have called for reforms, including driver monitoring and GPS surveillance.

Matt and Leanne Mullen enter Gosford Local Court. (ABC News)

Exposure to risk

A lack of protocols, monitoring and procedures are at the heart of the heavy vehicle breach charges the company and its directors have admitted to.

In March, Linq Buslines pleaded guilty to two counts of breaching the National Heavy Vehicle Law between November 2022 and June 2023.

The maximum penalty it faces for both breaches combined is a total of $2 million.

Linq admitted to exposing the public to risk during that time.

Investigators at the scene of the bus crash in which 10 people died. (AAP: Darren Pateman)

The court heard the company had no policies requiring potential drivers to undergo a medical assessment or fill out a medical fitness form.

It also heard there was no requirement for drivers to produce a driving record and provide valid references or referees from previous employers.

Valid licence

Defence barrister Bruce Hodgkinson SC said there was nothing to suggest Button was not fit for the role.

"He had to have a medical assessment sent to Transport for NSW, otherwise he wouldn't have had a licence at the time he approached [Linq] for employment," Mr Hodgkinson said.

"His long-term GP said he was not drug dependant and the only muscular disorder he had was arthritis."

Linq Buslines directors Christopher Terrence Fogg and Anthony John Royle pleaded guilty to breaching their duty of care in the six weeks leading up to the crash.

The company and directors are being sentenced in Gosford Local Court. (ABC Central Coast: Shauna Foley)

The charge was set out in the agreed facts which stated: "[Royle and Fogg] failed to take reasonable steps to ensure that appropriate action was undertaken to manage and address issues of identified over speeding in a timely manner."

Sentencing proceedings continue.

World.title: X-rays show skull of extinct thylacine in collector's auction find
World.content:
Testing of the mounted head of a thylacine discovered by accident in an auction house catalogue has confirmed its authenticity as the extinct Tasmanian tiger.

X-rays of the taxidermy head, which is believed to have been preserved sometime in the late 1800s, show that beneath wads of stuffing is a full, uncut skull.

An X-ray of the head confirmed James Cranfield's purchase to be the real deal. (Supplied: Instagram/thetaxidermist)

"It is indeed a thylacine," natural history collector and specimen owner James Cranfield said.

"It has been confirmed by experts as being a genuine, previously undocumented, newly discovered specimen of the extinct Tasmanian tiger.

"It is a ridiculously important and special specimen.

"The most amazing thing is the absolute completeness and the almost perfect state of the skull within."

James Cranfield and Francesca Hatcher hold what has been confirmed as a thylacine head. (Supplied: James Cranfield)

Mr Cranfield called the find "a discovery of a lifetime", saying "it is the holy grail of natural history collecting".

It has drawn interest from academics, museums and the scientific community, including a team of scientists who hope to "de-extinct" the species.

Thylacine pair, as depicted by John Gould in 1863. (Wikimedia Commons: John Gould)

The mounted head, which was sold in poor condition, had been listed as a fox's head in a UK auction house general sale and was expected to fetch between £30 ($57) to £50 ($95).

But an astute Mr Cranfield, who owns a curiosity shop in Bristol and has collected taxidermies and curiosities for his "entire life", said he immediately recognised the listing was incorrect after inspecting the animal's teeth.

Loading...

He noted that while foxes and dogs have six upper incisors between the canines, marsupials such as the thylacine have eight incisors.

After a heated bidding war with another collector, the thylacine was bought for £62,600 ($120,000), including auction fees.

Immediately afterwards, he held a sale of his private collection, as well as the contents of his shop, in a bid to recoup the cost.

James Cranfield says that when he inspected the teeth of the specimen, he was sure it was a thylacine. (Supplied: James Cranfield)

The verified specimen will now be listed in the International Thylacine Specimen Database (ITSD).

ITSD director, Steven Sleightholme, confirmed the skull's authenticity.

In a letter to Mr Cranfield, he wrote:

"I am pleased to confirm the radiographs of the skull, particularly the dentition, establishes that your mounted taxidermied head is indeed that of a thylacine. "It is unfortunate the specimen comes without any provenance, but nevertheless well done for recognising such a remarkable rarity."

A thylacine joey from the collections of the Natural History Museum, London. (Supplied: Penny Edmonds)

Dr Sleightholme stressed the importance of the find, saying that only 16 Tasmanian tiger specimens — including the mount — were held in private hands, with the remainder held in university or museum collections.

"Your specimen is particularly significant because there are only two known thylacine head mounts," he wrote.

"[Due to] the rarity and significance of the mount, it will be particularly important that any intervention is carried out with great care and kept to a minimum."

The ITSD has recorded 815 specimens around the world, which could range from a "microscopic slide" of tissue to a full mount.

Skull 'should be kept as is'

Mr Cranfield said other collectors may have been thrown off as to the specimen's true identity due to its "naive mount", with its googly eyes and a bulbous forehead that should have been more streamlined.

Thylacine head auction find a 'holy grail' for collector A British collector says he is now in possession of a "holy grail" — a mounted thylacine head.

X-rays have revealed the early techniques used, including a traditional "wood wool and tow" stuffing of shredded wood shavings with a smooth outer layer of coarse hemp to create the detailing.

Mr Cranfield said the radiograph showed that too much stuffing had been used, perhaps due to the taxidermist being unfamiliar with thylacines.

"The amount of stuffing within the skin has given it very different proportions to what a Tasmanian tiger would look like," he said.

Loading Instagram content

But despite the imperfections, Mr Cranfield argues the specimen should be left as is.

At some stage he may replace the existing eyes with antique glass eyes to be more in keeping with the time.

"I am of the personal opinion of leaving it as is. It is a historic piece and will never be perfect," he said.

"Even if you tried to rehydrate that skin and tried to remount it, we are losing an historically prepared piece. I think it can offer a lot more as it is, than trying to make it look pretty."

Specimen to inform de-extinction project

For the moment, the skull is no longer on display.

Mr Cranfield said that while the purpose of buying the mount was to share it with the world, the priority was to keep it safe.

He said the head was no longer on his shop premises and was in a safe in a secure location.

"The burden of being a custodian of such a special thing is now weighing heavily on my shoulders," he said.

"The next steps are to allow the continued availability of it to the academic community, get that DNA, and hopefully get it on display somewhere where the public can see it."

The last thylacine in captivity at Beaumaris Zoo Hobart in 1933. (Supplied: David Fleay)

University of Melbourne professor Andrew Pask, the chief biology officer at Colossal Laboratory and Biosciences, is part of a scientific team working to "de-extinct" the thylacine.

Researchers at the US science startup say they have brought dire wolves back from extinction and have worked on "de-extincting" the New Zealand moa.

He said while the taxidermy thylacine "was not a pristine specimen by any stretch" it could be a "really interesting one".

Thylacine skulls, from the collections of the Natural History Museum, London. (Supplied: Penny Edmonds)

Through genome sequencing and DNA testing, Dr Pask believed the provenance of this particular specimen could also be traced.

"We're hoping to sample it within the next couple of months and it won't take too long after that to get a genome," he said.

"We could possibly figure out where this specimen might have come from and which era it was collected in.

"Every single genome that we can get from a thylacine helps. It gives us a deeper understanding of what that population looked like so we can get an understanding of differences that existed between individuals in that population and that's important to creating a healthy population again, one that handles diseases and other changes in the environment."

In its work, the team used modified grey wolf genes to create embryos to be implanted into surrogates that gave birth to pups.

The modifications were based on analysis of DNA extracted from two dire wolf fossils.

It has been nearly 90 years to the day since Tasmania's last thylacine died in a Hobart zoo on September 7, 1936, a date that has since been commemorated as World Threatened Species Day.

World.title: Albanese says WA's GST deal won't change while he is PM
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has pledged there will be no change to Western Australia's GST arrangements after a report recommended scrapping the existing deal.

On his first visit to WA since an interim Productivity Commission report recommended the 2018 Morrison government GST arrangement be removed, Mr Albanese repeated the state deserved its "fair share".

'What I believe is very clearly, there will be no change to WA's GST arrangements whilst I'm prime minister," he told reporters.

"That is my view. That has consistently been my view."

The prime minister was pressed several times by Perth journalists on his promise and insisted: "There will be no change to WA's arrangements whatsoever on the GST."

Escape plan from 'costly' WA GST deal The Productivity Commission finds the WA GST deal is a "costly mistake" that has led to "perverse" outcomes, and recommends it be scrapped.

The Productivity Commission published its interim report into the GST carve up earlier this month, finding the 2018 WA GST deal was a "costly mistake" which had only benefited WA and should be scrapped.

That deal assured WA would receive a 75 cent floor in each dollar of GST contributed, with top-up arrangements for other states to ensure none were left worse off.

But the commission found this had cost the federal budget $23 billion in its first six years, $22 billion of which had flowed to WA.

The release of the report sparked an angry rebuke from the west, with Premier Roger Cook brandishing the report's authors as "east-coast clowns".

WA to get 'fair share'

Mr Albanese, whose government endorsed and extended the Morrison-era deal to at least 2029, had subsequently said WA would "get its fair share" of GST.

Mr Cook had said Mr Albanese told him over the phone WA's GST arrangements would not change.

Loading...

But the state opposition and the resources sector have been among those demanding Mr Albanese make that commitment publicly and explain what he means by "fair share".

"The floor of 75 per cent will absolutely stay. I think WA deserves that because WA contributes to the national economy and helps to drive that economy," Mr Albanese said on Monday.

WA government fights to keep current GST deal WA is desperate to retain the GST deal it struck with Scott Morrison as the Productivity Commission looks to rein in cost blowouts.

He had a message for state premiers and chief ministers on the "no worse off guarantee".

"An important thing that sometimes isn't understood from some of the critique of WA getting its fair share of the GST is that those additional payments have not come from states and territories. They have come from the Commonwealth," he said.

"I'm comfortable with that and what I say to premiers and chief ministers, though, is you need to bear that in mind when you are discussing federal-state financial relations."

WA premier 'relieved'

"I think every Western Australian is both relieved and pleased to hear the words from the prime minister today that Western Australia's arrangements for the GST will remain," Roger Cook said.

"We are very pleased that the prime minister has backed WA. As I've said before, he gets WA."

Mr Cook said it finalises the debate.

Anthony Albanese with Roger Cook in Henderson. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"The prime minister has provided an assurance to Western Australians that Western Australia's arrangement for the GST will remain," he said.

Mr Cook said WA would continue to fight for GST share in the lead up to the Productivity Commission's final report on the GST at the end of the year.

Mr Albanese was in Henderson, in Perth's south, for an announcement on the AUKUS nuclear submarine deal with the United States and the United Kingdom.

He declared a specific site in the centre of Henderson would be the location of a new defence precinct, which he described as a "major step" towards establishing a sovereign ship building and maintenance hub in WA.

"AUKUS is full steam ahead and WA is central to it," the prime minister said.

World.title: Crime rates up at suburban stations as police pull security officers
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Crime rates up at suburban stations as police pull security officers Alexander Darling August 24, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Crime rates were climbing steeply at suburban train stations across Melbourne in the years before Victoria Police decided to strip them of security officers, new data reveals. Protective services officers were stationed at the city’s 192 train stations between 6pm and the last train from 2010 but, in April, they were pulled from 119 stops and redeployed to the CBD and major suburban stations. Protective services officers at Southern Cross Station this year. Alexander Darling The force said the strategy would allow it to make best use of police resources. However, data obtained by this masthead shows the number of offences increased by nearly 180 per cent over five years to March this year at the 119 stations that have since lost their nightly PSO presence.



Teams of roaming PSOs now cover several of these smaller stations, riding trains between them, rather than being based permanently on station platforms. Crime Statistics Agency Victoria data suggests outer suburbs with growing populations face the largest increases in crime among those 119 stations, with Williams Landing station, on the Werribee train line, recording the highest number of offences in the past year. There were 138 offences at the station in the year to March 2026, double the number the year before. At Merinda Park station, on the Cranbourne line, there were fewer than three crimes in 2021, but 121 offences in the year to March 2026.



Almost 90 per cent of crimes recorded at train stations since 2021 are non-violent, such as car theft or drug possession. Crime data released to this masthead does not cover the period after PSOs were redeployed in April. That period will be covered by the next month’s release of Victoria Police’s official annual crime statistics, though concerns have been flagged that crime reports at many stations will have plateaued because there is nobody to report it to, rather than a real reduction in incidents. Superintendent Andrew Falconer, the architect of the new PSO system, said the redeployment was focused on using officers as effectively as possible to reduce crime. He said crime rates at stations such as Williams Landing had been largely driven by property offences like car theft, carried out at times when PSOs weren’t at the station.



He said he had seen internal data showing no increase in offences across the network after the PSOs were removed. “For vehicle theft, in particular, we’ve now got targeted operations on that, and we move between those areas of the high crime, and normally, once we’re able to arrest the primary offenders in the area, it significantly reduces it,” Falconer said. Superintendent Andrew Falconer of Victoria Police’s transit safety division. Alexander Darling “We’re seeing a reduction in the [busiest] category 1 stations by that additional deployment [of PSOs], and in the [less busy] category 3 we’re not seeing an increase.” Falconer said the arrest of five teenagers accused of assault in Sunshine on August 1 was an example of the new model’s effectiveness.



Related Article Exclusive

Public transport A stranger assaulted Hannah on a tram. She may never have reported him if not for this “The PSOs [left] the railway station because they were with police ... [to] make that arrest. We do have a number of examples like that now of different significant arrests by having additional deployment during the day,” he said. The state opposition has committed to hiring an extra 200 PSOs if elected in November, and opposition police spokesman Brad Battin said this would allow the bigger train stations and shopping centres to maintain their new level of coverage, while redeploying officers to suburban platforms overnight. “Some areas might need patrols a fraction early, particularly if you look at areas that have a high crime rate after school, so get them from 3pm until the last train, for example,” Battin said.



“It’s possible the numbers could steady because there is no one there [at the smaller stations] to make reports to. That’s why it’s really important to have PSOs there, so people do not just feel safe, but they’ve got someone to speak to at the station.” Related Article Crime Victoria’s most dangerous train stations revealed Falconer declined to answer what impact an extra 200 officers would have, but he reiterated the new model was already effectively addressing the growth areas in transport crime. In April, the government and police justified the reallocation of officers by noting that there were 79 stations which recorded no crimes against the person in 2024, and that a further 101 stations recorded fewer than six. Dr Berhan Ahmed hears many complaints about train station crime through his work as CEO of support service Africause, and not just from people who use the station nearby his office in Footscray.



Several weeks ago, Ahmed saw a woman who said she had been assaulted at Noble Park – a category 2 station in the south-east – where there is a permanent nightly PSO presence from 5pm. Dr Berhan Ahmed hears complaints about train station crime through his work at Africause. Jason South “She was at the station late afternoon and approached by a young man and woman and they asked her for money and her mobile phone,” Ahmed said. “She refused and they followed her to the car park, and when she started to shout they just bashed her. She yelled and they ran away. “She had bruises in her eye.” Ahmed said the woman came to him after being unable to find anyone at the station to report the crime to. He said he connected her with support for victims of crime.



Other commuters he saw felt so unsafe that PSOs were irrelevant to the decisions they were making. “Most of them are saying to me they wouldn’t go alone to [stations], they’re saying, ‘I need to go with someone’, rather than relying on police being there,” he said. “If it’s not safe, it’s not safe.” Falconer urged people to check a new website showing when and where PSOs would be, and that initiatives were under way to prevent at-risk people from committing crimes at certain stations. “I think one thing I’d encourage people to speak to the PSOs; they very much want to engage with people, ask them for advice,” he said. “We give them crime prevention advice to pass on.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘I’ve signed peoples’ arms for goodness’ sake’: Albanese vows WA’s GST system will stay put
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsWAGST ‘I’ve signed peoples’ arms for goodness’ sake’: Albanese vows WA’s GST system will stay put Hamish Hastie August 24, 2026 — 2:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has assured West Australians the GST arrangements that have boosted the state budget by billions annually will remain unchanged while he is in the top job. Albanese made the pledge during a press conference in Henderson in Perth’s south on Monday morning, in response to a Productivity Commission report that labelled the 2018 Morrison Government deal to introduce a 75-cents-in-the-dollar floor in the GST pool formula a “mistake”. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on a visit to BAE Systems Australia in Perth on Monday. AAP The Cook Labor government, industry groups, businesses and the WA community have heaped pressure on Albanese to be unequivocal about his support for the current arrangements. His public comments to date only included a promise the western state would keep its “fair share”.



“What I believe is very clearly there will be no change to WA’s GST arrangements whilst I’m prime minister. That is my view. That has consistently been my view,” he told reporters on Monday. “There will be no change.” The commission’s report was released on August 14 and Albanese denied he had waited until he came to WA to be more explicit in his position – referencing the time in 2024 when he used a marker to sign “no change to GST” on the arm of former West Australian journalist Dylan Caporn. “I didn’t wait. Although it was very clear, and I’ve said it multiple times ... I’ve signed peoples’ body parts, for goodness’ sake. I mean, seriously,” he said. The 2018 GST deal came with a no-worse-off guarantee to other states to get them across the line to agree to it.



That deal was expected to cost the Commonwealth about $2.3 billion, but now could balloon to $60 billion by 2030. Related Article GST ‘Angry’ WA premier tears into ‘dodgy, deceitful, dumb’ GST report Asked on Monday whether he would extend the no-worse-off guarantee beyond 2030 to satisfy the other states, Albanese said he would have discussions with the other premiers. “It is a good deal for the nation when you have an understanding and a clear, unequivocal position, being able to go forward with some certainty,” he said. WA Premier Roger Cook, who had been publicly urging Albanese to offer complete support for the deal, was ecstatic.



“Prime minister, can I just say, look, I think every Western Australian is both relieved and pleased to hear the words from the prime minister today that Western Australia’s arrangements for the GST will remain,” he said at the press conference in Henderson on Monday. “You don’t come to Western Australia on 45 occasions without appreciating that the Western Australian economy is driving the national economy, and we are very pleased that the prime minister has backed WA.” On Sunday, state opposition leader Basil Zempilas demanded Albanese clarify what “WA’s fair share” of the GST was. “‘A fair share’, prime minister, does not mean the same thing as ‘no change’,” Zempilas said. The Productivity Commission is due to produce its final report by December.



Albanese and Cook visited defence contractor BAE Systems in Henderson to unveil plans for the Henderson defence precinct, which will be used for a shipbuilding and sustainment facility.

AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon has taken a swipe at Ed Richards after the Western Bulldogs’ star suggested Friday night’s wildcard clash against Collingwood was not a real final. This weekend will be the first time the two do-or-die wildcard games will be held, the top eight having expanded to the top 10 in a bid to prolong supporter interest late into in the season. The eighth-placed Bulldogs will face the ninth-placed Magpies at the MCG, the clash expected to attract more than 85,000 supporters. Not quite a final: Western Bulldogs star Ed Richards doesn’t feel the wildcard round is an actual final. AFL 2026 No one wants to play the Blues, but the Swans are sitting ducks as finals race turns wild “I personally think that we haven’t [made finals yet],” he said. “I would like to win this one and then really have that cemented finals spot in an elimination. So, just treating this one as, I guess, another week – round 25, if you would.” It prompted a verbal whack from Dillon, speaking at the launch of the AFL finals series on Monday, who was unimpressed. “Yeah, look, I haven’t heard those comments, but I’m not sure the Bulldogs have played many home-and-away games in front of 90,000-plus, so you might have a different feeling after the game,” Dillon said.



The largest crowd the Bulldogs have played in front of this season was 59,556, against Hawthorn at the MCG in round 13. It’s one of only two occasions the Bulldogs have featured in games attracting more than 50,000 fans – the other being against Fremantle in Perth. Loading In the last clash between the two clubs at the MCG, in round two last year, 78,027 fans attended – the largest Bulldogs crowd of 2025. Scheduled to play the lower-ranked Magpies at the MCG off a shorter break, the Bulldogs would be entitled to complain that this game is not at Marvel Stadium – their home ground. But Richards insists the Bulldogs aren’t fazed, the AFL mandating that finals are held at the MCG.



“There’s been a bit of chat about that,” Richards said on Monday. Related Article Breaking

AFL 2026 Five Swans players banned from attending Brownlow “I love playing at the ’G, so I’m not too fussed. You’ve got to win finals [there], so you’ve got to be able to play finals at the MCG and play well. We’ve been pretty good there this year so, hopefully, we can continue some good form, play some good footy there on Friday.” Collingwood also get an extra day’s rest, having played Brisbane on Friday night before the Bulldogs beat Melbourne on Saturday. Spearhead Aaron Naughton, who rolled his ankle late against Melbourne, wasn’t involved in Monday’s light session but is expected to play.



“Needs to get rid of a bit of swelling and stuff from that ankle but, hopefully, he’ll be right,” Richards said. World.title: Kaiser airborne survey homes in on rich Victorian goldfield
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Kaiser airborne survey homes in on rich Victorian goldfield Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 24, 2026 — 2:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Gold producer Kaiser Reef has completed a high-resolution airborne magnetic survey over its Maldon gold project in Victoria, a move designed to zero in on the next batch of drill targets in one of Australia’s most historically rich goldfields. Kaiser’s latest work involved a low-altitude, helicopter-supported magnetic and radiometric survey flown with tight 35-metre line spacing over a 59-square-kilometre area. The survey aims to deliver a much clearer picture of the project’s underlying structural architecture and lithology. Kaiser Reef has completed a high-resolution helicopter-supported magnetic and radiometric survey over its Maldon gold project in Victoria. The new geophysical data follows recent soil sampling that identified multiple gold and arsenic pathfinder anomalies, giving the company a solid foundation to build upon. The company says the combined datasets will be an invaluable tool for locking in the next series of surface drill targets. The company is particularly interested in identifying cross-cutting structures that may intersect the region’s well-known north-south-trending reefs, as these intersections may be prime locations for gold mineralisation.



′ Maldon represents a district scale gold opportunity for Kaiser.′ Kaiser Reef managing director Brad Valiukas The Maldon goldfield, sitting in Victoria’s prolific Golden Triangle, has a serious pedigree, having historically produced an impressive 1.75 million ounces of gold at a bonanza grade of 28 grams per tonne. However, Kaiser says the district has been neglected by modern explorers for decades and remains substantially underexplored. The timing of the company’s expanded exploration program looks sharp, as the Australian gold sector continues to see a flurry of merger and acquisition activity, showing producers are willing to pay up for scale. At the same time, the recent spot gold price in Australian dollar terms is trading at higher levels, keeping the economics for new discoveries firmly in the spotlight. Kaiser Reef managing director Brad Valiukas said: “In the soils, we see some gold trends heading off the north-south alignment, and we are looking for the helicopter-based geophysics survey to confirm and better define the cross-cutting structures intersecting the multiple north-south reefs. This will be key to locking in the next series of surface targets for drill testing.” Kaiser is not just an explorer; it is also an established gold producer operating the Henty gold mine in Tasmania,providing it with valuable operational experience, a robust balance sheet and a source of cash flow to fund its growth ambitions. The company’s total group mineral resource currently stands at 5.42 million tonnes grading 3.59g/t gold for 625,000 ounces, including an inferred resource at Maldon’s Union Hill deposit of 1.31 million tonnes at 4.44g/t for 187,000 ounces. The company has reaffirmed its 2027 financial year production guidance of 32,000 ounces of gold across both the Maldon and Henty operations.



The Maldon project also comes with the significant advantage of the Porcupine Flats fully permitted and operating 200,000-tonne-per-annum processing plant and existing underground access, offering a potential fast-track to production should the current exploration program in Victoria prove successful. Kaiser isn’t sitting on its hands, with a 4350-metre surface drilling program also underway across four initial targets at Maldon. Standout results so far include a solid eight-metre hit at 4.16g/t gold from just 10m returned at its ‘Quill’ target. Follow-up drilling at Quill has now been completed with assays pending. In parallel, work has kicked off to refurbish the decline at the Union Hill mine and establish a new underground drill platform, giving the company freshangles to test the historic high-grade system from below. With a powerful new set of exploration data in hand and a clear geological model to test, Kaiser appears to be systematically working to unlock the modern potential of a classic Victorian goldfield. As the rods get ready to spin on a new follow-up drill program, the market will be watching to see if this old district still has a few secrets left to tell. World.title: Pauline Hanson’s deleted post deepens One Nation’s migration muddle
World.content:
Pauline Hanson has deleted a social media post containing her immigration targets from just five months ago, plunging One Nation into a deeper state of confusion as its MPs contradict themselves and each other over the party’s signature policy platform. Hanson posted on X on Sunday to say her party’s policy was to cut net overseas migration to 130,000 people a year after Farrer MP David Farley cast doubt on that target in a Sunday interview by saying it would inevitably be higher. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson in the Senate. Alex Ellinghausen New England MP Barnaby Joyce then backed Hanson on Monday morning, insisting the 130,000 net migration figure had been long-standing One Nation policy. “We’ve been saying that all along,” Joyce told Sunrise. “It’s 130,000 net overseas migration.” But One Nation’s public statements, including Hanson’s, contradict that claim and it was only defined as One Nation policy last week, when Joyce said 130,000 was a “net” figure.



A post from Pauline Hanson on X from March 1 this year, which states 130,000 arrivals, rather than net overseas migration, would be the cap under One Nation policy. X/@PaulineHansonOz Before that, Hanson had said the figure would be significantly lower. The One Nation leader has deleted a post on X she made on March 1 this year containing the lower target, which now conflicts with her most recent position from this weekend. In the deleted post, Hanson said One Nation was targeting a 130,000 cap on migrant arrivals. She said that would be compared with migrant departures, which had been 230,000 last year, to arrive at the net overseas migration figure. With those figures, NOM would be minus 100,000. The policy Hanson confirmed on Sunday would mean about 230,000 more people coming to Australia than her post from March. One Nation’s website still contains the previous policy, saying it would cap the number of visas granted each year to 130,000 – a metric that would lead to either zero or negative NOM depending on how many people left the country each year.



A screengrab of One Nation’s website, taken on August 24, 2026, which shows the party would cap visas at 130,000 people per year. This stands in contrast to recent comments by party MPs. onenation.org.au/immigration The party has been forced to clarify its position after the latest curveball was thrown over the weekend, when MP David Farley told the ABC that migration numbers under One Nation would be “not too different” to Labor’s. Farley suggested that was because One Nation had promised to quarantine certain visa classes – the Pacific Australian Labour Mobility scheme and aged care nurses – from its target. He said it meant the overall migrant influx would technically be significantly higher than 130,000 when those people were counted. The major parties have been grappling with how to neutralise One Nation’s campaign to clamp down on immigration without restricting crucial workforce numbers, harming the economy, or offending migrant communities. As One Nation ties itself in knots, the Coalition also vowed to protect backpackers from its visa cuts as the parties battle for Australia’s regional electorates.





Latest government data from June 30 this year shows this trend has continued: there were 225,648 working holidaymakers in the country at the end of the financial year, which is the highest June data on record. Housing spokesman Andrew Bragg earlier this month conceded that reality, when he pointed to backpackers as a potential way to reduce overall migration to about 180,000 – comments for which he has been counselled by party leadership. Related Article Immigration Taylor’s ‘historic’ migration cut could amount to just 5 per cent But the Nationals, who are on the front lines of battling One Nation for regional seats, don’t want working holidaymakers or those arriving under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme to be limited because they provide essential labour inflows for farms and manufacturers. Duniam said the Coalition wanted to make sure that its migration policy filled skill shortages, and that backpackers and PALM participants had minimal impact on net overseas migration.



Pauline Hanson has also said she does not want to touch those visa classes, and would instead focus on international students, temporary graduates and their dependents. Labor frontbencher Pat Conroy said One Nation’s migration “policy incoherence” proved the minor party was not fit to govern. “We had two different [One Nation] figures yesterday contradicting themselves about what their actual position is,” Conroy told Radio National. Labor has also been agonising over how to lower migration, and Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke pulled a keynote speech this month over cabinet concerns that the policy details were not ready.
