World.title: ‘No urgency’: Carey calls on selectors to back Labuschagne after another poor series
World.content:
SportCricketTest cricket ‘No urgency’: Carey calls on selectors to back Labuschagne after another poor series Nick Wright August 24, 2026 — 1:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alex Carey has urged Australian selectors to think carefully about their options before cutting No.3 Marnus Labuschagne from the Test team. Despite Australia cruising to victory by an innings and 51 runs inside two days and levelling the two-match series in Mackay, the nation’s woes with the willow have continued to raise questions about the top order. Loading Labuschagne’s struggles date back to the start of 2023. Since then, he has scored just one Test century and 1659 runs at an average of 29.69. The 32-year-old fell in limp fashion for four at Great Barrier Reef Arena when his attempted glance only resulted in the ball trickling off the bottom of his thigh pad into his stumps. Carey laughed when explaining the former world No.1 Test batsman had taken the scissors to his thigh guard in retribution.



“How unlucky is that, the old thigh pad onto the stumps. He cut it off,” Carey said. The reality is that if Labuschagne is to be dropped – skipper Pat Cummins refused to guarantee his selection for the upcoming tour of South Africa – the selectors must find someone capable of delivering more than a man with 11 Test centuries. None of the top 10 run scorers from the last Sheffield Shield season averaged more than 40, while very few have played red ball cricket recently – let alone batting in the top order. While rookie prospects Ollie Peake and Campbell Kellaway have been touted as long-term options, neither have knocked the door down through weight of runs.



Nathan McSweeney and Marcus Harris both played division two county cricket in England during the 2026 Australian winter, the former making three centuries and two half-centuries in nine matches for Northamptonshire, averaging 45.57. McSweeney toured Sri Lanka last year, having been thrown in as an opener against India at home when he struggled against a red-hot Jasprit Bumrah and averaged just 14.40 before making way for Sam Konstas. Marnus Labuschagne had another poor series against Bangladesh. Getty Images The 27-year-old McSweeney only averaged 28 last Shield season, but he did manage an unbeaten double century for Australia A against the England Lions. County runs did little to help Jake Weatherald, however. He averaged 60.37 in six division one clashes for Leicestershire in 2026 before finding himself on the scrapheap after the first Test against Bangladesh.



“Is Nathan the chat now, is he?” Carey said with a laugh after two questions about McSweeney. “Nathan has probably gone away from that [Test] experience and learned a lot about himself. He’s very calm, he’s got a very mature head for a young player. “He’s come back definitely a better player. He’s a great leader for South Australia. He’s had a taste of it [Test cricket], he’s hungry, but I also think the group we’ve got here are in a pretty good headspace as well in terms of grinding away, improving our game and trying to adapt to all conditions. Nathan McSweeney is one of the few players with recent red ball cricket under his belt who could put immediate pressure on Australia’s top order. Getty Images “You’ve had guys go away to England and play cricket through the winter, you’ve had guys last summer making scores on tough tracks in Sheffield Shield cricket, and had lots of guys experience the Test set-up, as well as one-day cricket. “There’s certainly some really good depth there, and some great options and headaches for selectors.”



Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket Australia’s had three two-day Tests in nine months. It’s damaging to cricket Labuschagne (36 runs at 12 against Bangladesh) was not the only struggler. Weatherald was axed for Matt Renshaw (who made eight in the second Test) after a run of lean performances at Test level – averaging 20.36 in six games in the Baggy Green. Beau Webster managed just 17 runs in three digs in the Bangladesh series, while Travis Head chopped onto his stumps in each knock after making decent starts. Only Steve Smith (157 runs at 52.33) and Cameron Green (184 at 61.33) played up to expectations. But while Carey admitted the batting group needed to find some form, he did not believe there was a need to rush into changes for the three-Test series in South Africa, starting on October 9, which follows ODI series against Zimbabwe and the Proteas. “No urgency from my point of view,” Carey said. “I guess there is a bit of time now between that next Test match – a month or so – and we’re always looking for ways to improve. “I’ll speak for Marnus; I think he’s shown some great signs. We know how good a player he is at his best, and I don’t think many batters found it easy out here. He’s working really hard, and a score is really close for him. “A 200-plus score [in Mackay] could’ve been a lot better, we understand that, but quality bowling as well. To get a 150-run lead is fantastic, but I think we felt a little bit like we left some runs out there.”

World.title: Crime rates up at suburban stations as police pull security officers
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Crime rates up at suburban stations as police pull security officers Alexander Darling August 24, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Crime rates were climbing steeply at suburban train stations across Melbourne in the years before Victoria Police decided to strip them of security officers, new data reveals. Protective services officers were stationed at the city’s 192 train stations between 6pm and the last train from 2010 but, in April, they were pulled from 119 stops and redeployed to the CBD and major suburban stations. Protective services officers at Southern Cross Station this year. Alexander Darling The force said the strategy would allow it to make best use of police resources. However, data obtained by this masthead shows the number of offences increased by nearly 180 per cent over five years to March this year at the 119 stations that have since lost their nightly PSO presence.



Teams of roaming PSOs now cover several of these smaller stations, riding trains between them, rather than being based permanently on station platforms. Crime Statistics Agency Victoria data suggests outer suburbs with growing populations face the largest increases in crime among those 119 stations, with Williams Landing station, on the Werribee train line, recording the highest number of offences in the past year. There were 138 offences at the station in the year to March 2026, double the number the year before. At Merinda Park station, on the Cranbourne line, there were fewer than three crimes in 2021, but 121 offences in the year to March 2026.



Almost 90 per cent of crimes recorded at train stations since 2021 are non-violent, such as car theft or drug possession. Crime data released to this masthead does not cover the period after PSOs were redeployed in April. That period will be covered by the next month’s release of Victoria Police’s official annual crime statistics, though concerns have been flagged that crime reports at many stations will have plateaued because there is nobody to report it to, rather than a real reduction in incidents. Superintendent Andrew Falconer, the architect of the new PSO system, said the redeployment was focused on using officers as effectively as possible to reduce crime. He said crime rates at stations such as Williams Landing had been largely driven by property offences like car theft, carried out at times when PSOs weren’t at the station.



He said he had seen internal data showing no increase in offences across the network after the PSOs were removed. “For vehicle theft, in particular, we’ve now got targeted operations on that, and we move between those areas of the high crime, and normally, once we’re able to arrest the primary offenders in the area, it significantly reduces it,” Falconer said. Superintendent Andrew Falconer of Victoria Police’s transit safety division. Alexander Darling “We’re seeing a reduction in the [busiest] category 1 stations by that additional deployment [of PSOs], and in the [less busy] category 3 we’re not seeing an increase.” Falconer said the arrest of five teenagers accused of assault in Sunshine on August 1 was an example of the new model’s effectiveness.



Related Article Exclusive

Public transport A stranger assaulted Hannah on a tram. She may never have reported him if not for this “The PSOs [left] the railway station because they were with police ... [to] make that arrest. We do have a number of examples like that now of different significant arrests by having additional deployment during the day,” he said. The state opposition has committed to hiring an extra 200 PSOs if elected in November, and opposition police spokesman Brad Battin said this would allow the bigger train stations and shopping centres to maintain their new level of coverage, while redeploying officers to suburban platforms overnight. “Some areas might need patrols a fraction early, particularly if you look at areas that have a high crime rate after school, so get them from 3pm until the last train, for example,” Battin said.



“It’s possible the numbers could steady because there is no one there [at the smaller stations] to make reports to. That’s why it’s really important to have PSOs there, so people do not just feel safe, but they’ve got someone to speak to at the station.” Related Article Crime Victoria’s most dangerous train stations revealed Falconer declined to answer what impact an extra 200 officers would have, but he reiterated the new model was already effectively addressing the growth areas in transport crime. In April, the government and police justified the reallocation of officers by noting that there were 79 stations which recorded no crimes against the person in 2024, and that a further 101 stations recorded fewer than six. Dr Berhan Ahmed hears many complaints about train station crime through his work as CEO of support service Africause, and not just from people who use the station nearby his office in Footscray.



Several weeks ago, Ahmed saw a woman who said she had been assaulted at Noble Park – a category 2 station in the south-east – where there is a permanent nightly PSO presence from 5pm. Dr Berhan Ahmed hears complaints about train station crime through his work at Africause. Jason South “She was at the station late afternoon and approached by a young man and woman and they asked her for money and her mobile phone,” Ahmed said. “She refused and they followed her to the car park, and when she started to shout they just bashed her. She yelled and they ran away. “She had bruises in her eye.” Ahmed said the woman came to him after being unable to find anyone at the station to report the crime to. He said he connected her with support for victims of crime.



Other commuters he saw felt so unsafe that PSOs were irrelevant to the decisions they were making. “Most of them are saying to me they wouldn’t go alone to [stations], they’re saying, ‘I need to go with someone’, rather than relying on police being there,” he said. “If it’s not safe, it’s not safe.” Falconer urged people to check a new website showing when and where PSOs would be, and that initiatives were under way to prevent at-risk people from committing crimes at certain stations. “I think one thing I’d encourage people to speak to the PSOs; they very much want to engage with people, ask them for advice,” he said. “We give them crime prevention advice to pass on.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘I’ve signed peoples’ arms for goodness’ sake’: Albanese vows WA’s GST system will stay put
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsWAGST ‘I’ve signed peoples’ arms for goodness’ sake’: Albanese vows WA’s GST system will stay put Hamish Hastie August 24, 2026 — 2:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has assured West Australians the GST arrangements that have boosted the state budget by billions annually will remain unchanged while he is in the top job. Albanese made the pledge during a press conference in Henderson in Perth’s south on Monday morning, in response to a Productivity Commission report that labelled the 2018 Morrison Government deal to introduce a 75-cents-in-the-dollar floor in the GST pool formula a “mistake”. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on a visit to BAE Systems Australia in Perth on Monday. AAP The Cook Labor government, industry groups, businesses and the WA community have heaped pressure on Albanese to be unequivocal about his support for the current arrangements. His public comments to date only included a promise the western state would keep its “fair share”.



“What I believe is very clearly there will be no change to WA’s GST arrangements whilst I’m prime minister. That is my view. That has consistently been my view,” he told reporters on Monday. “There will be no change.” The commission’s report was released on August 14 and Albanese denied he had waited until he came to WA to be more explicit in his position – referencing the time in 2024 when he used a marker to sign “no change to GST” on the arm of former West Australian journalist Dylan Caporn. “I didn’t wait. Although it was very clear, and I’ve said it multiple times ... I’ve signed peoples’ body parts, for goodness’ sake. I mean, seriously,” he said. The 2018 GST deal came with a no-worse-off guarantee to other states to get them across the line to agree to it.



That deal was expected to cost the Commonwealth about $2.3 billion, but now could balloon to $60 billion by 2030. Related Article GST ‘Angry’ WA premier tears into ‘dodgy, deceitful, dumb’ GST report Asked on Monday whether he would extend the no-worse-off guarantee beyond 2030 to satisfy the other states, Albanese said he would have discussions with the other premiers. “It is a good deal for the nation when you have an understanding and a clear, unequivocal position, being able to go forward with some certainty,” he said. WA Premier Roger Cook, who had been publicly urging Albanese to offer complete support for the deal, was ecstatic.



“Prime minister, can I just say, look, I think every Western Australian is both relieved and pleased to hear the words from the prime minister today that Western Australia’s arrangements for the GST will remain,” he said at the press conference in Henderson on Monday. “You don’t come to Western Australia on 45 occasions without appreciating that the Western Australian economy is driving the national economy, and we are very pleased that the prime minister has backed WA.” On Sunday, state opposition leader Basil Zempilas demanded Albanese clarify what “WA’s fair share” of the GST was. “‘A fair share’, prime minister, does not mean the same thing as ‘no change’,” Zempilas said. The Productivity Commission is due to produce its final report by December.



Albanese and Cook visited defence contractor BAE Systems in Henderson to unveil plans for the Henderson defence precinct, which will be used for a shipbuilding and sustainment facility.

World.title: Why the AFL CEO had a public crack at Dogs star Ed Richards
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Why the AFL CEO had a public crack at Dogs star Ed Richards Jon Pierik August 24, 2026 — 2:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon has taken a swipe at Ed Richards after the Western Bulldogs’ star suggested Friday night’s wildcard clash against Collingwood was not a real final. This weekend will be the first time the two do-or-die wildcard games will be held, the top eight having expanded to the top 10 in a bid to prolong supporter interest late into in the season. The eighth-placed Bulldogs will face the ninth-placed Magpies at the MCG, the clash expected to attract more than 85,000 supporters. Not quite a final: Western Bulldogs star Ed Richards doesn’t feel the wildcard round is an actual final. Getty Images The AFL has already said that its wildcard games are classified as finals, but Richards disagreed on Monday morning.



Related Article Four Points

AFL 2026 No one wants to play the Blues, but the Swans are sitting ducks as finals race turns wild “I personally think that we haven’t [made finals yet],” he said. “I would like to win this one and then really have that cemented finals spot in an elimination. So, just treating this one as, I guess, another week – round 25, if you would.” It prompted a verbal whack from Dillon, speaking at the launch of the AFL finals series on Monday, who was unimpressed. “Yeah, look, I haven’t heard those comments, but I’m not sure the Bulldogs have played many home-and-away games in front of 90,000-plus, so you might have a different feeling after the game,” Dillon said.



The largest crowd the Bulldogs have played in front of this season was 59,556, against Hawthorn at the MCG in round 13. It’s one of only two occasions the Bulldogs have featured in games attracting more than 50,000 fans – the other being against Fremantle in Perth. The Magpies and Bulldogs met in round 12, but that was held at Marvel Stadium before a crowd of 43,430, the Dogs winning by four points. Loading In the last clash between the two clubs at the MCG, in round two last year, 78,027 fans attended – the largest Bulldogs crowd of 2025. Scheduled to play the lower-ranked Magpies at the MCG off a shorter break, the Bulldogs would be entitled to complain that this game is not at Marvel Stadium – their home ground. But Richards insists the Bulldogs aren’t fazed, the AFL mandating that finals are held at the MCG.



“There’s been a bit of chat about that,” Richards said on Monday. Related Article Breaking

AFL 2026 Five Swans players banned from attending Brownlow “I love playing at the ’G, so I’m not too fussed. You’ve got to win finals [there], so you’ve got to be able to play finals at the MCG and play well. We’ve been pretty good there this year so, hopefully, we can continue some good form, play some good footy there on Friday.” Collingwood also get an extra day’s rest, having played Brisbane on Friday night before the Bulldogs beat Melbourne on Saturday. Spearhead Aaron Naughton, who rolled his ankle late against Melbourne, wasn’t involved in Monday’s light session but is expected to play.



“Needs to get rid of a bit of swelling and stuff from that ankle but, hopefully, he’ll be right,” Richards said. Ruckman Tim English hopes to return from injury, the 2022 All-Australian having missed the last two games because of an MCL strain. with AAP Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Kaiser airborne survey homes in on rich Victorian goldfield
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Kaiser airborne survey homes in on rich Victorian goldfield Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 24, 2026 — 2:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Gold producer Kaiser Reef has completed a high-resolution airborne magnetic survey over its Maldon gold project in Victoria, a move designed to zero in on the next batch of drill targets in one of Australia’s most historically rich goldfields. Kaiser’s latest work involved a low-altitude, helicopter-supported magnetic and radiometric survey flown with tight 35-metre line spacing over a 59-square-kilometre area. The survey aims to deliver a much clearer picture of the project’s underlying structural architecture and lithology. Kaiser Reef has completed a high-resolution helicopter-supported magnetic and radiometric survey over its Maldon gold project in Victoria. The new geophysical data follows recent soil sampling that identified multiple gold and arsenic pathfinder anomalies, giving the company a solid foundation to build upon. The company says the combined datasets will be an invaluable tool for locking in the next series of surface drill targets. The company is particularly interested in identifying cross-cutting structures that may intersect the region’s well-known north-south-trending reefs, as these intersections may be prime locations for gold mineralisation.



′ Maldon represents a district scale gold opportunity for Kaiser.′ Kaiser Reef managing director Brad Valiukas The Maldon goldfield, sitting in Victoria’s prolific Golden Triangle, has a serious pedigree, having historically produced an impressive 1.75 million ounces of gold at a bonanza grade of 28 grams per tonne. However, Kaiser says the district has been neglected by modern explorers for decades and remains substantially underexplored. The timing of the company’s expanded exploration program looks sharp, as the Australian gold sector continues to see a flurry of merger and acquisition activity, showing producers are willing to pay up for scale. At the same time, the recent spot gold price in Australian dollar terms is trading at higher levels, keeping the economics for new discoveries firmly in the spotlight. Kaiser Reef managing director Brad Valiukas said: “In the soils, we see some gold trends heading off the north-south alignment, and we are looking for the helicopter-based geophysics survey to confirm and better define the cross-cutting structures intersecting the multiple north-south reefs. This will be key to locking in the next series of surface targets for drill testing.” Kaiser is not just an explorer; it is also an established gold producer operating the Henty gold mine in Tasmania,providing it with valuable operational experience, a robust balance sheet and a source of cash flow to fund its growth ambitions. The company’s total group mineral resource currently stands at 5.42 million tonnes grading 3.59g/t gold for 625,000 ounces, including an inferred resource at Maldon’s Union Hill deposit of 1.31 million tonnes at 4.44g/t for 187,000 ounces. The company has reaffirmed its 2027 financial year production guidance of 32,000 ounces of gold across both the Maldon and Henty operations.



The Maldon project also comes with the significant advantage of the Porcupine Flats fully permitted and operating 200,000-tonne-per-annum processing plant and existing underground access, offering a potential fast-track to production should the current exploration program in Victoria prove successful. Kaiser isn’t sitting on its hands, with a 4350-metre surface drilling program also underway across four initial targets at Maldon. Standout results so far include a solid eight-metre hit at 4.16g/t gold from just 10m returned at its ‘Quill’ target. Follow-up drilling at Quill has now been completed with assays pending. In parallel, work has kicked off to refurbish the decline at the Union Hill mine and establish a new underground drill platform, giving the company freshangles to test the historic high-grade system from below. With a powerful new set of exploration data in hand and a clear geological model to test, Kaiser appears to be systematically working to unlock the modern potential of a classic Victorian goldfield. As the rods get ready to spin on a new follow-up drill program, the market will be watching to see if this old district still has a few secrets left to tell. World.title: Pauline Hanson’s deleted post deepens One Nation’s migration muddle
World.content:
Pauline Hanson has deleted a social media post containing her immigration targets from just five months ago, plunging One Nation into a deeper state of confusion as its MPs contradict themselves and each other over the party’s signature policy platform. Hanson posted on X on Sunday to say her party’s policy was to cut net overseas migration to 130,000 people a year after Farrer MP David Farley cast doubt on that target in a Sunday interview by saying it would inevitably be higher. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson in the Senate. Alex Ellinghausen New England MP Barnaby Joyce then backed Hanson on Monday morning, insisting the 130,000 net migration figure had been long-standing One Nation policy. “We’ve been saying that all along,” Joyce told Sunrise. “It’s 130,000 net overseas migration.” But One Nation’s public statements, including Hanson’s, contradict that claim and it was only defined as One Nation policy last week, when Joyce said 130,000 was a “net” figure.



A post from Pauline Hanson on X from March 1 this year, which states 130,000 arrivals, rather than net overseas migration, would be the cap under One Nation policy. X/@PaulineHansonOz Before that, Hanson had said the figure would be significantly lower. The One Nation leader has deleted a post on X she made on March 1 this year containing the lower target, which now conflicts with her most recent position from this weekend. In the deleted post, Hanson said One Nation was targeting a 130,000 cap on migrant arrivals. She said that would be compared with migrant departures, which had been 230,000 last year, to arrive at the net overseas migration figure. With those figures, NOM would be minus 100,000. The policy Hanson confirmed on Sunday would mean about 230,000 more people coming to Australia than her post from March. One Nation’s website still contains the previous policy, saying it would cap the number of visas granted each year to 130,000 – a metric that would lead to either zero or negative NOM depending on how many people left the country each year.



A screengrab of One Nation’s website, taken on August 24, 2026, which shows the party would cap visas at 130,000 people per year. This stands in contrast to recent comments by party MPs. onenation.org.au/immigration The party has been forced to clarify its position after the latest curveball was thrown over the weekend, when MP David Farley told the ABC that migration numbers under One Nation would be “not too different” to Labor’s. Farley suggested that was because One Nation had promised to quarantine certain visa classes – the Pacific Australian Labour Mobility scheme and aged care nurses – from its target. He said it meant the overall migrant influx would technically be significantly higher than 130,000 when those people were counted. The major parties have been grappling with how to neutralise One Nation’s campaign to clamp down on immigration without restricting crucial workforce numbers, harming the economy, or offending migrant communities. As One Nation ties itself in knots, the Coalition also vowed to protect backpackers from its visa cuts as the parties battle for Australia’s regional electorates.





Latest government data from June 30 this year shows this trend has continued: there were 225,648 working holidaymakers in the country at the end of the financial year, which is the highest June data on record. Housing spokesman Andrew Bragg earlier this month conceded that reality, when he pointed to backpackers as a potential way to reduce overall migration to about 180,000 – comments for which he has been counselled by party leadership. Related Article Immigration Taylor’s ‘historic’ migration cut could amount to just 5 per cent But the Nationals, who are on the front lines of battling One Nation for regional seats, don’t want working holidaymakers or those arriving under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme to be limited because they provide essential labour inflows for farms and manufacturers. Duniam said the Coalition wanted to make sure that its migration policy filled skill shortages, and that backpackers and PALM participants had minimal impact on net overseas migration.



Pauline Hanson has also said she does not want to touch those visa classes, and would instead focus on international students, temporary graduates and their dependents. Labor frontbencher Pat Conroy said One Nation’s migration “policy incoherence” proved the minor party was not fit to govern. “We had two different [One Nation] figures yesterday contradicting themselves about what their actual position is,” Conroy told Radio National. Labor has also been agonising over how to lower migration, and Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke pulled a keynote speech this month over cabinet concerns that the policy details were not ready. World.title: ‘No urgency’: Carey calls on selectors to back Labuschagne after another poor series
World.content:
SportCricketTest cricket ‘No urgency’: Carey calls on selectors to back Labuschagne after another poor series Nick Wright August 24, 2026 — 1:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alex Carey has urged Australian selectors to think carefully about their options before cutting No.3 Marnus Labuschagne from the Test team. Despite Australia cruising to victory by an innings and 51 runs inside two days and levelling the two-match series in Mackay, the nation’s woes with the willow have continued to raise questions about the top order. Loading Labuschagne’s struggles date back to the start of 2023. Since then, he has scored just one Test century and 1659 runs at an average of 29.69. The 32-year-old fell in limp fashion for four at Great Barrier Reef Arena when his attempted glance only resulted in the ball trickling off the bottom of his thigh pad into his stumps. Carey laughed when explaining the former world No.1 Test batsman had taken the scissors to his thigh guard in retribution.



“How unlucky is that, the old thigh pad onto the stumps. He cut it off,” Carey said. The reality is that if Labuschagne is to be dropped – skipper Pat Cummins refused to guarantee his selection for the upcoming tour of South Africa – the selectors must find someone capable of delivering more than a man with 11 Test centuries. None of the top 10 run scorers from the last Sheffield Shield season averaged more than 40, while very few have played red ball cricket recently – let alone batting in the top order. While rookie prospects Ollie Peake and Campbell Kellaway have been touted as long-term options, neither have knocked the door down through weight of runs.



Nathan McSweeney and Marcus Harris both played division two county cricket in England during the 2026 Australian winter, the former making three centuries and two half-centuries in nine matches for Northamptonshire, averaging 45.57. McSweeney toured Sri Lanka last year, having been thrown in as an opener against India at home when he struggled against a red-hot Jasprit Bumrah and averaged just 14.40 before making way for Sam Konstas. Marnus Labuschagne had another poor series against Bangladesh. Getty Images The 27-year-old McSweeney only averaged 28 last Shield season, but he did manage an unbeaten double century for Australia A against the England Lions. County runs did little to help Jake Weatherald, however. He averaged 60.37 in six division one clashes for Leicestershire in 2026 before finding himself on the scrapheap after the first Test against Bangladesh.



“Is Nathan the chat now, is he?” Carey said with a laugh after two questions about McSweeney. “Nathan has probably gone away from that [Test] experience and learned a lot about himself. He’s very calm, he’s got a very mature head for a young player. “He’s come back definitely a better player. He’s a great leader for South Australia. He’s had a taste of it [Test cricket], he’s hungry, but I also think the group we’ve got here are in a pretty good headspace as well in terms of grinding away, improving our game and trying to adapt to all conditions. Nathan McSweeney is one of the few players with recent red ball cricket under his belt who could put immediate pressure on Australia’s top order. Getty Images “You’ve had guys go away to England and play cricket through the winter, you’ve had guys last summer making scores on tough tracks in Sheffield Shield cricket, and had lots of guys experience the Test set-up, as well as one-day cricket. “There’s certainly some really good depth there, and some great options and headaches for selectors.”



Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket Australia’s had three two-day Tests in nine months. It’s damaging to cricket Labuschagne (36 runs at 12 against Bangladesh) was not the only struggler. Weatherald was axed for Matt Renshaw (who made eight in the second Test) after a run of lean performances at Test level – averaging 20.36 in six games in the Baggy Green. Beau Webster managed just 17 runs in three digs in the Bangladesh series, while Travis Head chopped onto his stumps in each knock after making decent starts. Only Steve Smith (157 runs at 52.33) and Cameron Green (184 at 61.33) played up to expectations. But while Carey admitted the batting group needed to find some form, he did not believe there was a need to rush into changes for the three-Test series in South Africa, starting on October 9, which follows ODI series against Zimbabwe and the Proteas. “No urgency from my point of view,” Carey said. “I guess there is a bit of time now between that next Test match – a month or so – and we’re always looking for ways to improve. “I’ll speak for Marnus; I think he’s shown some great signs. We know how good a player he is at his best, and I don’t think many batters found it easy out here. He’s working really hard, and a score is really close for him. “A 200-plus score [in Mackay] could’ve been a lot better, we understand that, but quality bowling as well. To get a 150-run lead is fantastic, but I think we felt a little bit like we left some runs out there.”

World.title: Govt pushes ahead with social media ban for under-16s
World.content:
The government is pressing ahead with its ban on social media for under-16 year olds, with the legislation set to be introduced on Monday.

But ACT and New Zealand First will not support the bill.

The bill puts the pressure on social media companies to comply, establishing an online safety regulator and setting up a penalty regime.

Watch the prime minister answer questions about the ban:

Education Minister Erica Stanford, who had been tasked with leading the work on the ban, said the bill would bring New Zealand into line with other countries that were placing greater responsibility on tech companies to protect children online.

"The bill places legal obligations on platforms. No penalties are proposed for children, their parents or caregivers," Stanford said.

"It doesn't just introduce a minimum age requirement. It creates an enduring framework that can evolve alongside technology and holds platforms responsible for understanding and reducing the risks they create for children."

Watch the government announcement here:

ACT and New Zealand First have invoked the 'agree to disagree clause', meaning National will need Labour's support to get the bill past its first reading.

ACT leader David Seymour said protecting children online was serious, but disagreed with National's approach.

"Unfortunately, the National Party have hitched their wagon to a terrible solution. The ban they propose won't work, and the side effects will leave us work off."

A New Zealand First spokesperson confirmed the party also opposed the bill.

But even Labour has indicated it may not support the bill, releasing a letter written by its science and technology spokesperson Reuben Davidson to Stanford.

The letter - which Davidson wrote on Friday - said there were still some matters Labour wanted addressed before it could offer its support.

"I want to be clear that we take this legislation very seriously. The safety of young people in Aotearoa New Zealand is at stake, and the risks they face in increasingly complex online environments are significant. It is critically important that this legislation is in the best possible shape at first reading to ensure it provides a robust safety net for those who need it most," he wrote.

Among the 79 things Labour was asking were the extent of consultation with children and young people on the bill, how a social media operator could show it has complied, whether the government would publish a full privacy impact assessment, and how the penalties would be enforced.

Davidson also wanted the whole Labour caucus to have access to the bill before deciding whether it could support it.

The bill would require "high risk" platforms, such as Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, X, and Facebook, to take "reasonable steps" to check users were over the age of 16.

The reasonable steps included using existing account information, facial age estimation, digital ID services, and formal ID.

Messaging apps such as WhatsApp or Discord, and online games like Roblox, are not included in the bill.

AI chatbots that are primarily for productivity, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are also out of scope, but social AI companions are covered by the ban.

File photo. AFP / Jonathan Raa

Platforms would also be required to regularly assess the risks they posed, and report on how those risks were being identified and reduced.

A factsheet released by the government said those risks included included illegal content, harmful content (such as grooming, cyberbullying, harassment, and AI deepfakes), advertising and behavioural profiling, and service design and function.

The regulator, which will be established within the Department of Internal Affairs, will be able to monitor, investigate and enforce compliance.

Its tools would range from simply gathering information or auditing the age assurance technology used by tech companies, all the way up to geo-blocking or criminal penalties.

A ban on VPNs is not in the legislation.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said parents did have a role to play in monitoring what social media platform their children were on, but so did social media companies.

World.title: Final emergency services test underway as opening date for Auckland's City Rail Link draws near
World.content:
More than 75 actors have been helping Auckland's emergency services test their responses to a range of scenarios ahead of the city's underground train network opening next month.

The City Rail Link (CRL), would open in three weeks on Sunday, September 13.

The last emergency exercise was taking place this week, simulating a fire on a train near one of the main stations.

In total, 15 emergency exercises have tested police, paramedics and fire fighters' responses to a range of scenarios including train derailments, station fires and mass evacuations.

These have each involved more than 300 volunteer passengers and also, actors, to help bring the scenario to life.

CRL Karanga-a-Hape Station on open day. (File photo) RNZ / Lucy Xia

The volunteers reflected the diversity of Auckland's daily commuters including older people, those with health conditions, people with limited English, and those with hearing, visual or mobility needs.

Auckland Transport (AT) General Manager Rail Services, Mark Lambert, said the testing programme has provided confidence the CRL was ready to welcome Aucklanders when it opened.

"The City Rail Link is unlike anything else in New Zealand's rail network, so it has been vital for everyone involved to practise how we would respond in a range of different situations. The strong collaboration between emergency services and our rail partners has helped build confidence that Aucklanders will be well supported should an incident ever occur."

The tests were comprehensive and looked at frontline responses through to the supporting systems behind the scenes, including ventilation and smoke extraction, alarms, communications, CCTV, lighting and control room operations.

Hato Hone St John Area Operations Manager, Kim Moser, said these realistic exercises help ensure emergency services were well prepared to respond safely and effectively if they were needed once the CRL opens.

"For Hato Hone St John, this testing has been an important opportunity for our ambulance personnel to build familiarity with the CRL's new underground environment and practise coordinated responses alongside our emergency service and transport partners."

The exercise builds on an extensive emergency testing programme completed last month, which involved more than 1400 volunteer passengers.

KiwiRail leads and coordinates emergency response to incidents in the CRL tunnels via its Auckland Rail Operations Centre. Auckland One Rail responds to unplanned events on trains and in the CRL stations - with the assistance of emergency services as needed.

City Rail Link chief executive Patrick Brockie said it was a unique environment.

"The City Rail Link's underground environment, with tunnels more than 40 metres below ground in some parts, presents unique challenges around access, evacuation and communication, requiring specialist planning and coordination."

Fire and Emergency New Zealand region manager Ron Devlin said they were carrying out site visits and additional training in the weeks leading up to opening.

"People may have seen our fire trucks parked outside the stations at all hours of the day," he said.

World.title: Decision to install fence at Wellington waterfront too 'highly charged' council says, despite death of teacher Isaac Levings
World.content:
Wellington City Council's chief operating officer is adamant the decision to install balustrades along the waterfront is too highly charged to be made by officials - despite multiple drownings.

The comments by James Roberts were made at the coroner's inquest into the 2023 drowning of Christchurch teacher Isaac Levings.

Since 2013, eight people have drowned in the harbour.

The inquest into Leving's death, following a concert by the band The 1975, resumed on Monday.

Earlier this month, the inquest heard from former council city and parks manager, Shane Binnie, who said recommendations from another inquest, into the death of Sandy Calkin two years earlier, weren't acted on.

He said while proposals to improve lighting went ahead, protection along the waterfront edge in the form of balustrades, or benches and bollards, didn't.

The Wellington waterfront pictured last year. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Binnie said in his opinion, the council senior executive refused to accept the safety options being put forward.

Lighting upgrades were undertaken in 2024, but a proposal to erect a waterfront fence was ultimately voted down by the council in August 2025.

In Wellington District Court on Monday, Roberts hit back at Binnie's claims and rejected any assertion that waterfront safety wasn't a council priority.

He said he did not agree with Binnie's assessment that edge protection - balustrades - was an operational matter.

Roberts said even in instances where officers and the executive had the authority to make decisions, "high-profile" or "politically sensitive matters" could be escalated to elected members.

"On this occasion, and in accordance with the relevant delegations, officers were required to put the decision to councillors and abide by the decision that they made.

"It was not a decision that could have been lawfully made by officers."

During his evidence, Binnie accepted temporary fencing erected on the waterfront following Leving's death would "catch a lot of heat" and was featured in the media. The fencing was removed in late 2025.

The temporary fencing which had now been removed. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Roberts said he acknowledged issues surrounding protection on the waterfront edge were "serious, ongoing and had been the subject of considerable work, debate and difficult decision making".

He said council had continued to invest "significant time, resources, and funding" into improving waterfront safety, including lighting upgrades, enhanced incident reporting and investigations, as well as the development of edge protection solutions - noting $11.1 million in funding for potential works had been carried forward to the 26-27 financial year.

He said the work undertaken since the inquest into Calkin's death demonstrated a "genuine commitment" to learning from past incidents, responding to the coroner's recommendations, and to pursuing proportionate measures to reduce the risk on the waterfront.

Calkin's father, Roger Calkin, who was sitting in the inquest on Monday, told RNZ he disagreed with Roberts' assertion and felt a Water Safety New Zealand Drowning Blackspots report, received by the council in May this year, was dismissed.

Roger Calkin said the report made it clear that there had been no deaths along Auckland's CBD waterfront since balustrades were installed in 2017, while there had been five deaths on Wellington's waterfront.

The report said the difference between the cities was observational but consistent with "edge protection acting as a mitigating factor".

Notion that advice was watered-down rejected

Under questioning from Josh Shaw, the counsel assisting the Coroner, Roberts defended the advice put to councillors regarding a proposal to erect balustrades on the waterfront.

A former council staffer, Shane Binnie has previously told the court that he had been sidelined after presenting options for protection around the waterfront edge.

Shaw put to Roberts that the exclusion of staff perceived to be advocates for barriers, weakened the advice ultimately given to elected members.

"What I'm suggesting is that this focus on neutrality and balance, this removal of anyone who you think might be straying into the territory of advocating for a particular position, it runs the risk of watering down and removing the urgency, the imperative, the need to deal with something that's a 20-year-plus issue to make sure that more people don't die."

Roberts rejected the notion that the advice was watered-down.

"We have to be careful how we construct and provide advice and guidance to council and the processes we follow to get that," he said.

"We have on a number of occasions been subject to judicial review for decisions and the processes related to those decisions made by council."

Roberts said balustrades was the option recommended to councillors, which followed multiple discussions, briefings, workshops and evidence provided to elected members, such as previous coroners' reports into waterfront deaths.

"Ultimately, we got a decision in front of councillors as soon as we could, as thoroughly as we could, with the right information that would be robust and would hold up to a future interrogation.

"And I believe we did emphasise the balustrade option as the recommended one."

World.title: Christchurch business evacuates over hazardous, unidentified substance
World.content:
A person has been taken to hospital in a moderate condition after a hazardous substance forced the evacuation of a Christchurch business.

Fire and Emergency crews were called to Buchan Street in Sydenham just before 1pm on Monday.

St John treated two people, with one taken to Christchurch Hospital.

A cordon was put in place but has since lifted and FENZ left the scene at 3.30pm.

World.title: Woman appears in court after death of Northland man
World.content:
A woman has appeared in court over the death of a Northland man during the weekend.

Emergency services were called to Haruru, near Paihia, about 4.30am on Saturday. Police, St John Ambulance and the Paihia Volunteer Fire Brigade responded to the emergency.

A man found unresponsive at the property died a short time later.

A 56-year-old woman was arrested at the scene and appeared in the Kaikohe District Court this afternoon.

She has been charged with injuring with intent to injure, and wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm.

The woman was granted interim name suppression and remanded in custody. She is next due in court by audio-visual link on 8 September for a bail application.

The victim's name has yet to be formally released.

Northland's top investigator Detective Inspector Rhys Johnston initially described the man's death as unexplained.

A post-mortem was carried out on Sunday and enquiries into his death were continuing.

Haruru residents could expect to see an increased police presence in the area, Johnston said.

World.title: Former ambulance paramedics called back out to help with 'exceptional' demand
World.content:
Former St John paramedics now working in other parts of the organisation are being asked to jump back into ambulances to meet "exceptional" demand.

Hato Hone St John received 16,794 calls through 111 for the week ending 23 August, another all-time high.

A new daily record of 2606 calls was set on Friday 14 August, compared with an average of 2061 a day last August.

Hato Hone St John director of ambulance operations Doug Gallagher said the sustained workload was having an impact.

Since they put the call out over the weekend, 30 to 35 staff had volunteered to do ambulance shifts outside of their regular duties.

These were people in support roles, like quality and research staff, or tutors.

"Our people have been working through exceptional demand for more than two weeks," he said.

"They continue to do an outstanding job, but repeated high-workload shifts, winter illness affecting our people and their dependants, and pressure across the health system are taking a toll."

Some staff who held ambulance or clinical qualifications - but were now working in education, leadership or other non-patient-facing roles - were stepping up to work in frontline operations, he said.

The organisation's major incident arrangements remained in place, providing national oversight of demand, ambulance availability, workforce capacity and patient-safety risks.

Some of the greatest pressure was in Auckland, he said, particularly during the evening and overnight.

The period of highest demand across the board tended to be 1pm till midnight.

Ambulance crews have been experiencing delays with handing over patients at hospital emergency departments, particularly in the largest cities including Auckland, Hamilton, Palmerston North and Christchurch.

Patients continued to be prioritised according to clinical need. However, during the most intense periods, some patients assessed as time-critical might wait longer than Hato Hone St John would want.

People should still call 111 when there was a threat to life, he said.

"Please do not delay calling in an emergency. If the patient's condition worsens after calling 111, call again and tell us what has changed.

"We also ask everyone to treat our call handlers, dispatchers, clinicians and ambulance crews with patience and respect. They are working incredibly hard to help patients and communities."

World.title: Ex-NBA player who says he identifies as woman ejected from WNBA game
World.content:
Former NBA centre Enes Kanter Freedom has been ejected from an Indiana-Chicago WNBA game after Sky guard Natasha Cloud yelled and pointed in his direction late in the third quarter.

Freedom was sitting along the baseline on Sunday night (Monday AEST). He had on a black shirt that read "WOMAN noun. adult human female".

The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then went to confront Kanter, who held his arms out and took one step on the court. Security and a handful of Sky players stepped in between the two before the dispute escalated.

Freedom was then escorted from the court area. He displayed his shirt as he walked toward the lobby. He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing Wintrust Arena.

Sky coach Tyler Marsh said the team had rallied around Cloud.

"Tash didn't wanna feel like she was a distraction and I told her she wasn't," he said.

"I told her that we all embrace her as someone that protects our team and protects people that need to be protected. Tash is always going to stand on that, and we stand for Tash."

Freedom and Royce White, another former NBA player, declared themselves eligible for the WNBA draft this month, saying they identified as women.

The argument that's hijacking the WNBA Sophie Cunningham insists she wants to protect the sanctity of women's sport, but her comments have opened her league up to an unprecedented attack.

"I'm transgender. I'm a woman … I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purposes of … professional basketball," White previously said.

"I think I'd be unstoppable."

Freedom said he and his team had reviewed the WNBA's eligibility criteria and its approach to self-identification and inclusion, and argued that if declaring an identity were sufficient, then he met the requirements to compete.

The confrontation came in a game that Indiana star Sophie Cunningham was playing in. Cunningham previously voiced support for barring transgender girls and women from girls' and women's sports in an extensive ESPN profile.

"I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans," Cunningham said.

"And I'm like, 'I never once said that.' I think that I am here to extend love.

"But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

Protesters from both sides of the argument have gathered outside a number of WNBA games, with fans at the Sky-Fever game calling out Kanter as he entered the arena.

Sophie Cunningham (left) has been at the centre of the controversy, highlighted by Enes Kanter's (right) stunt. (Getty Images: Michael Reaves)

One was heard telling the former NBA centre to get his "bitch ass out of Chicago", while another said "I'm not touching him I'm just saying f*** you, bitch".

"Knowing that rallies are happening on both sides shows the platform that the W has and the stunts for attention are just continuing to try and ride the wave that we have,” New York Liberty star Breanna Stewart said.

"I want Liberty fans and even Indy fans that are going to come here tonight to be able to have this arena be a safe space."

There has never been a transgender woman player in the WNBA.

Commissioner Cathy Engelbert last week denounced people she said were trying to "sow divisiveness" over the issue.

Engelbert's comments in a pre-game gathering before a Fever-Wings game in Dallas were her first public remarks since the league called out what it said were bad faith efforts to use the debate to "demean or marginalise others".

"People are trying to use the league to sow divisiveness," Engelbert said.

"We're being the centre of political football for people who have never watched the WNBA, never have written about the WNBA or reported on the WNBA."

The league's collective bargaining agreement states that "only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA", but it does not include any more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.

Engelbert sent a memo this month to team presidents and general managers saying the league would discuss the subject of transgender women in women's basketball.

"There's always going to be haters out there and we denounce it," Engelbert said last week.

"But that's what happens when you have made it as a legitimate sports media and entertainment product."

World.title: AFL boss says suspended Swans will not be invited to Brownlow ceremony
World.content:
AFL boss Andrew Dillon has spoken to the media about the Sydney Swans scandal, saying "the actions of a few don't define the actions of the entire industry".

Dillon was at the launch of the men's AFL finals series and the first-ever wildcard round but was mainly asked about the AFL's handling of the Sydney Swans scandal, as well as details on allegations of drug use by the players.

Players Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon have been stood down by the Sydney Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late after last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are separately investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching a woman without her consent.

A police investigation is still underway, but no charges have been laid or arrests made.

Dillon and the AFL released a statement on Tuesday evening, the day after the story emerged, but today marked the first time Dillon or any of the league's higher-ups had fronted the media on the matter.

Chief executive Dillon said it was fair to say the scandal had "overshadowed" the start of the finals, but that he hoped football could bring people together, as evidenced by the emotional scenes after the Swans' men's and women's double header at the SCG on Sunday.

Swans fans descend on SCG amid club scandal Sydney Swans fans react to an emotional week, where a scandal continues to engulf the club, as they prepare to watch a historic double header at the SCG.

"The actions of a few do not take away from the thousands of people involved in football at all different levels who do great things all the time," he said.

"But what we do know is that we can do things better and we will continue to do that and we will continue to learn to be better.

"I think the actions of a few don't define the actions of the entire industry."

Dillon said the five suspended players would not be invited to the Brownlow Medal ceremony, held on the Monday before the grand final, but remained eligible for the award.

Dillon said the league would not conduct its own enquiries into the incident until after the police investigation was finished.

On Saturday, police provided an update about the investigation being undertaken by detectives from the Sexual Crimes Squad.

"The exact circumstances of the matter are still being established, and a number of people have been spoken to," the statement read.

"As the investigation remains active and ongoing, we will not be commenting further, including providing information on the specific circumstances of the matter, movements of detectives and any statements or interviews taken."

In a statement, the Sydney Swans said the club "supports the action taken by Victoria Police in releasing today's statement regarding the investigation".

The club's statement also addressed comments relating to other men, beyond the five players identified by the club, being present in the hotel room at the centre of the allegations.

"The Sydney Swans categorically confirms that no member of staff is involved in the investigation. This includes being in the hotel room central to the police investigation," it read.

"The club reiterates that no player has been interviewed by police at this stage."

That's the end of the press conference 'It is a privilege to play AFL': Dillon Dillon is asked a follow up whether the five named players relating to the scandal have been held accountable. "There's been accountability for those players," he says. "It is a privilege to play AFL and with that comes responsibilities." AFL has reviewed illicit drugs policy Dillon is asked whether the alleged drug use that has created part of the story around the Swans scandal has prompted a rethink over the league's illicit drugs policy. "We've just undergone an extensive review of the illicit drugs policy," Dillon says. "That will be taking effect from this off season. "There's accountability for the players and there will continue to be." Show more

World.title: Runner smashes half-marathon record, heads straight to the football
World.content:
Yomif Kejelcha has smashed the half-marathon world record, running a staggering 56 minutes and 51 seconds at the Media Maratón Ciudad de Buenos Aires in Argentina on Sunday.

The Ethiopian shaved 29 seconds off the previous mark of 57:20, which had been set by Uganda's Jacob Kiplimo in Lisbon in March.

Kejelcha's time and that of the record he just beat are still subject to ratification by World Athletics.

The Media Maratón Ciudad de Buenos Aires is a World Athletics Label road race and took place under favourable conditions of 6 degrees Celsius and with a slight breeze.

As ever, the super shoe gets plenty of post-race love from Yomif Kejelcha. (Instagram: @maratondebuenosaires)

Tadese Worku (59:20) and Bereket Nega (1:00:20) of Ethiopia completed the podium.

"I'm over the moon," Kejelcha told World Athletics.

"I'm super happy and right now I don't feel any tiredness. The travel from Ethiopia was too long and I was tired the first days here, but later I felt better and today I was full of beans.

"I had planned to run conservatively over the early stages, but I felt good and decided to give it my all.

"This time is unbelievable. I can't describe it with words.

"I now hope to try the Argentinian meat, which has a very good reputation, and this afternoon I have been invited to watch the River Plate-Vélez football match. I'm very grateful."

At the historic Estadio Monumental, Kejelcha showed off his new record on a new River Plate shirt, although would have been disappointed as Vélez Sarsfield came from 2-0 down to draw 2-2 in their Argentine Primera División clash.

Clearly Los Millonarios don't share Kejelcha's stamina.

Yomif Kejelcha showed off his record on a new River Plate kit at at the Estadio Monumental. (Instagram: @maratondebuenosaires)

Kejelcha's time allowed him to reclaim the record, which he previously held with a 57:30 in Valencia in October 2024.

The time is slower than that recorded by Kiplimo in Barcelona last year, when he ran what he described as "the perfect race" to stop the clock in 56:42.

But World Athletics did not ratify that time because race conditions did not comply with their regulations.

Kejelcha ran the race at an average pace of 2 minutes and 42 seconds per kilometre — which would give you a 5km parkrun time of 13 minutes and 28 seconds.

However, as was the case when he became the second man to run an official race marathon in less than two hours in London last year, he negative split the race, running the second half faster than the first.

Super shoes won't be banned despite 'technological doping' claims Lord Sebastian Coe says World Athletics has a duty to "enable" super shoe development despite concerns.

He set out behind two pacemakers, going through the first 5km at 13:45, while the second 5km was run in 13:34.

His subsequent 5km split was a remarkable 13:22, with the Ethiopian holding that pace through the next 5km, running it in 13:23.

Last April at the London Marathon, the 29-year-old two-time Olympian ran 1:59:41, finishing second behind Kenya's Sabastian Sawe, who set the world record with a 1:59:30.

In the women's race, Ethiopia's Fotyen Tesfay stormed to victory in 1:03:57, comfortably beating her two Kenyan rivals Nelvin Jepkemboi (1:05:06) and Catherine Amanang'ole (1:05:11).

World.title: 'Disappointed' Hird congratulates McVeigh ahead of Bombers coach call
World.content:
Mark McVeigh appears set to be unveiled as Essendon's next senior coach, with fellow applicant James Hird congratulating his former teammate on the impending appointment.

Bombers legend Hird had been vocal in expressing his desire to return for another stint as coach, after Brad Scott was sacked in May.

Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham and Adelaide assistant Murray Davis were also in the mix.

But McVeigh, an assistant to Dean Cox at Sydney, is reportedly on the verge of being appointed, with an announcement expected as soon as tomorrow.

Mark McVeigh is in the box seat to be offered the Bombers job. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Interim coach Dean Solomon hands over the reins after the Bombers (2-21) completed the worst season in club history with a 10-point defeat to Port Adelaide on Sunday.

"Firstly, congratulations to Mark. He's a great friend of mine and I'm very proud of him that he's going to be named the coach, so good on him," Hird said on Nine yesterday night.

"From a personal point of view, it's very disappointing. I'm disappointed. I put my heart and soul into the effort, but obviously fell short and that's the way it goes."

Hird indicated he was yet to hear an official decision from Essendon, but said "maybe that's coming".

The 53-year-old ruled out returning to the Bombers in a different role, but said he still had the passion to coach.

James Hird, Dean Solomon and Mark McVeigh together in 2022 when they were all at the Giants. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Hird is director of coaching with VFL club Port Melbourne.

"We have a finals series to play," Hird said.

"We'll see what plays out at the end of the year with some other clubs who have contacted me and we'll see what happens."

McVeigh is reportedly set to present to the Essendon board again today, with an announcement imminent.

The 45-year-old played 232 games for Essendon and was one of the 34 players suspended over the club's devastating drugs saga, when Hird was coach.

McVeigh currently serves as Sydney's defensive coach, but could leave the club immediately to play a role in the Bombers' end-of-season exit meetings and list management decisions.

The second-placed Swans are preparing for a finals campaign while bracing for more fallout from the scandal that has rocked the club.

"That's one thing this football club's done well for a long period of time … be ready for the unexpected or if something does arise," Sydney coach Cox said last week about the potential of losing McVeigh to the Bombers.

"We've had those meetings [and] discussions. We're really clear on what will happen if he was or wasn't to get the [Essendon] position."

Two-time Essendon premiership champion and former captain Hird first took over as Bombers coach in 2010.

He was suspended for the 2014 season amid the fallout from the drugs saga, returned as coach in 2015 and resigned in August that year.

Hird had garnered plenty of support from Bombers fans in his latest bid to return as coach, after he narrowly missed out when Scott was appointed in 2022.

World.title: Former Roosters premiership star unveiled as PNG Chiefs' '007' signing
World.content:
Joey Manu has been unveiled as the much-hyped PNG Chief 007, with the two-time premiership winner to return to the NRL in 2028.

The Chiefs officially confirmed today the former Sydney Roosters utility signed a two-year deal with the club, which now boasts a backline that will be the envy of the NRL.

PNG had long hyped their seventh signing, with speculation Penrith superstar Nathan Cleary was bound for the club as their inaugural halfback.

But with a staircase at their home base showing each of their signings and "007" listed as "reserved", that honour will now go to code-hopper Manu ahead of the 2028 season.

Loading Instagram content

"We're thrilled to add Joey to our squad moving forward," Chiefs general manager Michael Chammas said.

"He is a world-class footballer with versatility across several positions and can change a game in a single moment with the skills he possesses.

"His experience and demonstrated success at the highest level will be a great benefit to our team and we can't wait to see him have a significant impact in the Chiefs jersey."

Manu joins a list that already includes Jarome Luai, Alex Johnston, Connor Watson, Zac Lomax, Brian To'o and Englishman Matty Lees.

But the move appears likely to have ended the 30-year-old's boyhood dream of representing the All Blacks.

To'o is still just the beginning for PNG Brian To'o is the fourth player to sign for Papua New Guinea who has played State of Origin in the past two years. It's a sign of things to come, with the NRL's richest club yet to truly enter free agency.

Manu left the NRL for an overseas rugby union career after the 2024 season, starting in Japan before a move to French team Racing 92 last year.

But his French rugby deal runs to the end of 2027, and New Zealand Rugby only selects players for the All Blacks if they play domestically.

Manu will be 33 by the time his Chiefs deal finishes.

Manu became one of the NRL's most prized utility players across 181 games, including the 2018 and 2019 premiership wins, with the Roosters.

He was named Dally M centre of the year in 2022 and won the Golden Boot award as the sport's best international player later that year.

The athletic New Zealand representative is equally adept in the centres and at fullback, and can also capably slot into the halves in a pinch.

On leaving the NRL after the Roosters' 2024 finals campaign, Manu offered no guarantees of ever returning to the 13-man code.

But any possible comeback had widely been expected to come with the Roosters, who scouted him as a teenager.

Instead, Manu becomes the latest jewel in the crown of the NRL's forthcoming 19th team, which can offer lucrative tax-free salaries to its signings.

PNG will be able to officially hit the market on November 1, with Cleary headlining a list of players who could still become free agents at that time.

The club has also been linked to Gold Coast utility AJ Brimson and Canberra second-rower Hudson Young, both of whom are State of Origin players, in recent weeks.

Isaah Yeo, Latrell Mitchell and Bradman Best are among other household names without deals beyond the 2027 season.

World.title: Aussie athletes continue top form with trio of medals at Diamond League
World.content:
Commonwealth Games champions Eleanor Patterson and Rose Davies have kicked on from their Glasgow triumphs, along with double silver medallist Jessica Hull, as Australia's athletes have continued to shine on the Diamond League circuit in Poland.

All three made the podium at the Diamond League Silesia meet in Chorzów overnight, with high jump champion Patterson soaring to third place, Glasgow 5,000/10,000 metre double winner Davies grabbing bronze in the 5,000m and Hull running her fastest race of the year to finish 1,500m runner-up.

But there was disappointment for Glasgow sprint hero Lachlan Kennedy, who after his Australian-record run for silver at Glasgow's Scotstoun Stadium, failed to make the 100m final in Chorzów.

Pride of place went to Olympic silver medallist Hull, who tried out new tactics, sitting back in the field in the Silesian Stadium and kicking for home at the top of the straight, only to be reeled in by Ethiopia's Tsige Duguma. She needed a 2026 world-leading time of three minutes and 55.06 seconds to pip Hull's 3:55.20.

"I got caught in the last few metres but it was a big step forwards in confidence today," said Hull, who is eyeing the inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest next month.

"That's the fastest I've run all year and we have some good races to come over the next few weeks."

Davies earned her second career Diamond League podium as she pursued Italian favourite Nadia Battocletti, fresh from her own 5,000/10,000 double at the European Championships.

Davies eventually finished third in 14:55.39, pipped by Ethiopia's Freweyni Hailu and Battocletti, who won in 14:54.09.

"Every race is a step forward and to come top three at a Diamond League shows I'm in good form," Davies said.

"I really look up to Battocletti, she's a great athlete and I would love to be like her."

Australia's Eleanor Patterson earned bronze during the women's high jump final. (Getty Images: Maja Hitij)

Patterson again defeated teammate, world champion Nicola Olyslagers, just as she had done in Glasgow when they took gold and silver.

It was a strong effort considering Patterson was battling illness, but she had to settle for third behind Ukrainian rivals, Olympic champion Yaroslava Mahuchikh and Iryna Gerashchenko.

Kennedy took his first strides back on the international circuit after his historic 9.85sec silver medal-winning run in Glasgow, but his 10.08sec run in the heats in Chorzów was not enough to earn him a place in the final, which was later won by Jamaica's world champion, Oblique Seville, in a searing 9.83sec.

"I didn't come out as well as I would've liked but I'm just trying to shake the rust off a bit. I'll get back into some training and better form — I'm happy," Kennedy said.

Triple Commonwealth pole vault champion Kurtis Marschall cleared 5.90m but it only earned him fifth place while his mate Armand Duplantis earned yet another effortless triumph with a 6.20m winner.

Queensland's two-time Diamond League champion Matthew Denny finished eighth in the discus (66.38m), as Lithuania's world record holder Mykolas Alekna won with a competition record 72.58m.

The international highlight was world champion Melissa Jefferson-Wooden handing Olympic champion Julien Alfred her first loss of the season to win the women's 100m, 10.78sec to 10.83.

World.title: AFL wildcard matches and times confirmed
World.content:
Carlton are confident they can "do some damage" in the AFL finals from 10th spot as they eye a wildcard round clash with Melbourne.

Josh Fraser's men will take on the Demons on Saturday night at the MCG in the second of two knockout wildcard clashes next weekend under the new format.

The Western Bulldogs will meet Collingwood in the first wildcard match on Friday night, also at the MCG.

AFL wildcard matches, dates and times Western Bulldogs [8th] vs Collingwood [9th]: Friday, August 28, 7:40pm AEST, Melbourne Cricket Ground Melbourne [7th] vs Carlton [10th]: Saturday, August 29, 7:35pm AEST, Melbourne Cricket Ground

If Melbourne win, they will travel to Adelaide while the winner out of Western Bulldogs and Collingwood will visit Geelong.

If Carlton win, they will travel to Geelong while the winner of the other wildcard match will play away to Adelaide.

Carlton are the hottest team in the lower finals bracket after a comprehensive win over ladder leaders Fremantle in round 24 on Saturday.

It extended their unbeaten streak to five matches, with 11 wins and a draw in 14 outings since Fraser took the coaching reins in May.

Carlton previously sneaked into the finals from ninth when arch-rivals Essendon were banished from the 2013 campaign as punishment over the supplements scandal.

The Blues were knocked out in week two that year but appear capable of making a deep finals run this time from the platform of the league's first wildcard round.

"You need to show up and if you play the right way then I feel like you can do some damage," Blues forward Brodie Kemp told AAP.

"We've got some momentum going into wildcard and [beating Fremantle] was a great way to do it.

"Wins on the board means that you've got evidence that you can play a good brand and it stacks up against good sides."

Initially appointed on an interim basis after Michael Voss was sacked, Fraser secured the job as full-time coach when he engineered one of the great in-season turnarounds to steer Carlton to a wildcard spot.

Kemp said the 44-year-old had put a greater emphasis on skills during the week to add another dimension to the Blues' game style, which is reaping rewards.

"We always had that contest and stoppage game with Vossy, and he did a lot of work on the foundations of our game," Kemp said.

"[Now we have] the ability to possess the ball a bit more while nailing the fundamentals, and that's probably the biggest shift for us.

"We're playing for each other and it's really fun to be a part of … but finals-type heat adds a different layer.

"It's not going to go all our way the whole time, so we need to adapt and stay connected and we're in a really good position to be able to do that."

Carlton expect to welcome back Will Hayward and Nick Haynes from ankle injuries against Melbourne, who are monitoring fresh knee problems for Matt Jefferson and Dan Turner.

The Bulldogs could be without spearhead Aaron Naughton (ankle) for their meeting with Collingwood, who have lost veteran Scott Pendlebury and Brayden Maynard to knee issues.

Dogs ruckman Tim English (knee) is an outside chance to return.
